Pour les aficionados de X, n'hésitez pas à suivre notre compte Clubic Bons Plans pour être au courant en direct des meilleures offres.

articles.title: PlayStation Plus dará gratis un juego de Dragon Ball y otros dos títulos
articles.text:
Los suscriptores de PlayStation Plus podrán descargar gratis tres videojuegos a partir del 1 de diciembre de 2026, entre ellos una popular entrega de la franquicia Dragon Ball. La nueva selección de Sony también incluye una colección de skateboarding y una aventura de terror psicológico, disponibles para los usuarios de PS4 y PS5 sin importar el nivel de suscripción que tengan contratado.
La promoción estará vigente hasta el 4 de enero de 2027 y forma parte de los juegos mensuales que la compañía ofrece a los miembros de su servicio. Los títulos anunciados son Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3+4 y Amnesia: The Bunker.
Los tres videojuegos podrán reclamarse sin costo adicional para quienes tengan una membresía activa de PS Plus Essential, Extra o Premium (Deluxe). Una vez añadidos a la biblioteca durante el período de la promoción, los usuarios podrán seguir jugándolos mientras mantengan activa su suscripción.
Cuáles son los tres juegos gratis de PlayStation Plus en diciembre
La selección de diciembre reúne propuestas de distintos géneros. El título de Dragon Ball destaca por su sistema de combate y su historia ambientada en el universo creado por Akira Toriyama, mientras que las otras dos opciones ofrecen experiencias centradas en el deporte y el terror.
Estos son los videojuegos que estarán disponibles:
- Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 (PS4 y PS5): un RPG de acción y lucha que permite crear un personaje propio y participar en una historia original dentro del universo de Dragon Ball.
- Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3+4 – Cross-Gen Edition (PS4 y PS5): una colección remasterizada que reúne dos entregas de la reconocida franquicia de skateboarding.
- Amnesia: The Bunker (PS4): un videojuego de terror psicológico en el que los jugadores deben sobrevivir a una criatura que los persigue dentro de un búnker durante la Primera Guerra Mundial.
La promoción comenzará el 1 de diciembre y finalizará el 4 de enero de 2027. Por ello, los suscriptores tendrán poco más de un mes para reclamar los tres títulos y agregarlos a sus bibliotecas digitales.
Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 celebra diez años con nuevo contenido
De los tres videojuegos anunciados, Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 es probablemente el que más interés despertará entre los seguidores de la franquicia japonesa. Desarrollado por Dimps y publicado por Bandai Namco, llegó al mercado en 2016 y, desde entonces, recibió numerosas actualizaciones y expansiones.
El título propone una aventura de acción y rol en la que los jugadores pueden crear su propio guerrero y participar en combates inspirados en diferentes momentos de la historia de Dragon Ball. Su argumento gira alrededor de las alteraciones en la línea temporal, por lo que los personajes deben intervenir para evitar que acontecimientos importantes del universo cambien.
Durante sus diez años de existencia, el videojuego incorporó nuevos luchadores, escenarios, misiones y habilidades. Sin embargo, quienes lo reclamen mediante PlayStation Plus recibirán la edición básica, por lo que el contenido adicional disponible a través de expansiones deberá adquirirse por separado.
Además, el juego recibió contenido especial por su décimo aniversario, mientras que los seguidores de la saga esperan Dragon Ball Xenoverse 3, cuya llegada está prevista para la segunda mitad de 2027.
Tony Hawk y Amnesia completan los regalos de diciembre
La segunda propuesta es Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3+4, una colección que recupera dos entregas clásicas de la serie de skateboarding. El videojuego incluye pistas, desafíos y personajes de ambas versiones, con gráficos renovados y mecánicas adaptadas a las plataformas actuales.
Por su parte, Amnesia: The Bunker ofrece una experiencia completamente diferente. Lanzado en 2023 por Frictional Games, el título sigue al soldado francés Henri Clément, quien queda atrapado en una instalación militar durante la Primera Guerra Mundial.
El jugador debe explorar el lugar, administrar recursos y evitar a una criatura que representa una amenaza constante. Su propuesta combina exploración, supervivencia y terror psicológico, con situaciones que cambian según las decisiones tomadas durante la partida.
Qué otros juegos llegarán al catálogo de PlayStation Plus
Los regalos mensuales no serán las únicas novedades del servicio durante diciembre. Sony también confirmó que Dynasty Warriors: Origins se incorporará al catálogo de PS Plus Extra y Premium (Deluxe).
Asimismo, el catálogo de clásicos recibirá Ratchet & Clank, la primera entrega de la popular franquicia desarrollada por Insomniac Games.
Mientras se anuncian las próximas incorporaciones, los suscriptores todavía podrán reclamar los juegos de noviembre: Dead Island 2, Monster Train 2 y Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered. Estos títulos estarán disponibles hasta el 30 de noviembre de 2026.

articles.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.text:
The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.
What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.
Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.
The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.
What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)
Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.
None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, though.
From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.
The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.
Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.
The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:
- Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.
- If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?
- Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.
There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

articles.title: 1Password sofre invasão e alerta clientes sobre vazamento de dados
articles.text:
1Password sofre invasão e alerta clientes sobre vazamento de dados
A 1Password sofreu uma invasão após hackers comprometerem a conta corporativa de um funcionário no GitHub.
Se você tem conta na 1Password, atenção: o serviço de gerenciamento de senhas emitiu um comunicado para alertar clientes sobre uma invasão aos seus sistemas. Os hackers não tiveram acesso a cofres de senhas e chaves de recuperação de acesso, mas dados como nome e endereço de e-mail foram expostos.
De acordo com uma investigação iniciada pela própria 1Password em 19 de novembro de 2026, o problema teve origem no comprometimento da conta corporativa de um de seus funcionários no GitHub.
Ao acessar essa conta, os invasores puderam entrar nos repositórios privados da empresa e inserir um código malicioso em serviços internos que, por sua vez, foi capaz de captura dados relacionados a clientes.
Para completar, os hackers conseguiram copiar um código-fonte interno da empresa, bem como acessar o ambiente de CI/CD (Continuous Integration e Continuous Delivery/Deployment), um conjunto de ferramentas e processos que automatiza testes, compilação e distribuição de software.
Ambientes de CI/CD podem conter credenciais de acesso e dados críticos de infraestrutura, por isso, o acesso indevido a ele configura um importante problema de segurança.
Segundo a 1Password, o vazamento expôs os seguintes dados de clientes:
- nome
- endereço de e-mail
- chaves públicas
- datas e horários de criação de conta ou último login
- tokens de links enviados por e-mail relacionados a convites, provisionamento de contas e recuperação de acesso
- parâmetros do protocolo SRP (Secure Remote Password), usado para autenticação
- metadados internos
A 1Password ressaltou que os cofres que armazenam senhas e dados relacionados não foram comprometidos, o mesmo valendo para as chaves que protegem esses cofres e para os aplicativos ou extensões do serviço.
Quanto aos tokens expostos, a companhia explica que eles não são suficientes para as contas dos clientes serem acessadas, pois esse procedimento também exige um código de verificação de seis dígitos enviado por e-mail ou autenticação de login único (SSO, na sigla em inglês).
Já a exposição de chaves públicas não chega a ser um problema grave, pois esse tipo de informação foi projetada para ser compartilhada sem que isso permita decifrar informações protegidas. A exposição de chaves privadas é que seria um problema, mas isso não aconteceu.
A 1Password afirma que apenas um pequeno número de usuários foi afetado pela invasão e que eles foram notificados individualmente sobre o problema. Em todos os casos, não é preciso que os clientes alterem senhas ou chaves de acesso.
Por outro lado, os usuários devem ficar atentos para possíveis ações de phishing que usam os dados expostos para aplicar golpes em nome da 1Password.
Do seu lado, a companhia informou já ter adotado medidas para deter a invasão e evitar outros incidentes do tipo. Entre elas está a desativação da conta no GitHub comprometida, o reforço da segurança do ambiente de CI/CD e a contratação de especialistas em segurança para validação e aplicação de ajustes nos procedimentos adotados.

articles.title: Qatar's Tech Startup Community Awards return for third edition
articles.text:
Qatar's Tech Startup Community Awards return for third edition
- Startup Grind Doha has partnered with Business Leaders Middle East Magazine to launch the third edition of the Tech Startup Community Awards 2026, recognising founders, investors, mentors and ecosystem enablers contributing to Qatar's entrepreneurial and technology landscape.
- Held under the theme Built by the Community, for the Community, this year's awards will recognise achievements across 11 categories, covering fintech, AI, deeptech, idea-stage and growth-stage startups, female founders, investors, mentors, community builders and startup enablers.
- The 2026 edition introduces a dedicated review committee comprising Dalia Al-Khalaf, Munera Al-Dosari, Majed Lababidi, Ramzan Al Naimi and Marcel Dridje, responsible for assessing nominations and selecting winners based on category-specific criteria.
- The initiative aims to strengthen collaboration across Qatar's startup ecosystem and increase visibility for its entrepreneurial community. Details regarding nominations, submission deadlines and the awards ceremony will be announced through the organisers' official channels.
Press release:
Startup Grind Doha has teamed up with Business Leaders Middle East magazine to launch the Tech Startup Community Awards 2026, the yearly awards that shine a light on the people building Qatar’s startup scene: the founders and their teams, the investors who back them, the mentors who guide them, and the enablers who help the whole system work.
This is the third year the awards have run, and working with Business Leaders Middle East Magazine gives them a bigger stage than ever before. The goal is simple: make sure the people driving entrepreneurship, innovation and technology in Qatar get the recognition they have earned.
This year’s theme, “Built by the Community, for the Community", says a lot about the spirit behind the awards. Handing out trophies is only part of the story. The bigger aim is to bring founders, investors and supporters together, give them a reason to cheer each other on, and build the kind of relationships a healthy startup ecosystem depends on.
The 2026 Categories
Winners will be named across 11 categories this year:
- Fintech Startup of the Year
- Community Builder of the Year
- Mentor of the Year
- Best Idea Stage Startup of the Year
- Best Growth Stage Startup of the Year
- Most Value Added Investor
- AI Startup of the Year
- Breakthrough Startup of the Year
- Best Female Founder
- Startup Enabler of the Year
- Deep Tech Startup of the Year
New for 2026 is a dedicated Review Committee made up of well-known figures from Qatar’s entrepreneurial, business and investment communities: Dalia Al-Khalaf, Munera Al-Dosari, Majed Lababidi, Ramzan Al Naimi and Marcel Dridje.
The committee will have the final say. Its members will review and assess the nominations against the criteria set for each category and pick the winners, which gives everyone taking part extra confidence that the results are fair and credible.
For both organisations, this partnership is about telling more of the stories coming out of Qatar’s startup community and giving real credit to the people with the big ideas, the people doing the hard work of building, and the people who believed in them along the way.
Everyone in the community is invited to take part in the nominations, so if you know a founder, mentor, investor or organisation that deserves recognition, keep them in mind. The programme will end with an awards ceremony that brings Qatar’s startup and business community together to celebrate great work, fresh ideas and what can be achieved together.
Details on how to nominate, submission deadlines and the ceremony itself will be shared soon on the official channels of Startup Grind Doha and Business Leaders Middle East Magazine.
For more information on the awards programme and to submit nominations, visit the official website.

articles.title: Vardhaman Jain: Who is the industrialist behind Tirumala’s gold donation?
articles.text:
Vardhaman Jain: Who is the industrialist behind Tirumala’s gold donation?
Vardhaman Jain, a Chennai-based entrepreneur linked to Access Healthcare and Asia Engineering, has donated 121 kg of gold ornaments worth Rs 206 crore to Tirumala.
A donation of 121 kg of gold is difficult to overlook. But behind the Rs 206 crore offering made to Venkateswara at Tirumala is a businessman whose career has largely unfolded in healthcare services and Asia engineering and technology.
Chennai-based industrialist and philanthropist Vardhaman Jain, along with his wife Radhika Jain, made the offering on Thursday, November 26, 2026. The donation comprises 46 gold ornaments and is among the largest contributions received by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD).
The ornaments were presented in the presence of Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu and senior TTD officials. They were first displayed at Ranganayakula Mandapam before being ceremonially taken to the sanctum sanctorum.
From building healthcare services businesses to taking up leadership roles in large technology companies, Vardhaman Jain's professional journey has covered several areas. Here's a look at the entrepreneur behind the offering.
From Vision HealthSource to Access Healthcare
Before Access Healthcare became a part of his business journey, Vardhaman had already worked in the healthcare services industry. He co-founded Vision HealthSource, a healthcare services company that was acquired by Perot Systems in 2003.
Following the acquisition, he held senior positions at Perot Systems and Dell Services. His responsibilities included managing director of Dell Services' BPO operations, giving him experience in managing large-scale business process services.
In 2011, he went on to establish Access Healthcare with Shaji Ravi and others. The company provides technology-enabled revenue cycle management services to healthcare providers, primarily in the US. Its offerings cover medical billing, coding, accounts receivable management, analytics and automation-led services. The company has also had Anurag Jain as its chairman and CEO, while Shaji Ravi has served as founder, president and managing director.
Healthcare services are not the only area in which Vardhaman has worked. His professional interests also include business process automation and technology development. Public company profiles credit him with patents related to medical image processing and the use of data extracted from electronic images.
Vardhaman studied statistics at Loyola College in Chennai before pursuing computer science at the University of Texas at Austin.
A career that extends beyond business
Alongside his business interests, Vardhaman has been associated with initiatives in healthcare, education and skill development.
His philanthropic work includes the Shree Sarita Jain Foundation Trust and Aavishkaar, a skill-development initiative for underprivileged youth. He is also listed as the managing trustee of Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital.
His association with Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams is not limited to the latest offering. Earlier contributions include electric buses for pilgrim transport and financial support for the Sri Venkateswara Bhakti Channel, besides other temple-related initiatives.
What went into the 121-kg offering?
According to TTD, the couple's donation used 121 kg of 24-carat gold to prepare ornaments for two temples. Of this, 106 kg was used for jewellery intended for Venkateswara at Tirumala, while the remaining 15 kg will go towards a vastram for Sri Padmavathi Ammavari at the Tiruchanoor temple.
The collection includes a crown, necklaces, anklets, armlets, waist ornaments, hand ornaments and pada kavachams, along with covers for the conch and chakra. Diamonds, blue and yellow sapphires, rubies, emeralds and saligrama stones also feature in the ornaments.
The Rs 206 crore offering has brought Vardhaman's philanthropic contributions into the spotlight. Yet, his work across healthcare, technology, education and temple initiatives shows that his interests extend well beyond a single business or industry.

articles.title: Black Friday Asus : le Zenbook 14 avait déjà de sérieux arguments… avec -250 € il devient juste incontournable !
articles.text:
Black Friday Asus : le Zenbook 14 avait déjà de sérieux arguments… avec -250 € il devient juste incontournable !
Le Black Friday réserve parfois de très belles surprises, et celle-ci mérite clairement le détour ! Avec son écran OLED de 14 pouces, son autonomie impressionnante et son design soigné, l’ASUS Zenbook 14 avait déjà de quoi séduire. Mais avec 250 € de ristourne à la FNAC et un prix remisé à 749,99 €, il devient encore plus difficile de ne pas le conseiller.
Alors, comme ça, vous avez décidé de vous offrir un nouvel ordinateur portable ? Eh bien, félicitations, vous ne pouviez pas mieux tomber ! Et pas uniquement parce que le Black Friday est une période propice aux bonnes affaires. Surtout, parce que les fabricants sont parvenus à gommer les principaux défauts des générations précédentes. Et croyez-nous, ça change tout !
Le Zenbook 14 en est l’exemple parfait : autonomie exceptionnelle, un écran OLED à couper le souffle, des finitions irréprochables… il coche clairement toutes les cases ! Et avec un prix qui dégringole à seulement 749,99 € chez la FNAC, soit une remise immédiate de 250 €, difficile de ne pas voir là une superbe opportunité.
Zenbook 14 : premium et abordable, c’est vraiment possible ?
On l’a dit, le marché des PC portables est dynamique depuis quelque temps. Et cette concurrence pousse les fabricants à redoubler d’efforts pour se démarquer. ASUS l’a bien compris et semble avoir trouvé une formule plutôt convaincante avec son Zenbook 14 : proposer une machine élégante, bien équipée et agréable à utiliser, sans pour autant réclamer un montant démesuré.
5 bonnes raisons de se laisser tenter :
•	250 € d’économie immédiate : un ultraportable premium à seulement 749,99 €
•	Un écran OLED de 14 pouces : résolution Full HD et format 16:10 idéal pour travailler.
•	Jusqu’à 30 heures d’autonomie annoncées : de quoi tenir toute une journée
•	Des performances efficaces pour des tâches quotidiennes en bureautique ou consommation de contenus
•	Un design premium sans compromis : un châssis en Ceraluminum™ et connectique complète
Avant même de s’intéresser à ce qu’il embarque sous le capot, c’est sa conception qui attire l’attention. Lignes épurées, finition soignée, châssis robuste en Ceraluminum™ et écran bord à bord, le Zenbook 14 joue dans la cour des ultraportables premium. Le tout dans un format adapté aux voyageurs. Alors oui, le design ne fait pas tout, mais quitte à passer ses journées devant un ordinateur, autant qu’il soit agréable à regarder.
Un écran OLED ça change tout !
La technologie OLED a déjà largement fait ses preuves, et ce n’est pas un hasard si elle s’invite sur les appareils haut de gamme, des ordinateurs portables aux téléviseurs. ASUS a donc eu la bonne idée d’équiper son Zenbook 14 d’une dalle OLED de 14 pouces. Le résultat, ce sont des noirs profonds, un contraste saisissant et des couleurs qui en mettent plein les yeux. Le constructeur annonce même une couverture de 100 % de l’espace colorimétrique DCI-P3. L’écran affiche une définition de 1 920 × 1 200 pixels et adopte un format 16:10 adapté à la bureautique. Ce n’est pas la définition la plus spectaculaire du marché, mais sur une diagonale de 14 pouces, elle fait parfaitement l’affaire.
Un ordinateur efficace et endurant
ASUS a confié les rênes de son Zenbook 14 à une puce Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100, un choix qui mérite qu’on s’y attarde. Ce processeur à huit cœurs, capable de grimper jusqu’à 2,97 GHz, repose sur une architecture ARM qui fait preuve d’une grande agilité.
Il intègre une puce spécifique, dédiée à l’intelligence artificielle et capable de développer jusqu’à 45 TOPS. Les 16 Go de mémoire vive LPDDR5 assurent une expérience fluide au quotidien, entre bureautique, navigation Web et multitâche.
Mais son véritable tour de force se joue du côté de l’autonomie. Grâce à l’efficience de sa puce ARM, associée à une batterie de 50 Wh, ASUS annonce jusqu’à 30 heures de lecture vidéo hors ligne ! Oui, vous avez bien lu.
Pour couronner le tout, malgré une finesse remarquable, il embarque une connectique complète : on retrouve notamment deux ports USB-C prenant en charge l’alimentation et la sortie vidéo, un port USB-A, une sortie HDMI ainsi qu’une prise audio de 3,5 mm. Côté connexions sans fil, le Wi-Fi 6E et le Bluetooth 5.3 sont de la partie. Enfin, ASUS a prévu une webcam Full HD avec reconnaissance faciale infrarouge compatible Windows Hello.
Le Zenbook 14 a tout pour plaire, surtout à ce prix !
Étudiants, professionnels en déplacement ou utilisateurs désireux de remplacer leur vieux PC portable… le Zenbook 14 s’adresse à vous ! Son écran OLED, l’autonomie généreuse et son format compact en font un choix naturel, d’autant qu’il est proposé à 749,99 €.
D’autres configurations sont disponibles :
Et comme il en faut pour tous les goûts, ASUS décline son Zenbook 14 en plusieurs coloris et configurations :

articles.title: Des iPad sous macOS : Apple en aurait sous la main, mais il ne voudrait jamais les vendre
articles.text:
On parle souvent des usages bureautiques des iPad, mais son système d’exploitation iPadOS est jugé limitant. Beaucoup ont rêvé d’un iPad sous macOS, Apple l’aurait fait. Mais pas pour ses clients, seulement pour ses salariés, selon Mark Gurman, journaliste de Bloomberg. C’est ce qu’il a expliqué dans le dernier podcast Power On ce 25 novembre.
Les iPad pourraient faire tourner macOS
Le journaliste explique dans ce podcast qu’Apple disposerait « depuis un certain temps » d’iPad faisant tourner macOS, en interne. Selon lui, ce serait possible puisque les iPad et les Mac récents reposent sur la même architecture Apple Silicon. Puisqu’ils partagent les mêmes puces, leur proximité technique est telle qu’ils peuvent utiliser les mêmes systèmes d’exploitation.
Ces iPad seraient surtout utilisés dans les laboratoires pour des tests. On peut d’ailleurs imaginer qu’ils ont servi à tester l’usage tactile de macOS pour préparer l’arrivée du dernier MacBook Pro Oled tactile, sorti tout récemment. Ils pourraient aujourd’hui être utilisés pour tester de nouvelles fonctions ou applications venues de macOS pour être apportées sur iPadOS. Malheureusement, Mark Gurman ne nous en apprendra pas davantage sur ce qu’en ferait Apple.
Pourquoi Apple ne vous vendra pas des iPad sous macOS
Malheureusement pour ceux qui en rêvaient, Apple ne chercherait pas à commercialiser ses tablettes tactiles avec le système d’exploitation de ses ordinateurs. Selon Mark Gurman toujours, aucun projet ne serait en cours chez Apple pour apporter macOS aux iPad. Il ajoute ne pas avoir connaissance d’un nouveau système d’exploitation dédié à l’iPad, ni même de projet de fusion entre iPadOS et macOS. D’autant plus que début novembre, le dirigeant d’Apple John Ternus avait écarté l’idée d’une telle fusion lors d’une conférence téléphonique sur les derniers résultats financiers, comme le rappelle MacRumors.
Néanmoins, Apple continuerait à vouloir apporter des améliorations à iPadOS venues de macOS, qu’il s’agisse de fonctions ou d’applications. Par exemple, Final Cut Pro et Logic Pro étaient arrivé sur les tablettes d’Apple en 2023 ; une application tout droit venue des Mac.
Autre explication, réglementaire cette fois-ci. Dans l’Union européenne, le Digital Markets Act impose des obligations différentes selon la popularité des systèmes d’exploitation. Aujourd’hui, iPadOS est tellement utilisé sur le Vieux Continent qu’Apple est obligée de se soumettre à des règles plus strictes. Ce n’est pas le cas de macOS ; en le laissant, Apple s’assure de ne pas avoir à respecter ces règles. Une stratégie qui permet aujourd’hui d’avoir Siri AI sur les Mac en Europe, mais pas sur les iPhone ou les iPad.

articles.title: Llevamos décadas tratando de unir la relatividad y la física cuántica. Un investigador de OpenAI dice que lo ha conseguido
articles.text:
El miércoles 25 de noviembre, a las 18:58 (hora universal), llegó a arXiv un documento de 54 páginas, 34 figuras y un solo autor. No me voy a andar por las ramas: si lo que se dice en ese paper es cierto, estaríamos ante uno de los avances más importantes de la física teórica en décadas.
Después de la conjetura de Riemann, de VP ≠ VNP o la multiplicación de matrices, ahora hay investigadores que (a lomos de la IA) quieren unificar la física cuántica y la teoría de la relatividad (al menos en aspectos sustanciales). Pero vayamos por partes.
Una teoría cuántica de la gravedad. La relatividad general describe la gravedad como la forma del espacio-tiempo; la mecánica cuántica describe el resto de fuerzas y la materia. Se suele decir que la primera se encarga de lo muy grande y la segunda de lo muy pequeño: unificarlas conllevaría estar muy cerca de una teoría del todo. Una herramienta que permita explicar toda la realidad.
Pero, tranquilos, aún no hemos llegado a eso. Durante décadas se ha tratado de juntar ambas teorías de una forma u otra. Por ejemplo, una receta habitual consiste en fijar un espacio-tiempo de fondo y cuantizar las pequeñas ondulaciones que lo recorren (cuyos cuantos serían los gravitones).
La idea es buena y, de hecho, funciona a baja energía. Pero en cuanto se afina el cálculo, aparecen infinitos que no hay manera de esconder debajo de controlar.
A este callejón llegamos en 1985 y en él seguimos.
¿Y qué ha hecho Chandrasekaran? El investigador de Stanford (y trabajador de OpenAI) ha decidido usar otra vía. En lugar de intentar cuantizar el universo entero, selecciona dos sucesos, uno detrás de otro (dos destellos, por poner un ejemplo), y se fija en lo que hay entre el cono de luz que sale del primero y el que converge en el segundo.
Hay muchas cosas que sabemos de ese "diamante causal" y la relatividad nos da herramientas para trabajar ahí. Además, ese diamante se puede cuantizar. El problema es que, sin espacio-tiempo de fondo, el investigador tiene que construir un reloj que permita organizar conceptualmente lo que pasa dentro.
Así que usa cuánto avanzan los haces de luz y cómo se deforman para medir el borde, resolverlo con ecuaciones clásicas y, ya sí, cuantizarlo. Salvando todas las distancias, es como alicatar un baño: el investigador va poniendo azulejos en el borde hasta tenerlo cerrado.
¿Y qué conseguimos con todo esto? Según el paper, Chandrasekaran ha logrado varias cosas:
- Que esas sumas den resultados finitos, incluso con gravitones de longitud de onda arbitrariamente corta.
- Que un diamante con el reloj limitado admite un número finito de estados.
- Que de ahí sale la entropía de los agujeros negros, el famoso "área entre cuatro" (la entropía es el área del horizonte, medida en unidades de Planck, dividida entre cuatro) de Bekenstein y Hawking.
- Y que, a gran escala, todo ello evoluciona según las ecuaciones de Einstein.
Sin entrar en el fondo de la cuestión, el paper tiene flecos por resolver. El propio paper lo reconoce: describe gravedad en el vacío, sin materia; la existencia de estados dentro del diamante se apoya en un paso que una nota al pie califica de heurístico (razonable, pero no demostrado); y no ofrece, hoy por hoy, nada que se pueda medir. ¿Es un trabajo notable? A falta de que lo revisen los expertos, lo parece. Y eso ya es mucho.
Lo que no sabemos es si será suficiente. Hemos tenido una semana de resultados matemáticos que pueden ser históricos y lo ha sido, en buena medida, por Lean, un verificador automático que nos permite comprobar si una demostración es sólida. Ahora no tenemos esa ayuda.
Las teorías físicas, además de ser coherentes, tienen que funcionar en el mundo real (y experimental). Ahora decenas de personas deben leer el texto y ponerlo a prueba. Uno de los primeros en hacerlo, Jonathan Oppenheim del University College de Londres, dice que no resuelve ninguno de los grandes problemas abiertos. También es cierto que Oppenheim defiende una teoría rival (y colabora con Claude)..
A día de hoy nadie puede decir si estamos ante un momento histórico o ante otra "alucinación de la IA". Lo que sí parece es que los cimientos de la ciencia moderna se están moviendo y no está claro dónde podemos terminar.

articles.title: Senate committee makes amendments to lawful access bill
articles.text:
The Senate committee has requested several changes to the federal government’s Lawful Access (Bill C-22) bill.
The national security, defence, and veterans affairs committee spent parts of Tuesday and Wednesday reviewing Bill C-22 clause by clause and agreed to further amend it.
As CTV News pointed out, with the Senate requesting changes, the bill will now have to pass through third reading in the Senate again before returning to the House of Commons to review the latest changes.
For context, Bill C-22 is designed to make it easier for both police and intelligence agencies to intercept private or encrypted data as part of an investigation (which a UN human rights watchdog said violates human rights). The bill would allow the government to compel tech companies to change their systems to preserve data and then turn it over to intelligence or law enforcement.
Part of the changes include amending the bill to further clarify the definition of “systemic vulnerability” to cover the risk that secure information could be accessed. Another change made Wednesday would allow telecom providers to ask the Public Safety Minister to consult a new technical advisory committee on whether a directive would introduce a new vulnerability. The minister would also be able to consult this advisory committee proactively.
Interestingly, Nova Scotia Senator Colin Deacon moved an amendment that would have prevented the government from basically compelling tech companies to retain metadata if they don’t otherwise do so for business purposes, but it didn’t pass.
The committee also debated changes to the provision requiring providers to retain metadata for six months, but ultimately it wasn’t amended.
Eventually, senators will vote on whether to approve the bill with the new amendments. From there, it will then be sent back to the House of Commons to decide whether to accept, reject, or further amend the bill.
Source: CBC News

articles.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.text:
Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:
Jeremy Hsu
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.
I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).
Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.
I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.
Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).
Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.
Nick Indge
Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”
My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.
The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.
Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.
The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.
The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.
Ryan Whitwam
I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.
The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.
I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.
Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.
Aurich Lawson
I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.
To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.
My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.
On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.
The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.
Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.
I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.
When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

When I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is currently a Logitech MX Master 3S.
To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought new in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a big purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.
Tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.
Eric Bangeman
I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.
My office mate is a bull terrier named Ralph who likes to say “woof” at passing dogs and pedestrians.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica

The bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.
Lee Hutchinson
This is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.
The paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.
One of the Apollo bits I’m most proud of is this printout of Sy Liebergot’s EECOM console as it was configured during the Apollo 13 explosion, with the displays showing the exact data and everything. Sy was kind enough to sign it for me.

The rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it said that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!)

My office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.
An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.
Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

articles.title: Elon Musk veut offrir 2 actions SpaceX à chaque enfant américain
articles.text:
Elon Musk sait comment se faire de la publicité. Il vient ainsi d'annoncer une opération inédite de transfert d'actions de SpaceX !
On a l'habitude de dire qu'Elon Musk aime vivre dans l'espace public de bad buzz et de polémiques pouvant écorner son image de businessman. Mais il est aussi capable semble-t-il de se payer une bonne publicité de temps en temps. En tout cas, celle qu'il vient d'annoncer devrait lui gagner des fans, mais à un prix, il faut le dire, monumental !
Elon Musk promet deux actions SpaceX par enfant américain, un cadeau à 18 milliards de dollars
SpaceX et Tesla vont fusionner prochainement. Un mastodonte qui va avoir de nombreux nouveaux actionnaires, vu l'annonce qu'Elon Musk vient de faire dans un message posté sur son réseau social X.
« Chaque enfant aux États-Unis recevra deux actions SpaceX, l'une offerte par l'entreprise et l'autre de ma part personnellement » a-t-il ainsi annoncé. Un cadeau qui va clairement coûter, même à quelqu'un qui a brièvement été billionnaire, puisque l'on estime que ce don d'actions SpaceX représente aujourd'hui une valeur de près de 18 milliards de dollars.
Un transfert qui commencera dès le mois prochain
Et pour ceux qui sont sceptiques quant à cette opération, ils pourront très rapidement juger sur pièce. Car Elon Musk annonce que la première des deux actions - celle provenant de SpaceX - sera transférée aux enfants américains dès le mois prochain.
« Les actions provenant directement de moi seront transférées à l'expiration de ma période de blocage, en juin de l'année prochaine » a-t-il ajouté, dans un message séparé. Et au-delà de la question de la publicité, il y aussi à long terme un intérêt bien senti pour Elon Musk dans cette opération promotionnelle. « Cela permet de constituer une base massive et durable d'actionnaires particuliers » émet ainsi comme hypothèse le conseiller en marchés mondiaux chez Mitrade Group, Christopher Brankin.
Avoir des investisseurs particuliers qui possèdent une part importante du capital d'une entreprise est souvent considéré comme un avantage pour une société, en ce que cette configuration protège plus facilement d'une OPA. Cela offre aussi un actionnariat plus ouvert aux investissements lourds à long terme que les investisseurs institutionnels - en France, on a ainsi l'exemple d'Air Liquide qui fonctionne de cette manière. Et pour une entreprise comme SpaceX, qui souhaite pouvoir développer la conquête spatiale, il n'est pas imprudent de dire que d'énormes investissements à long terme devraient être au programme !
Source : Reuters

articles.title: A Caltech nanorobot got cancer drugs into mouse brains, and Parkinson's could be next
articles.text:
First look: Researchers at Caltech have built a nanorobot small enough to travel through the bloodstream and carry medicine into the brain. The device, called a BrainBot, crosses the blood-brain barrier, the layer of cells that shields the organ from germs but can also keep out the drugs meant to treat it. In mice with a type of brain cancer, light-activated bots delivered about five times more medication into the brain than the same bots without light activation.
The barrier does its job almost too well. It keeps pathogens, toxins and other threats out of the brain, but it can also stop medicines from reaching the organ. That leaves doctors with drugs that might work against a disease but cannot get to it.
Wei Gao, a professor of medical engineering at Caltech, ranks that gap among the biggest challenges in treating brain diseases. The same obstacle shapes cancer care. Karen Noble, director of research and policy at the charity Brain Tumour Research, told The Independent that the barrier "prevents many potentially effective drugs from reaching brain tumours and finding ways to overcome this could transform treatment and improve outcomes."
The Caltech team describes its solution in the journal Science Robotics. Each BrainBot is a balloon-like structure that is injected into the bloodstream. The bots are made of biocompatible and biodegradable materials and measure 250 nanometers, hundreds of times smaller than the width of a human hair.
Getting something that small to the right place is the core engineering problem, and the design relies on two mechanisms working together. The first is biological. The bots carry aptamers, specialized DNA molecules that recognize and bind to the cells lining the barrier.
The second is physical. Near-infrared light is directed through the skull at the brain, heating the bots and triggering a burst of "light-activated propulsion" that pushes them toward the barrier. Once the bots bind to the cells lining it, those cells ferry the BrainBots into the brain, where they release their payload. The authors describe the system as "designed to actively traverse the BBB through on-demand propulsion coupled with biological targeting."
Gao said the researchers did not know how well this would work. "Because the BrainBots are so small and the blood circulation is so fast, we initially were not sure how much a method based on nanoscale propulsion would increase the passage of drugs through the BBB; we are thrilled to see it worked so well."
For the first test, the team chose glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. They loaded the bots with a type of chemotherapy and injected them into mice that had the disease. The authors report "enhanced brain delivery" of the drug, which in turn suppressed tumor growth. They also say the approach can "markedly reduce systemic toxicity" linked to chemotherapy, compared with usual chemotherapy administration.
So far, the results come only from mice. The researchers hope to move to human trials in the future, though they have given no timeline. First, they say, they need to optimize the near-infrared light delivery and evaluate the bots' long-term safety, stability and degradation in the body.
Gao framed the brain tumor work as a starting point. "Our new nanorobot is not limited to brain delivery, but we are trying to address one of the biggest problems in medicine – crossing the blood – brain barrier – as a starting point." He added: "We targeted cancer, but there are a lot of neurological diseases, such as Parkinson's, for example, that we hope could benefit from this technology."

articles.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
articles.text:
After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.
The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.
The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.
The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.
X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.
“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

Galaxy S25 despenca para menos de R$ 3 mil na véspera da Black Friday
Galaxy S25 (256 GB) com 12 GB de RAM e chip Snapdragon recebe 60% de desconto no Pix com cupom exclusivo Prime, a menos de 24 horas para a Black Friday 2026
O Galaxy S25 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 2.999 no Pix com cupom 25IMPERDIVEL exclusivo para assinantes do Amazon Prime. O celular da Samsung, com 12 GB de RAM e chip Snapdragon 8 Elite, atinge o 2.º menor preço de 2026 com desconto de 60% sobre o base de R$ 7.499, na véspera da Black Friday.
O menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy S25 5G 256 GB foi R$ 2.899, no Magalu, em 31/7/2026. Esta oferta está R$ 100,20 acima desse recorde, mas 15% abaixo da média (R$ 3.514) das 41 ofertas que publicamos desde fevereiro de 2026.
O Galaxy S25 é um celular premium compacto e potente, capaz de rodar soluções do Galaxy AI localmente graças ao chip Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite e aos 12 GB de RAM. Os 256 GB de espaço interno são adequados para guardar fotos e vídeos.
Sua tela LTPO AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,2″ com taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de até 2.600 nits reproduz imagens com cores vibrantes, alta fluidez e visibilidade garantida.
O kit principal de câmeras filma em 8K. Ele é formado por wide de 50 MP com OIS e ultrawide de 12 MP, que captam belas cenas em ambientes abertos, e telefoto de 10 MP com zoom óptico 3x para aproximações. A frontal de 12 MP tira ótimas selfies e filma em 4K a 60 fps.
O corpo em alumínio Armor 2 do S25 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus 2, resistente a pancadas e arranhões. A certificação IP68 confere proteção em cenários como ambientes empoeirados e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 4.000 mAh tem autonomia de até 29 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O carregamento de 25 W via cabo USB-C e de 15 W sem fio permite que ele seja usado por um dia inteiro.
O Galaxy S25 de 256 GB (R$ 2.999 no Pix com cupom 25IMPERDIVEL exclusivo Prime) será atualizado até o Android 22 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.
A Black Friday 2026 chega amanhã (27) trazendo cupons de promoções em gadgets com condições especiais oferecidos por lojas como a Amazon, que continuarão chegando até a Cyber Monday na próxima segunda-feira (30).
