articles.title: Bevorstehendes Aus: Wo der Cybertruck plötzlich beliebt ist
articles.text:
Bevorstehendes Aus: Wo der Cybertruck plötzlich beliebt ist
In drei Jahren nur 70.000 bis 80.000 verkaufte Exemplare – hergestellt in einer Fabrik mit einer Kapazität von jährlich 250.000: Teslas Cybertruck gilt als größter Flop in der Geschichte des Automobils. Mitte November 2026 zog Elon Musk die Reißleine und kündigte das Produktionsaus für den kantigen E-Pickup-Truck an.
Gebrauchte Cybertrucks sind gefragt
In der Fabrik sollen ab Mitte 2027 Cybercabs gebaut werden, Robotaxis ohne Strompedal und Lenkrad. Doch auf einem Markt ist der Cybertruck jetzt überraschend erfolgreich. Wie Techcrunch unter Berufung auf eine Analyse von Iseecars berichtet, war Teslas E-Pickup-Truck auf dem Gebrauchtwagenmarkt der am schnellsten verkaufte Truck.
Von dem Einstellen einer entsprechenden Anzeige auf einem Marktplatz bis zum Verkauf vergingen im Schnitt 39,1 Tage. Im Vergleich dazu dauerte das im Truck-Segment im Schnitt 65,5 Tage. In dem Schnellverkaufsranking folgten hinter dem Cybertruck der Ford Maverick Hybrid und der Rivian R1T.
Für das Zwischenhoch des Cybertrucks auf dem Gebrauchtwagenmarkt sind mehrere Faktoren verantwortlich. Das Produktionsaus kann es aber nicht sein. Die analysierten Verkaufszahlen stammen vom Oktober 2026. Da hatte Musk dies noch nicht offiziell verkündet.
Hohe Benzinpreise treiben Nachfrage
Vielmehr sorgen die hohen Benzinpreise für eine erhöhte Nachfrage nach gebrauchten Stromern, wie Iseecars-Analyst Karl Brauer Techcrunch sagte. Im Schnitt hatten Elektroautos laut Analyse nach 45,6 neue Besitzer:innen gefunden. Bei Hybriden waren es 54,5 Tage und bei Verbrennern 61 Tage.
Neben den hohen Benzinpreisen spielte zudem das allgemein knappe Angebot an auf dem Markt verfügbaren Cybertrucks eine Rolle für die große Nachfrage. „Den Cybertruck gibt es erst seit wenigen Jahren. Daher kommen nun zahlreiche gebrauchte Exemplare aus Leasingverträgen auf den Gebrauchtwagenmarkt“, so Brauer. Und: Im Vergleich zum ursprünglichen Listenpreis seien gebrauchte Cybertrucks günstig.
Cybertruck: Neuer Run wohl ab Sommer 2027
In den kommenden Monaten könnten die Cybertruck-Verkäufe auf dem Gebrauchtmarkt weiter anziehen. Einen dauerhaft anhaltenden Run nach Bekanntwerden des Produktionsaus sieht der Iseecars-Analyst aber nicht. Im Spätsommer oder Herbst 2027, also nach dem tatsächlichen Stopp der Produktion, könnten die Verkäufe von gebrauchten Cybertrucks aber noch einmal deutlich anziehen.

articles.title: After a decade in Nigeria, Bolt is looking beyond rides
articles.text:
When Bolt, the Estonian mobility company, launched as Taxify in Lagos in November 2016, it entered a market where Uber, the American ride-hailing giant, had already established a lead after arriving two years earlier.
By July 2016, Uber had completed more than one million trips across Lagos and Abuja. Taxify was not only competing with an established rival; it also had to win commuters over from yellow taxis and public transportation by offering another way to get around.
A decade later, Nigeria’s ride-hailing market looks very different. Yellow taxis have lost most of their prominence, while the market has attracted other international players like inDrive, and local operators such as LagRide and Rida. In September, Uber announced it was winding down its Nigerian operations, marking the exit of the company that had once led the market.
Meanwhile, Bolt has expanded its footprint to 31 cities and says it has reached more than 14 million riders in Nigeria since it entered the market. The company also says it has invested more than ₦140 billion ($102.4 million) in the country. Beyond ride-hailing, it has expanded into other ride categories, vehicle financing, food delivery and electric mobility.
Early beginnings and price wars
Weyinmi Aghadiuno, Bolt’s Head of Regulatory and Policy, Africa, said Bolt entered into Nigeria at a time when getting around the country’s cities was often unpredictable.
“When we launched as Taxify in 2016, getting around Nigerian cities was unpredictable. People mixed traditional taxis, private arrangements, and public transport, and finding a reliable ride, knowing the fare upfront or trusting the service, was hard,” she said in an email response to TechCabal on Friday. “At the same time, smartphone adoption was rising, and Nigerians were getting comfortable using their phones for everyday services. We saw those two trends meeting.”
Nigeria’s smartphone penetration stood at 30% in 2016, proving a market for app-based services to grow. However, the competitive landscape meant Taxify needed to persuade passengers to try another app while convincing drivers to switch from a familiar platform. It approached the problem with a penetration-pricing strategy at launch.
Taxify went live in Lagos, promising rides at 30% less than its closest competitors and charging drivers a 15% commission, compared with Uber’s 25%. Drivers dissatisfied with Uber’s commission structure began migrating to the new platform, allowing Taxify to build its vehicle supply.
After Taxify lowered its prices in Lagos, Uber followed with a 40% fare reduction. The move aimed to stimulate demand, and Uber said it had introduced temporary payment guarantees to protect drivers’ earnings while the new fares took effect. However, drivers were unconvinced and argued that lower fares, combined with Uber’s 25% commission, left them with less money after operating costs.
The Los Angeles Times later reported that drivers organised on WhatsApp and moved to Taxify in numbers. Bolt describes those years as building two sides of a market at once.
“Ride-hailing wasn’t unfamiliar by then, so we had to give people a reason to download Bolt and try it,” the company said. “That took awareness campaigns, onboarding support and promotions that encouraged riders to experience the service for themselves. Word of mouth did a lot of the heavy lifting. One good ride usually became a recommendation to a friend, colleague or family member.”
Taxify maintained the same pricing strategy when it launched in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, in November 2017, offering passengers a 40% discount for the month and retaining its 15% commission on drivers’ earnings. Uche Okafor, the company’s operations manager in Nigeria at the time, said the expansion aimed to introduce more competition in the capital and lower transportation costs for commuters.
In 2018, after entering Owerri and Ibadan, Taxify launched in Benin City in December, making it the company’s fifth Nigerian city. The company said it wanted to reach markets beyond the country’s obvious commercial centres, where ride-hailing could offer passengers another transportation option and create earning opportunities for drivers.
In 2019, Taxify changed its name to Bolt, a name that the company’s founder and chief executive said was meant to evoke speed.
New ways to keep moving
As Bolt expanded its operations across Nigerian cities, it faced a market where commuters still relied on cheaper or locally established transport options. In Uyo, Akwa Ibom State in Southeastern Nigeria, tricycles had become an important part of everyday transportation after the state banned commercial motorcycles, popularly known as okada, in 2011.
Bolt said it wanted to reflect how people already moved around different cities, and in January 2020, introduced tricycle-hailing in Uyo.
“For us, mobility solutions have to be locally relevant,” Aghadiuno told TechCabal in March. “That’s why we began by integrating a transport mode that already exists and plays a significant role in local economies.”
The COVID-19 pandemic tested the resilience of Bolt’s Nigerian business. In March 2020, movement restrictions introduced to contain the spread of the disease brought economic activity in Lagos and other cities to a near standstill. This left ride-hailing companies with fewer passengers and fewer trips.
“COVID-19 was among the hardest for transport,” Aghadiuno said. “Movement restrictions and reduced economic activity hit demand directly.”
The company tried to adapt by introducing Bolt Business Delivery in April in Lagos and Abuja, connecting businesses with couriers on its platform to deliver essential goods to customers. The company also faced tougher regulatory restrictions, as Lagos State moved to enforce new licencing rules for ride-hailing platforms. Under the regulations, third-party operators with more than 1,000 drivers faced a ₦10 million ($7,138) licence fee and a ₦5 million ($3,659) annual renewal fee, raising operational costs.
Despite these setbacks, Bolt continued to expand as demand for ride-hailing services grew beyond Lagos. In September 2020, it launched in Jos, taking its Nigerian footprint to 12 cities. Femi Akin-Laguda, the company’s country manager at the time, said more Nigerians were seeking flexible ways to move around, and rising car ownership costs made access to vehicles difficult. Against the constraint of vehicle ownership, Bolt expanded into 10 more cities in December 2020, including Akure, Asaba, Warri, Kaduna, and Uyo, taking its Nigerian footprint to 21 cities.
To address the barrier of vehicle acquisition for drivers, in June 2021, Bolt partnered with Sterling Bank’s Alternative Finance to launch a vehicle financing programme to help eligible drivers buy new or used cars. It expanded the programme in November through a partnership with Metro Africa Xpress (MAX), using the mobility company’s alternative credit-scoring technology alongside Bolt’s driver activity data to assess drivers for financing.
With pandemic-era demand for delivery still strong, Bolt launched Bolt Food, its food delivery business, in Nigeria in October 2021, entering a market that already included Jumia Food and Gokada. The market opportunity was clear: In 2019, Lagos residents spent ₦827 billion ($605.3 million) eating out, according to National Bureau of Statistics data.
During the COVID-19 lockdowns, Jumia Food also recorded 30% month-on-month growth in orders. At Bolt Food’s launch, customers were offered access to over 100 restaurants on Lagos Island. The company also pitched the service as an opportunity for restaurants to reach more customers and for couriers to earn through its platform.
Tough market
As Bolt expanded its operations in Nigeria, ride-hailing’s economics became harder to manage. In February 2023, the company laid off 17 of its 70 employees in Nigeria, as part of a strategy to improve its operational processes. After the removal of the petrol subsidy in May 2023, Bolt raised its base fare from ₦650 ($0.48) to ₦800 ($0.59). However, drivers and their unions argued that the adjustment did not reflect the jump in operating costs. Disputes over fares and the commission deducted from each trip led to repeated driver protests and strikes.
Later that year, Bolt announced that it would shut down Bolt Food in Nigeria, saying it wanted to streamline resources and maximise efficiency. By then, the service said it had partnered with more than 10,000 restaurants, delivered more than a million meals and onboarded 12,000 merchants.
According to Aghadiuno, Bolt responded to these pressures by continually adjusting its services and operating model.
“Our job is to keep both sides of that equation workable: fares passengers can manage and earnings that make driving sustainable,” she said. “That means listening to both groups and regularly reassessing our services and operating model. It has also made efficiency and innovation essential. We can’t run the business the way we did in 2016 and expect it to work in today’s economy.”
She also pointed to its expanded range of services, including Bolt Comfort, the lower-cost Bolt Lite category, tricycle rides, Bolt Send and Bolt Business, as ways of serving different mobility needs. In April 2025, Bolt launched electric tricycles in Lagos, in partnership with local electric mobility company SGX Mobility. The company said its ₦140 billion ($102.4 million) investment in Nigeria covers technology, local operations, safety initiatives and engagement with drivers and passengers.
“What got us through was staying close to the market,” Bolt said, reflecting on the difficult periods it had faced. “We kept engaging with drivers, responded to changing consumer needs, worked with relevant stakeholders and kept evolving our services, without losing sight of the long-term opportunity.”
A decade after entering Nigeria, Bolt says it is operating in a market that looks different from the one it encountered in 2016. Ride-hailing has become part of everyday urban transportation, and passengers have become more discerning about what they expect from the service. The company says growth now transcends bringing more riders and drivers onto the platform, and instead is about making the platform useful across a wide range of mobility needs.
“The next decade is about depth: more value for Nigerians and a broader idea of what mobility can mean for the communities we serve,” Aghadiuno said. “That means continuing to improve the ride experience, strengthening safety, expanding relevant services and exploring opportunities across the wider mobility ecosystem.”

articles.title: Elon Musk now promises two free SpaceX shares to every child in America
articles.text:
What just happened? Just over a month after he promised to give every child in America a free SpaceX share next year, Elon Musk has changed the terms of his promise: he now says he'll hand over two shares, one from the company and one from himself. The billionaire added that the company's shares will be transferred next month, while his shares will be transferred in June 2027.
SpaceX offered some specifics on its website about who qualifies. The company announced that it would issue one new share of its Class A common stock for every currently active Trump Account. Musk will match the number of shares SpaceX gives away, though the company hasn't said whether a child without an active Trump Account would receive either share.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026
Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for children under 18. Eligible US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 get a $1,000 contribution from the federal government, and families, employers, and other donors can add to the pot. SpaceX president and COO Gwynne Shotwell and her husband have separately pledged more than two million of their own SpaceX shares to children in the program.
SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, putting the value of the two shares at $254.88. The White House said in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been opened. Using 70 million as a round figure puts the combined giveaway at about $17.8 billion, with Musk's half coming to roughly $8.9 billion at Wednesday's price.
SpaceX plans to hand out its shares in December, but Musk said on X that he'll have to wait until June 2027 to give away his own. That's when the restriction on transferring his shares expires.
Musk advised people not to rush into selling their shares. "If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun's energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy. These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them. I recommend holding on to your shares," he wrote in a follow-up post.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026
Musk's original pledge came after xAI rival Anthropic announced it would set aside 5% of its stock for a fund that could make donations for the "public good." Musk had his own suggestion at the time. "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," he wrote. "This is what I will be doing."

articles.title: Ramiro Aurín, ingeniero de caminos, sobre las autopistas: "Una carretera sin agujeros es una carretera segura y ahora es un auténtico desastre"
articles.text:
Ramiro Aurín, ingeniero de caminos, canales y puertos, cree que la falta de mantenimiento en España no se queda en las vías del tren. En una entrevista en el pódcast A Contraluz asegura que también alcanza a las autopistas y a la gestión de los ríos, y que esto es algo preocupante.
Del peaje a la gratuidad. Sus críticas se centran sobre todo en la AP-7, que fue liberada en la mayoría de tramos para pasar a ser gratuita. Para Aurín esa decisión ha tenido un precio, porque según su análisis el asfalto se está deteriorando a toda velocidad desde que se levantaron las barreras.
El argumento del pago por uso. Según defiende, el peaje garantizaba una calzada en perfecto estado y permitía a conductores y flotas de transporte ganar tiempo con seguridad. Y opina que desde que pasó a ser gratuita ha estado saturada de camiones, provocando unos desperfectos en el asfalto que el dinero público no consigue reparar a un ritmo suficiente. Vamos, que en su opinión la vía se desgasta más deprisa de lo que se arregla, asegurando que que “una carretera sin agujeros es una carretera segura y ahora es un auténtico desastre”. También acusa al Ejecutivo de haber antepuesto el rédito propagandístico de abrir las barreras a garantizar el dinero para su conservación diaria.
Las presas que no llegaron. El daño que ve en las obras hidráulicas contra inundaciones y sequías es todavía mayor. Aurín recuerda que la planificación hidrológica moderna la impulsó Josep Borrell, que a principios de los noventa compareció en el Congreso como ministro de Obras Públicas y Transportes para hablar del Plan Hidrológico Nacional, y que los gobiernos posteriores le dieron continuidad hasta que, a su juicio, las dinámicas de coalición más recientes giraron en contra de contener los cauces.
Un sesgo contra los embalses. Explica que los acuerdos de Gobierno con formaciones como Podemos, que entró en el Ejecutivo con el nombramiento de ministros de enero de 2020, asentaron la idea de que “las infraestructuras eran algo malo” y de que “hacer un embalse era algo malo en sí mismo”. Esa visión acabó frenando, siempre según el ingeniero, presas y diques de defensa ya proyectados en zonas vulnerables.
Para Aurín, las catástrofes que provocan los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos tienen que prevenirse con ingeniería y criterios científicos contrastados, dejando a un lado los discursos dogmáticos y retomando las obras pendientes. La política de aguas, insiste, “hay que afrontarla con tecnología, con valor y con audacia”.

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review
articles.text:
Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a company that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me."
The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain said the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been."
A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain said, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.
To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.
Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.
He closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

articles.title: Criptomonedas: el costo de ethereum para este día
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda digital #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.3M de unidades creadas.
La cotización de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 1700.8 dólares, es decir, que la criptomoneda reportó un cambio de 4.13 % en las últimas 24 horas.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0 % con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #2.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
La nueva era de Ether
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

articles.title: ‘We know first-hand what a great artist she is’ — 007 First Light composers say IOI ‘proved their ambition’ by wanting a star artist and cinematic sequence and were ‘delighted’ that it was Lana Del Rey and David Arnold
articles.text:
007 First Light composers recall learning that Lana Del Rey and Bond composer David Arnold would be the star artists — ‘To say we were delighted would be an understatement’
The Flight has collaborated with Lana Del Rey in the past
- 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith recall learning that Lana Del Rey and David Arnold would be the game's star artists
- The music duo say IO Interactive "proved their ambition" by wanting a star artist and a cinematic title sequence
- Henson and Smith have always been fans of Arnold and his Bond scores, and have worked with Lana Del Rey in the past
007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have shared their reaction to learning that Lana Del Rey was the star artist of IO Interactive's Bond game.
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the duo known as The Flight discussed how they defined a great Bond score and their inspirations for the game's soundtrack, the composers said that IOI had great ambitions for First Light's opening cinematic and music and were very happy to hear that singer-songwriter Lana Del Rey and British composer David Arnold were chosen.
Henson and Smith have both worked with Del Rey in the past, and the official theme song, 'First Light,' marked the return of Arnold, the renowned Bond franchise composer with credits for multiple movie scores, including Tomorrow Never Dies, The World Is Not Enough, Die Another Day, Casino Royale, and Quantum of Solace.
"Even before we came on board, we were aware that IO wanted an original Bond song for First Light complete with star artist and cinematic title sequence, and this was one of the things that really proved their ambition," Smith said.
"Soon after signing and beginning our work, Dom Vega revealed to us that it was going to be David Arnold and Lana Del Rey – to say we were delighted would be an understatement."
Henson added that he and Smith have "always looked up to David" and have been fans of his iconic scores, "especially Casino Royale."
"We worked with Lana in her very early days, writing and recording demo songs when we had just formed The Flight," the composer added. "None of them made her debut album, but we know first-hand what a great artist she is."

articles.title: The Download: Better bionic hands and AI’s natural-gas boom
articles.text:
The Download: Better bionic hands and AI’s natural-gas boom
Plus: SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellites.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he's cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it's wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one's hand.
Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he's the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.
Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
— Casey Crownhart
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I've lost count of how many times he's been proven right.
Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta's emissions are up 45% over last year's.
Across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand. Here’s what that means for the future of the grid.
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellites
The FCC says they'll help meet AI computing demand. (Reuters $)
+ But they could overcrowd the orbit and obscure the stars. (Bloomberg $)
+ SpaceX must start deploying them by 2033 under its license. (BBC)
+ Europe has opened a megafactory to build a Starlink rival. (CNBC)
+ Can data centers really work in orbit? (MIT Technology Review)
2 The US Army just blew up nearly five tons of unstable explosives
The EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following the detonation. (Verge)
+ Scientists are now testing soil and water for contamination. (Wired $)
+ Officials were criticized for poor communication beforehand. (Axios)
3 Earth just had its first six-day streak above 2°C
Scientists say it’s an early warning of what's to come. (Guardian)
4 Ukraine has claimed the first-ever laser takedown of a jet drone
Its Blysk laser downed a Russian kamikaze drone. (Bloomberg $)
5 Neuralink has won approval for a brain-implant trial in ALS patients
It's the final stage of testing before seeking market clearance. (Gizmodo)
+ China is racing to catch up in brain-computer interfaces. (SCMP)
+ A BCI gave a man with ALS his voice back. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Hackers have breached the US Treasury's financial crime watchdog
It's taken systems used to report money laundering offline. (FT $)
7 Bankrupt startup Character.ai wants to sell millions of user chats
42 attorneys general are trying to block the sale. (TechCrunch)
8 The hunt for dark matter is getting weirder
Scientists are using levitating magnets and nuclear clocks. (Quanta)
+ Dark matter's hiding places keep growing. (MIT Technology Review)
9 Scientists used seabird spies to track ships that had gone dark
Recorders on the birds detected ships with trackers off. (404 Media)
10 This Thanksgiving, AI is becoming a popular sous-chef
But food bloggers say its recipes are often "total nonsense." (Axios)
Quote of the day
“Hey, by the way, this might be the last time we see each other—potentially, probably not, but maybe—because of AI.”
—Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and author of the "AI 2027" forecast, tells The New York Times how he plans to bring up AI extinction risks with his wife’s family this Thanksgiving.
One more thing
AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some could solve them nearly perfectly.
But puzzles do more than highlight AI's progress. Seeing where models succeed and fail, and where humans still beat them, offers a window into the technology's strengths and weaknesses.
We've gathered seven puzzles that have stumped models. Try them yourself to find out whether you can outsmart AI.
—Grace Huckins

articles.title: Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM) lanza una función que ayuda a recordar información sin tanto esfuerzo
articles.text:
Google ha lanzado un cúmulo de funciones para Gemini Notebook que ayudarán a las personas que estudian o necesitan memorizar las cosas. La actualización más reciente añade soporte para imágenes en las tarjetas didácticas (flashcards). Esto ayudará a que los usuarios comprendan mejor los conceptos combinando información textual y gráfica.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, las tarjetas didácticas ya pueden cargar elementos visuales desde las fuentes originales. Este agregado cambia el formato habitual de las flashcards, que se centraba en preguntas y respuestas de texto. Si bien este modelo funciona para practicar la memoria, en ocasiones nos encontramos con temas que son más difíciles de asimilar y es ahí en donde entra la parte visual.
Además de esto, la actualización también añade un cronómetro integrado para las sesiones de estudio. Los usuarios pueden activarlo mientras repasan sus tarjetas y tiene como objetivo medir cuánto tardan en recuperar la información. El cronómetro será de gran utilidad para quienes están por presentar un examen con límite de tiempo, ya que la IA permite simular condiciones similares a las de una evaluación real.
Por último, Gemini Notebook ya permite programar recordatorios para revisar las tarjetas generadas. Esta función está disponible dentro de la aplicación de Gemini Notebook para el móvil, desde la cual ajustarás las alertas para crear una rutina de estudio. Google afirma que estos recordatorios ayudan a mantener las sesiones periódicas de repaso sin depender únicamente de la memoria o disciplina personal.
Gemini Notebook también mejoró las notas y ahora son herramientas interactivas
La actualización llega a unos días de que Google lanzara una función para transformar notas, investigaciones y otras fuentes en webs interactivas. Los usuarios solo tienen que escribir "crear un sitio" dentro del chat de Gemini Notebook y añadir la descripción de lo que quieren construir. A partir de ese prompt, la IA genera una experiencia interactiva que puede abrirse en una pestaña independiente o compartir con otras personas.
Entre los ejemplos de uso que plantea Google se encuentra una tabla periódica interactiva para explicar cada uno de los elementos, una línea de tiempo histórica, paneles interactivos para explorar datos o herramientas para realizar seguimiento de proyectos. La complejidad del proyecto dependerá de las fuentes y de lo específico que seas al escribir el prompt.
Las nuevas funciones de las tarjetas didácticas y las páginas interactivas ya están disponibles para los clientes de Google Workspace, suscriptores de Workspace Individual y los usuarios con cuentas personales de Google. Como ocurre con cada lanzamiento, el despliegue es gradual y podría tardar en aplicarse en algunos países, por lo que tendrás que revisar más tarde si todavía no aparece en tu sesión.
Aunque el boom de NotebookLM cayó un poco cuando cambió de nombre, Google ha mantenido una estrategia de actualización constante. Gemini Notebook ha recibido varias funciones desde mediados de agosto, como la inteligencia experta, la grabadora de audio para capturar clases o notas, los cuadernos de estudio o las presentaciones y videos personalizables.

articles.title: Finnable raises Rs 405 Cr in Series C to expand multi-product lending
articles.text:
Finnable raises Rs 405 Cr in Series C to expand multi-product lending
The Bengaluru-based lender has crossed Rs 4,600 crore in assets under management and says it made Rs 51 crore in profit after tax in the first half of FY27.
Fintech company Finnable has raised Rs 405 crore in a Series C round. The new investors are Bharat Value Fund, part of the Pantomath Group, along with Pratithi Investments and NKSquared. Pratithi is the investment vehicle of Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan's family, and NKSquared is the firm of Zerodha co-founders Nithin and Nikhil Kamath.
Existing backers Z47, TVS Capital and Claypond Capital continue in the company. TVS Capital and Claypond Capital put in more money in this round. The Rs 405 crore figure carries an asterisk in the company's release. A disclaimer says final allotments and regulatory filings are still being completed and the figure is subject to final subscription numbers.
Profit ahead of last year's full-year total
Finnable said its assets under management crossed Rs 4,600 crore in October 2026. It reported a profit after tax of Rs 51 crore for April to September 2026, which already exceeds the Rs 46 crore it earned in the whole of FY26.
On asset quality, the company said its latest PAR 90 at six months on books stands at 0.24%. This measures loans overdue by more than 90 days among those that have been on the books for six months. Finnable pairs digital loan journeys and technology-led credit assessment with in-house collections.
Three lending lines
Finnable runs three businesses. Its personal loans target salaried professionals, mainly in metros and Tier I cities. Its loan against property (LAP) business offers secured credit to small business owners in Tier II and Tier IV markets. Its consumer finance arm provides instant checkout credit on leading e-commerce platforms, giving it access to younger, digitally active customers.
The company said it combines on-book lending with co-lending partnerships, which co-founder Amit Arora described as a capital-efficient model built to hold up across credit cycles.
Where the money will go
The funds will go towards taking the LAP business into new geographies, scaling consumer finance partnerships and strengthening technology. Finnable also plans to keep investing in AI across underwriting, fraud detection, collections and customer service.
Over the past year the company has also reinforced its board. It has appointed Shrimohan Yadav, a former chief general manager at the Reserve Bank of India, and Sreeram R. Iyer, a former global COO of the corporate and institutional business at ANZ Banking Group. The most recent addition is Sekhar Garisa, managing director at Claypond Capital.

articles.title: Cheaper Zuku wins back customers, but losses continue under Axian
articles.text:
Zuku, the Kenyan home internet service provider (ISP) once dominant in Nairobi, is winning back subscribers with cheaper packages and faster speeds. But one year after Axian Telecom acquired its parent company, Wananchi Group, the business is still losing money. It posted a $2 million loss in the third quarter as revenue fell to $11.5 million.
The figures reflect the challenge facing Axian, the pan-African telecoms group that acquired Wananchi for $69.4 million. It bought a fibre network with an established customer base, but one that had lost ground to Safaricom and Faiba, and was already struggling financially.
Zuku is now cutting prices to win back subscribers in a market where Safaricom has more than a third of fixed-internet connections. The strategy is bringing customers back, but has yet to deliver a financial recovery.
Wananchi’s revenue fell by about a fifth from the first quarter, according to unaudited financial results published on Monday. Its quarterly loss narrowed from $3.9 million in the second quarter, but the group has accumulated $8.1 million in losses since January.
The results also cover Wananchi’s operations in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Malawi.
Buying back market share
Zuku was once one of Kenya’s largest home-internet providers. It was among the first companies to wire Nairobi homes with fibre and, a decade ago, held about half of the country’s fixed-internet subscriptions. It now ranks third, according to the Communications Authority of Kenya.
Axian’s acquisition gave it an entry into a market where Safaricom has built a lead through its nationwide distribution network and growing fibre footprint.
Zuku’s response has been to make home internet cheaper and faster. In May, the ISP doubled speeds across its fibre packages without raising prices. Three months later, it cut monthly subscription rates on several plans.
The changes appear to be working. Zuku’s fixed-internet subscriptions grew 10.4% in the first half of 2026, with much of the increase coming after the speed upgrade, according to the communications regulator. This follows a difficult period in which Wananchi lost more than 24,000 internet and pay-TV subscriptions in the three months to September 2025.
The gains come as Kenya’s home-internet market expands. Fixed-internet subscriptions rose by about a third through June, while Safaricom crossed one million home-internet customers, more than Faiba and Zuku combined.
Yet more subscribers have not translated into higher revenue for Wananchi. Lower subscription prices are one explanation. The group also said weaker currencies in Tanzania and Uganda reduced the dollar value of its earnings.
Wananchi’s cost base makes the recovery harder. Network capacity, television content and bandwidth account for some of its largest expenses, alongside staff costs and depreciation. These costs continue to weigh on its financial performance even as it attracts more customers.
A costly acquisition
Axian agreed to buy 99.63% of Wananchi in August 2024 and completed the transaction on October 30, 2025, after securing regulatory approvals, including from the COMESA Competition Commission.
The $69.4 million acquisition price included just $8.3 million in cash paid to the sellers. The remainder settled a loan owed to the Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the US government’s development lender.
Wananchi’s liabilities exceeded its assets by $48.6 million when Axian took control. The sellers refunded $1.6 million in May after the parties agreed on the final acquisition accounts. In September, Axian also reduced the value it assigned to the acquired network.
“Management does not expect these conditions to be met, and therefore no accrual has been recognised,” the company said.
The acquisition was a small part of Axian’s wider business. Group revenue rose 17% to $525.5 million in the third quarter, driven by mobile and mobile-money growth in Tanzania and Madagascar. Wananchi contributed about 2% of that revenue.
Axian said the Wananchi deal, alongside a smaller fibre acquisition in Tanzania, was not material enough to require pro forma financial disclosures to bondholders.
“Given the value of revenue, gross assets, and adjusted EBITDA of the Wananchi Group and Aptus these acquisitions are not considered to be material acquisitions,” it said.
The group adopted the Yas name in September, replacing Axian Telecom as its operating brand. When the Wananchi deal closed, chief executive Hassan Jaber said the acquisition would support its ambition to expand broadband connectivity across Africa.
Zuku’s subscriber growth signals the acquisition is beginning to deliver on its commercial promise and turn those customers into sustainable revenue without relying on price cuts.

articles.title: GTA VI unofficial PC ports are already rendering in-game graphics despite Take-Two's takedowns
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Grand Theft Auto VI has been available on consoles for less than a week, and the cat-and-mouse game between Rockstar and users trying to play it on PC is in full swing. The game isn't playable on PC yet, but progress toward that goal continues steadily despite Take-Two's aggressive moves against unofficial ports.
Social media videos demonstrated early progress on vibe-coded PC ports of Grand Theft Auto VI just two days after the game's console launch. Other users also claim to have taken a crucial step toward running the game on emulators and uncovered the exact graphics settings for each console.
Although clips from this week reveal modders have successfully rendered GTA VI's in-game graphics on PC, framerates remain in the single digits, and glitches are clearly visible. Further development will likely have to happen underground, as a Take-Two DMCA notice struck down a port called Leonida and more than 3,000 GitHub forks. Leonida was the first project known to have booted the game on PC.
 – __cxc__ (@ChenXuchuan) November 24, 2026
 – Brackz (@Brackzmeta) November 25, 2026
The website PortWatch VI is tracking the race between several porting attempts. None have achieved a playable frame rate, but several have at least reached GTA VI's first chapter. In the lead is AvatarManz, who forked a port called Victory and achieved frame rates of between 6 and 20fps on an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX. However, his project currently uses up to 46GB of RAM.
Meanwhile, unconfirmed reports claim some users have dumped the files from the PS5 version and run it on jailbroken consoles. Playing GTA VI on PS5 normally requires firmware version 26.07-14.23.00 or newer, which hasn't been jailbroken so far. If reports of the dump are genuine, the game might become playable on PS5 emulators, which have made significant progress in recent weeks.
Data mining might also have revealed a list of graphics settings Rockstar used for each console. The original posts listing the settings on X and gtaforums.com were deleted, but not before several outlets copied them. If the list represents a potential graphics menu for an official PC version, then the wait might be shorter than for Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption II, both of which took over a year to reach PC.
Unsurprisingly, the standard PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use identical settings, which vary between medium and high for effects like global illumination and shadows. The PlayStation 5 Pro engages ray-traced shadows and sets them to high, while the Xbox Series S lowers many settings to medium or low and adjusts motion blur.
Since experts have described GTA VI as CPU-heavy, settings related to pedestrians are likely crucial to predictions about what kind of CPU a PC version would need to hit 60fps. The settings menu reveals three such options: AI behavior & motion, pedestrian and vehicle density, and physics quality, with all set to medium on Series S and high on all other consoles. GTA VI is locked to 30fps on all consoles, so reaching 60fps on many CPUs might require turning these settings down.

articles.title: Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills Through SRE-based Training
articles.text:
Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. In her talk, Engineer Confidence with Reliable Training Programs at GOTO Copenhagen, Jennifer Petoff showed how we can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself.
Software ownership is a human challenge as much as it is a technical one. Most formal education programs are geared towards the first 10% of the software development life cycle, the build phase, Petoff said. Engineers and operators are tasked with maintaining, debugging, securing, and evolving systems they may not even have written:
There’s this implicit assumption that coding proficiency translates seamlessly to operational confidence, but it doesn’t. Without systematic training, this may create imposter syndrome, stress, and maybe even attrition in your organization.
AI has magnified the relative cost and complexity of post-build operations. Petoff suggested thinking about how to equip developers and operators with skills to run their services scalably in production.
Culture is not some grand mindset you need to shift. It’s much more tactical. You can change your culture by changing what people do every day, Petoff said. Training people acts as a confidence engine, giving engineers the self-efficacy to adopt new operational behaviors. When behaviors are repeated over time and across teams, they become habits, and those habits comprise your organizational culture. Petoff suggests avoiding a sink-or-swim mentality (letting people fend for themselves rather than training them), as it can breed stress or frustration.
Training needs depend on the maturity of your organization in adopting key principles and practices, the familiarity of engineers with the organization and infrastructure, and the experience of individuals. For organizations starting their DevOps or SRE journey, she suggested addressing skill gaps and tailoring the message to who is on your team. Organizations that already have well-developed production best practices should aim at reinforcing their culture and building upon their practices to foster confidence.
Your training program should take into account the size of your organization and how fast it’s growing to get the most from your investment. If your organization is small and growing slowly, focus on one-on-one knowledge transfer through mentoring and shadowing, Petoff suggested. For a large and slowly growing organization, invest in ongoing education. When it’s small but growing rapidly, invest in onboarding. If you’re both large and growing rapidly, invest in a full life cycle training program, onboarding, all the way through ongoing education and beyond, she said.
The foundational principles of SRE and elements of the service reliability hierarchy can be applied to the training program itself, Petoff explained:
Monitor through attendance tracking and survey feedback. Address issues that surface via the monitoring. Write postmortems when something goes wrong to learn from that failure. Observe concrete job-related behaviors to more effectively tie the training to business impact.
To scale production safety training to tens of thousands of developers, they created a self-paced training and piloted it with a 1% cohort, making changes based on audience feedback before scaling it up. Petoff said they automated the distribution, enrollment, and escalation notifications up the management chain.
A production-ready workforce and organizational culture is non-negotiable in the generative AI era, Petoff stated. Learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and behavior repeated over time drives culture. You need to look at the training costs and benefits to make the right level of investment based on the specific organizational situation. Applying SRE principles to the training program itself led to a more consistent, reliable, and scalable experience, she concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Jennifer Petoff after her talk.
InfoQ: How can we tailor the training message to individual team members?
Jennifer Petoff: In the Generative AI era, we are all moving faster than ever, and it’s easy for training to get sacrificed as something important, but not urgent. Developers and operators may also look upon training with skepticism: Is this training tied to some fleeting corporate hype that will quickly be forgotten?
You need to convince them "what’s in it for me?" (WIIFM). The answer ties directly to what motivates people and varies among team members.
- For the practically-minded: Tie the training to reductions in toil or on-call load.
- For the growth-minded: Connect it to higher-value skills that can unlock career opportunities.
- For people motivated by self-preservation: Explain how the training will build future-proof skills.
These "WIIFM" elements can be conveyed in written communications, through talking points to managers, or peer-to-peer discussions incorporated into the program.
InfoQ: How did you observe job-related behaviors?
Petoff: We built a hands-on training environment using real production infrastructure, but without real-world users and associated stakes. We could "break" our training infrastructure on demand, and students would work in groups of three to troubleshoot realistic production issues.
By structuring the training in this way, instructors could directly observe how participants used system diagrams, diagnosed production issues, and mitigated an outage. We looked at how people engaged with production during the exercises instead of quizzing them or asking for a simple nod of understanding.
InfoQ: What have you learned from applying SRE principles to training programs?
Petoff: Reliability is about mastering the operational "how" of any complex initiative. Training programs are just the tip of the iceberg. I believe that you can "SRE" anything in work, life, and for your well-being. Building is time-bound, but operations are forever. Planning a project beyond launch to include mechanisms to streamline operations and drive continuous improvement will pay you back tenfold and free up time to work on more impactful initiatives without getting buried under a mountain of toil.

articles.title: Windows 11 distribue des pilotes Intel obsolètes et vulnérables via Windows update
articles.text:
Les outils de Microsoft ont visiblement un gros problème de communication. Le site allemand Deskmodder rapporte en effet que le système d’exploitation a distribué, par l’intermédiaire de Windows Update, un pilote obsolète et vulnérable déclenchant une alerte de sécurité de Microsoft Defender.
Un pilote vulnérable, mais légitime, distribué par Windows Update
C’est après avoir mis à jour un système Intel NUC de 11e génération que Deskmodder a vu s’afficher une alerte de sécurité émise par Microsoft Defender. Celle-ci a mis en lumière un problème provenant du paquet Intel Performance Driver Extension dans sa version 1.0.0.38. Ce module lié au service Intel NUC Software Studio Service et qui a pour objectif de fournir une surveillance matérielle de bas niveau, comporte une importante faille de sécurité. Une brèche qui touche plus particulièrement le composant WinRing0 de ce pilote et dont la vulnérabilité est connue depuis 2020.
Cette faille, identifiée sous la référence CVE-2020-14979 permet une élévation locale des privilèges. Cela signifie concrètement que des attaquants disposant déjà d’un accès à la machine pourraient exploiter ce pilote légitime pour mener des attaques de type Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver et ainsi contourner les protections du noyau de Windows.
Windows Update réinstalle automatiquement le pilote après suppression
Mais le plus gros problème avec ce pilote, c’est que bien qu’il soit clairement identifié comme étant vulnérable par Microsoft Defender, Windows Update continue de le distribuer. Et cela, même après l’avoir supprimé.
Le module de mise à jour de Windows ne communique pas avec l’antivirus natif et continue de le délivrer en boucle ce pilote vulnérable lors des recherches de mises à jour. Un problème de taille alors que Microsoft a dévoilé il y a quelques mois son Driver Quality Initiative, censée corriger toute seule les pilotes problématiques.

articles.title: El Black Friday más allá de teléfonos y ordenadores: areneros autolimpiables, proyectores y cámaras dashcams
articles.text:
Muchas personas aprovechan el Black Friday para comprar teléfonos, televisores, portátiles y otros productos bastante caros. Sin embargo, el Black Friday afecta a todo y puedes encontrar novedades en sectores muy interesantes, por ejemplo el del cuidado de mascotas con areneros o impresoras 3D.
En PowerPlanet van a lanzar una ambiciosa campaña de ofertas, que ya está disponible y que durará hasta el 7 de diciembre, alargando casi una semana el CyberMonday. Hemos dejado aquí dividido por categorías las mejores ofertas que puedes encontrar.
Areneros autolimpiables
A la hora de tener una mascota en casa, sobre todo gatos, el principal incoveniente es la limpieza del arenero. En Power Planet puedes encontrar dos modelos en oferta, los dos con una capacidad de 76 litros y que se pueden controlar desde el teléfono móvil. Son estos dos:
PETKIT Pura Max 2 de 309 euros: es el más silencioso, con hasta 35 dB, y su depósito sellado aguanta hasta 15 días. Admite gatos de hasta 8 kg y mayores de 6 meses. Baja casi a la mitad.
PETKIT Pura Max 3 de 439 euros: admite gatos de 1,5 a 10 kg y hasta 3 o 4 gatos, e incluye el desodorizador N50.
Para nosotros, compensa más el Pura Max 2; pero si tienes varios gatos o gatos grandes, entonces el Pura Max 3. Más modelos en los areneros y productos para mascotas en oferta.
Proyectores de calidad
No hay nada como sentarse en el sofá a ver una película un viernes por la noche. Mucho más si lo hacemos en un buen proyector con una gran calidad de imagen. Hemos encontrado dos modelos que tienen una resolución FHD e incluyen Netflix de manera preinstalada.
Wanbo X5S de 259,90 euros: 1.100 lúmenes ANSI, HDR10 e imagen de hasta 140 pulgadas. Trae Netflix, YouTube, Disney+ y Prime Video preinstalados, y tiene HDMI 2.1 con eARC para conectar una barra de sonido.
Wanbo Mozart 1 Pro de 359,90 euros: 1.200 lúmenes ANSI, Android TV 11, autoenfoque y corrección trapezoidal automática. Su sonido es más completo, con dos altavoces de 10 W y subwoofer.
Si dudas entre ambos, el X5S es la opción más económica y con más plataformas mientras que el Mozart 1 Pro es el que mejor suena y el más fácil de colocar. Tienes más modelos en los proyectores en oferta.
Dos dashcam: una compra barata que seguro que valoras
Cada vez más coches y motos llevan cámaras integradas para grabar el entorno, especialmente útil en caso de accidente o de atropello y que ayuda a esclarecer el motivo de cara a las aseguradoras. Si tu coche no la trae de serie, te dejamos dos modelos de dashcams con una increíble calidad de imagen y que no se va mucho de precio.
DDPAI N5 Pro de 119,95 euros: cámara delantera 4K con sensor Sony Starvis 2 y 143° de visión, trasera en 2K, visión nocturna NightVIS 2.0, 64 GB internos y asistente de conducción ADAS. No tiene pantalla: se maneja desde la app por Wi-Fi 6.
DDPAI Z60 2026 de 109 euros: pantalla IPS de 3 pulgadas, cámara delantera 4K, trasera 1080p por cable y GPS integrado sin suscripción.
Si quieres ver la imagen en la propia cámara, entonces la elección es la Z60 2026. Pero si prefieres más resolución atrás y asistente de conducción, la N5 Pro. Más modelos en las cámaras y accesorios para coche en oferta.
Empieza a imprimir en 3D
La impresión en 3D está de moda. Si tienes espacio para poner una en tu casa, aprovecha este Black Friday con ofertas muy interesantes y ponte a imprimir desde ya. No necesitas conocimientos demasiado técnicos. Tienes dos modelos en oferta:
Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo  de 399,99 euros, con unas dimensiones de 256 × 256 × 256 mm, hasta 500 mm/s y sistema CANVAS de cuatro colores. Su boquilla de acero endurecido permite imprimir PLA con fibra de carbono, y nivela sola en 121 puntos. 
Creality K2 Combo de 529 euros: 260 × 260 × 260 mm y hasta 600 mm/s. Su sistema CFS se amplía hasta 16 colores, y la cámara con IA pausa la impresión si falla una capa.
Si quieres empezar pero no gastarte mucho dinero, elige entonces la Elegoo. Si quieres algo más pro, para crecer hasta 16 colores, entonces tu elección debería ser la Creality. Más modelos en las impresoras 3D en oferta.
Bonus: dos monitores gaming de Xiaomi, de 24 y 27 pulgadas
Una magnífica compra teniendo en cuenta los precios que suele tener Xiaomi en su día a día para todo lo que ofrece, que es mucho en el caso de los monitores gaming.
Xiaomi G24i 2026 de 105 euros: 23,8 pulgadas Full HD, panel Fast IPS a 200 Hz, 1 ms y FreeSync Premium. Baja un 47 %.
Xiaomi G Pro 27Qi 2026 de 309 euros: 27 pulgadas 2K a 180 Hz con Mini LED de 1.152 zonas, hasta 2.000 nits y HDR1000. Su soporte se ajusta en altura, gira y pivota.
Para elegir el correcto tienes que tener en cuenta a qué vas a jugar. Para jugar a shooters con poco presupuesto, el G24i; pero si quieres la mejor imagen HDR en juegos y series, el G Pro 27Qi. Más pantallas en las ofertas de informática.

articles.title: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
articles.text:
The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.
Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.
If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.
What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.
But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.
And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.
But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

articles.title: Kenyan, Nigerian, Ugandan startups named as Latitude59 Kenya finalists
articles.text:
Ten startups from Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have been selected as finalists for the Latitude59 Kenya Pitch Competition, and will now pitch on the main stage at the event in Nairobi on December 4.
Disrupt Africa reported last month startup and technology event Latitude59 was returning to Kenya for the fourth year, with startups invited to compete for non-equity funding, partner prizes, and the opportunity to pitch on the main stage.
Ten finalists have now been chosen from a record 509 applications from 25 countries – seven from Kenya, two from Nigeria and one from Uganda.
The Kenyan ventures include Inner Circle, which runs a marketplace where African creators earn money from their audiences through mobile money, paid sessions, subscriptions and direct messages in six markets; Farmsky, which builds AI-powered infrastructure for farmers and agricultural SMEs; Sustainable Africa, which builds data infrastructure designed to make African businesses and value chains verifiable and financeable; and ElementPay, which gives businesses in emerging markets bank accounts in their own names in more than 27 countries.
The other Kenyan startups are MasomoGPT, which helps users learn by drawing on things they already enjoy; Chargebyte, which makes solar-powered charging and Wi-Fi stations to widen access to energy and connectivity; and Bahari Mezani, which provides solar-powered cold storage and logistics to reduce fish spoilage and post-harvest losses along the Kenyan coast.
The Nigerian finalists are Ruralpass, which provides identity verification and risk assessment tools that help banks and insurers serve smallholder farmers, and BetaLife, which connects hospitals, blood banks and donors to improve the delivery of blood and medical supplies.
Uganda’s Kyuka Ventures, the remaining finalist, converts plastic waste into clean LPG cooking fuel.
“What stands out about this year’s TOP10 is the range of founders and ideas,” said Krista Meinarde, head of investor-startup relations at Latitude59. “Put them on one stage, and you get a real picture of where African tech is heading, and these are the teams to watch.”
Before the final, the startups will get pitch training and mentoring from pitch coach Gleb Maltsev.
The winner will receive a “golden ticket” to Tallinn, Estonia. The prize fast-tracks them into the top 30 of the Latitude59 2027 Pitch Competition and covers their return trip. It also gives them the chance to meet investors and potential partners in Estonia’s startup ecosystem.
