articles.title: AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works?
articles.text:
AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works?
As organizations invest in AI, many are discovering a new bottleneck: obtaining data that is both protected and useful. Engineering teams need realistic, production-like data to validate AI-generated changes, train models, test applications, and generate business insights.
Yet, privacy initiatives can sometimes make that data harder to access, less representative of real-world conditions, or unable to preserve critical relationships between records.
The Perforce Delphix “2026 State of AI and Data Privacy Report” highlights this challenge. Among surveyed organizations, 26% say privacy controls make production-quality data harder to obtain, 25% struggle to preserve relationships across data entities, and 51% cite data quality challenges.
“Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it.”
Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it. For engineering teams, the question is whether their data protection strategies can preserve the qualities that make data valuable in the first place. You need a well-rounded data strategy with tools that maintain referential integrity and relationships across your environments.
What these statistics mean for practitioners
At first glance, statistics from the report, like “51% of enterprises cite data quality challenges,” may sound like a purely governance issue.
In practice, they represent engineering problems. Low-quality datasets can produce:
- Inaccurate analytics.
- Poorly trained AI models.
- Incomplete test coverage.
- Increased rework.
- Delayed releases.
- Reduced confidence in data automation.
“When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable.”
When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable. When test environments contain unrealistic data, defects can escape into production. When analytics datasets lack consistency, teams spend more time validating results than acting on them.
Data protection and utility are not opposing goals
A common misconception is that organizations must choose between privacy and innovation, but the most successful organizations know that compliance, quality, and speed can and need to work together.
Protected data still needs to be:
- Realistic enough for testing and validation.
- Representative enough for analytics.
- Accessible enough for engineering teams.
- Governed enough for regulatory requirements.
- Connected enough to preserve referential integrity.
There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection. All too often, enterprises sacrifice compliance for innovation or speed. That’s a big reason 84% of respondents in our report have a data privacy exception in their non-production environments.
“There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection.”
Organizations can only move at AI speed when they have access to trustworthy data that accurately represents production conditions. When privacy controls degrade quality, limit realism, or restrict access to representative datasets, the data layer becomes the new bottleneck.
Why referential integrity matters more than ever
Many discussions about data privacy focus on masking sensitive fields. However, masked data that loses referential integrity between entities can create a different kind of risk.
A customer, order, or payment record may still exist, but if the relationships connecting those records break during protection processes, the data no longer resembles reality. Take billing validation, for example. It needs referential integrity when a customer has multiple products, charges, and invoices across several database tables to produce the correct products or make accurate charges.
Broken relationships are especially problematic for modern AI and analytics systems. Analytics pipelines depend on consistent identifiers to join information across sources. AI and machine learning workflows depend on complete business context to identify patterns and make predictions. Software testing depends on realistic relationships between records to validate application behavior accurately.
When referential integrity is lost:
- Analytics can produce incomplete or misleading results.
- AI models can learn from flawed datasets.
- Testing environments can fail to expose production issues.
- Teams lose trust in protected datasets.
Importantly, these failures are often difficult to detect. Pipelines may continue running successfully while quietly producing degraded outcomes, which can be a very costly mistake.
This helps explain why 25% of surveyed organizations cited preserving relationships across data entities as a significant challenge. For practitioners, that statistic is a warning that privacy controls can unintentionally undermine the quality of AI and analytics initiatives if they fail to preserve business context.
Keep in mind that not all data protection solutions are created equal — enterprise-grade masking algorithms are key to preserving relationships. When applied consistently and at scale, these algorithms ensure the same input produces the same masked output across your systems and environments. Other masking approaches might be done piecemeal, resulting in broken relationships.
What engineering teams should measure
Many organizations measure privacy success through compliance metrics alone. However, AI-driven environments require a broader definition of success. Engineering leaders should evaluate privacy initiatives against several dimensions:
- Data quality: Does the protected dataset accurately reflect production conditions?
- Realism: Can developers, data scientists, and analysts use the data confidently for their intended purpose?
- Referential integrity: Do relationships remain consistent across applications, tables, environments, and data sources?
- Accessibility: Can teams obtain compliant data without introducing delays?
- Provisioning speed: How quickly can trusted datasets be delivered when needed?
These measurements help organizations determine whether privacy efforts enable AI outcomes or create new obstacles.
Designing for governance by default
As AI adoption grows, privacy cannot remain a separate process that occurs after development begins. Organizations should instead map the entire data lifecycle, from data request and discovery to reuse and retirement.
This approach helps ensure governance is built into workflows rather than applied as a late-stage checkpoint. It also provides stronger auditability, reduces compliance exceptions, and gives teams greater confidence that protected datasets remain fit for purpose.
Most importantly, it aligns privacy objectives with business outcomes instead of treating them as competing priorities.
Trusted data will become a competitive differentiator
The need for test data — in volume, coverage, and scale — is booming as agentic development continues to rise. AI has also increased the volume of change enterprises can generate, but the challenge of validating that change remains unsolved.
That responsibility still belongs to data. The organizations that gain the most value from AI will not necessarily be the ones with the most advanced models. They will be the ones with the most trustworthy data foundations — using a portfolio approach that combines data virtualization for speed, masking for security, and synthetic data for coverage as needed.
“In the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.”
The research points to a clear lesson: If privacy controls uphold realism, quality, relationships between records, or access to representative datasets, they can enable AI success.
As enterprises continue investing in AI and data privacy, the real objective should be ensuring protection and utility coexist. Because in the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.

articles.title: Effondrement de jetée, routes inondées : comment El Niño fait déborder la Californie sans tempête
articles.text:
Les images viennent de Californie, mais le phénomène à leur origine touche toute la planète. Un homme pagayant sur une route inondée à Mill Valley, au nord de San Francisco, ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, alors que la ville a battu son record de marée pour un mois de novembre, rapporte le Time.
Le lendemain, les vagues ont emporté une partie de la jetée en bois de Pacifica, par temps clair, selon le récit du Guardian. Plus au sud, Santa Cruz a fermé ses plages, et environ 200 maisons ont reçu un avis d’évacuation.
Comment El Niño fait monter le niveau de l’océan
Mais pourquoi l’eau monte-t-elle si haut sans grosse tempête ? L’agence océanique américaine (NOAA) a expliqué le mécanisme dès le 4 novembre, après une première série de records fin octobre. San Diego avait alors atteint 85 centimètres au-dessus de la moyenne de ses plus hautes marées.
Tout part d’une marée de vives-eaux, quand la Lune est pleine et au plus près de la Terre. El Niño, ce réchauffement des eaux du Pacifique tropical, y ajoute des ondes de Kelvin, d’immenses vagues lentes qui poussent l’eau chaude vers l’Amérique et rehaussent l’océan de 15 à 30 centimètres pendant plusieurs semaines. Une vague de chaleur marine fait le reste, car l’eau chaude prend plus de place que l’eau froide.
« Les effets combinés de ces facteurs ont fait grimper le niveau de l’eau à des niveaux record, provoquant l’inondation de routes, de logements et de commerce, et perturbant la vie quotidienne », explique la NOAA.
Ce mercredi, San Diego et Los Angeles ont encore battu leurs records, selon le météorologue Jeff Masters.
Un El Niño parti pour battre des records
Or El Niño ne s’arrête pas à la Californie. Dans son bulletin mensuel publié le jeudi 12 novembre, le centre de prévision climatique du service météo américain (CPC) estimait à environ 60 % la probabilité d’un épisode plus fort que tous ceux mesurés depuis 1950.
Ses effets bousculent déjà le climat mondial. Auprès de Numerama, le climatologue Éric Guilyardi détaille ce qu’El Niño nous réserve pour les prochains mois.
En Californie, l’épisode n’est pas terminé : la NOAA prévoit de nouvelles marées anormalement hautes jusqu’au 27 novembre, puis du 22 au 26 décembre.

articles.title: 2K, IP65 et deux ans d'autonomie : le pack Blink caméra et sonnette à moins de 35 €
articles.text:
Blink est la marque de caméras connectées d’Amazon, positionnée en entrée et milieu de gamme face à des concurrents comme Netatmo ou EZVIZ. Ce pack 2K+ marque un saut par rapport aux modèles 1080p de la gamme : la caméra extérieure passe à 2560 × 1440 pixels, avec vision nocturne en couleur, zoom numérique 4x et certification IP65. La sonnette vidéo adopte un format carré 1:1, pensé pour cadrer le visiteur des pieds à la tête, et elle accepte aussi bien les piles qu’un câblage existant. Le tout est pilotable depuis une seule application, avec une intégration Alexa pour afficher le flux sur un Echo Show. Ce Black Friday, le pack passe à 34,99 euros.
Les atouts du pack Blink 2K+
- Caméra en 2K (2560 × 1440) avec vision nocturne couleur
- Sonnette au format 1:1, 140° horizontal, filaire ou sur piles
- Certification IP65 et jusqu’à 2 ans d’autonomie sur piles AA lithium
Affiché à 82,10 euros en temps normal, le pack Blink 2K+ est disponible à 34,99 euros sur Amazon pour le Black Friday, soit une réduction de plus de 57 %.
Successeur du Saros 10R annoncé en début d’année, le Saros 20 Set passe de 1 299 à 799 euros. C’est l’une des meilleures affaires du Black Friday pour s’offrir la nouveauté à petit prix !
Une caméra extérieure qui monte en résolution
La Blink Outdoor 2K+ filme en 2560 × 1440 pixels, là où les modèles 1080p de la même gamme restent en dessous. La différence se voit concrètement : un visage ou une plaque, identifiable là où l’image basse résolution donne un carré flou. Le zoom numérique 4x prolonge cet avantage. La vision nocturne passe en couleur sous faible éclairage, puis bascule en infrarouge noir et blanc quand la lumière disparaît vraiment.
Côté installation, deux piles AA lithium suffisent, Blink annonce jusqu’à deux ans d’autonomie dans les conditions d’utilisation par défaut, avec les réglages de fréquence de détection au minimum. Dans la pratique, cela dépend du volume de clips enregistrés. La certification IP65 couvre la pluie et la poussière, et le fonctionnement est garanti entre -20 °C et 45 °C.
La sonnette et le piège du stockage sans abonnement
La sonnette vidéo 2K+ adopte un format carré 1:1 avec 140° de champ horizontal, ce qui permet de voir un visiteur en entier, colis posé devant la porte compris. L’audio bidirectionnel laisse répondre depuis l’application sans ouvrir la porte. Elle fonctionne sur piles ou sur un câblage existant, ce qui la rend compatible avec les installations filaires déjà en place. Jusqu’ici, tout est solide. Le Sync Module Core fourni dans le pack connecte les deux appareils à la box, mais attention : il n’a ni port USB ni emplacement microSD. Passé l’essai gratuit de 30 jours, sans abonnement Blink, l’historique vidéo et la détection des personnes disparaissent. Il reste les alertes de mouvement et la vue en direct limitée à cinq minutes. Pour débloquer l’enregistrement sans frais récurrents, il faut acheter séparément un Sync Module 2 (environ 44,99 euros) avec une clé USB, ou un Sync Module XR avec microSD. L’alternative est de souscrire à l’abonnement Blink Plus, autour de 10 euros par mois pour couvrir plusieurs appareils. Ce pack à 35 euros est donc une bonne base, à condition d’avoir prévu l’un ou l’autre de ces ajouts.
Pour comparer le Blink 2K+ à d’autres modèles du marché, consultez notre guide des meilleures caméras de surveillance, qui recense les modèles que nous recommandons selon les usages.

articles.title: Une chaine de TV 24/7 dopée à l'IA et personnalisée : la nouvelle idée qui germe chez Google
articles.text:
Google a déposé une demande de brevet pour « My Channel », une chaîne de télévision dont les vidéos seraient créées par une IA à partir de votre historique de visionnage, de votre position et de votre âge. Elle pourrait même vous donner le rôle principal, avec votre visage et votre voix.
Allumer sa télé et tomber sur « La chaîne de Jean », pleine de scènes d'aventures aux quatre coins du monde que personne n’a tournées : c’est ce que décrit une demande de brevet publiée le 19 novembre par Google.
Vos données en entrée, une vidéo sur mesure en sortie
Le principe est relativement basique. Le brevet en question décrit un serveur capable de récupérer ce que vous regardez (genres et titres, sur YouTube par exemple), des infos sur votre appareil (adresse IP, langue, position GPS) et des données démographiques, comme votre tranche d’âge. Il en tire un prompt envoyé à un grand modèle de langage. Ce dernier génère une vidéo, stockée puis diffusée sur votre écran sous forme de vignette avec un titre et un résumé. Ces contenus générés peuvent aussi varier selon l’appareil, téléphone ou télé.
Google précise que la génération peut être programmée sur une minuterie (hebdomadaire, mensuelle ou annuelle) ou à la demande, et même sans aucune action de l’utilisateur. Un second modèle peut aussi piocher dans l’actualité, les tendances sociales ou les scores sportifs. Un fan de foot pourrait se retrouver dans les gradins de la Coupe du monde, à soutenir la France. Dans la version complète, l’utilisateur se place au centre du scénario et le système construit un avatar à partir de vos photos tout en clonant votre voix pour les répliques. Évidemment, des publicités peuvent aussi venir se glisser dans la vidéo avant sa lecture.
Le sujet n’est pas nouveau. En avril, nous rapportions que YouTube laissait ses créateurs générer un avatar photoréaliste à leur image et à leur voix pour leurs Shorts, à partir d’un selfie vidéo. Début novembre, c’est Microsoft qui déposé un brevet pour réécrire en direct les paroles d’un orateur selon le profil du spectateur (âge, langues parlées).
Quoi qu’il en soit à ce stade, l’USPTO, l’organisme chargé d’examiner les brevets aux Etats-Unis, a rejeté celui-ci et Google peut encore le modifier pour obtenir une approbation. D’un côté, l’idée n’est pas ultra novatrice. 404 media, qui rapporte l’affaire, note qu’il existe déjà des chaînes gratuites pointues sur Samsung TV Plus et TCLtv+, des pubs déclinées par l’IA chez Meta, ou FairgroundTV, la chaîne gratuite entièrement générée par IA lancée par Roku.

articles.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
articles.text:
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
Avi Davidson is the first at-home user of an experimental prosthetic hand that lets him feel his wife’s hand in his own.
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.
Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb
In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.
The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.
Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”
Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections
A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.
Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.
A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”
In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic
Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.
He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.
At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.
Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.
The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”
Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Iñaki Gabilondo: “Cuando ya tienes una edad, ya tienes el piso pagado, ya los hijos son mayores, ya tienes los reconocimientos que has podido tener, ¿qué motor puedes tener?”
articles.text:
El periodista Iñaki Gabilondo lleva más de medio siglo dedicado a su profesión. Tras una larga vida profesional, reflexiona sobre qué pasa cuando los motivos que nos mueven (las cargas familiares o los objetivos profesionales) dejan de tener validez. “Cuando ya tienes una edad, ya tienes el piso pagado, ya los hijos son mayores, ya tienes los reconocimientos que has podido tener, ¿qué motor puedes tener?”
Esta reflexión la hace en una charla que mantiene con Ricardo Moya en el programa “El sentido de la birra”. Tras décadas de ejercicio profesional como periodista, habla en esta ocasión de cómo envejece y de cómo trata la muerte.
Habla desde su propia experiencia y reflexiona sobre cómo cambian los motivos. Al envejecer, se da cuenta de que había hecho muchas cosas por gusto. Pero también había hecho cosas por otras razones. Por ejemplo, pagar el piso o sacar adelante a los hijos. También podía haber hecho algo por reconocimiento. En cualquier caso, estas razones podían ir asociadas a algo que creía que hacía porque quería. Cuando las razones dejan de estar ahí… ¿Qué queda?
Para explicarlo, habla de cómo entiende el paso del tiempo. Tiene claro que hay un número limitado de botellas de vino que podrá tomar. También tiene claro que hay un número limitado de veces que podrá hacer el amor o que podrá volver a París.
Se define como alguien que ha disfrutado bastante de la vida. Ha sabido valorar todo lo que le pasaba porque no sabía cuánto iba a durar. ¿Cómo se puede disfrutar sin saber que hay un límite? Ha sido la conciencia de la muerte lo que le ha ayudado a disfrutar de las cosas en el momento. Sin pensar que siempre puede volver a hacerlo.
Ha sabido aceptar el desgaste que implica la existencia. No ha tenido una especial inquietud por la muerte.
La compañía de Lola y el tiempo a solas
Cuando habla de su propia muerte, destaca el aspecto que más le inquieta. “Lo que más me angustia de morirme es separarme de Lola”. Es un hombre felizmente casado. Considera que es una suerte que tenga a su lado a Lola. Es un regalo (sobre todo a su edad).
Sabe estar solo. Tiene placer en leer o escuchar música. También puede estar pensativo, pasear o mirar. Le resulta difícil imaginar cómo pueden pasar estos momentos aquellos que no encuentran placer en estas actividades.
Por ejemplo, compara la vida con un paseo por el bosque. Sabemos que acabará. En el camino hay belleza y exaltación, pero también hay miedos y sufrimientos. Para él, hay que ser responsable de nuestra vida. Hay que darle sentido, haciéndolo bien y siendo responsable.

Black Friday 2026 : L'aspirateur balai Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW à 299,99 € (-40%)
Actuellement noté 4/5 par notre rédaction, l'aspirateur balai Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW assure d'excellentes performances d'aspiration, notamment sur tapis à poils longs, avec une filtration parfaite. Le Black Friday fait descendre son prix à 299,99 € chez Darty.com, soit une baisse d'environ 40 % et 200,00 € d'économie.
Samsung déploie son aspirateur balai Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW, un modèle stick à filtration multicyclonique pensé pour nettoyer les sols sans station de vidange automatique. Livré avec une mini-brosse motorisée pour traquer les poils d'animaux, cet appareil s'est distingué lors de son passage dans notre labo par son efficacité de nettoyage.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW descend à 299,99 € chez Darty.com, soit environ 40 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (499,99 €). Cela représente une économie de 200,00 €.
Une aspiration redoutable et une filtration exemplaire
Cet aspirateur balai fait valoir de très solides prestations de nettoyage, notamment sur les tapis à poils longs où la brosse ramasse la poussière en profondeur sans blocage. Le système de filtration multicyclonique retient parfaitement les particules fines dans le collecteur de 0,8 l, ce qui évite de rejeter les saletés dans l'air de la pièce. Comme le détaille notre test complet, l'écran affiche une estimation de l'autonomie restante exprimée en minutes et en secondes, une donnée précise pour gérer sa séance de ménage sans interruption imprévue.
Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW
Points forts
- Filtration parfaite.
- Excellentes performances d'aspiration, notamment sur tapis à poils longs.
- Estimation de l'autonomie exprimée en minutes et secondes.
Points faibles
- Très peu de fonctionnalités annexes (rampe de leds inexistante, aspiration continue obligatoire…).
- Vidange du collecteur.
- Autonomie limitée.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Des concessions sur les options et l'entretien au quotidien
Pour modérer la facture face aux versions équipées d'une tour de vidange, Samsung impose ici de vider manuellement le bac à poussière, une manipulation qui réclame un peu de patience. La tête d'aspiration fait également l'impasse sur une rampe de leds pour repérer la poussière sous les meubles, et l'autonomie globale reste mesurée lors des sessions intensives. Ces limites gênent principalement les très grands logements, mais la présence d'une seconde batterie amovible dans la boîte permet de doubler le temps de nettoyage.
Dyson V8 Cyclone : l'autre option face au Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW

Actuellement noté 4,5/5 par notre rédaction, le modèle britannique soigne particulièrement le confort acoustique et la facilité de vidange de son bac, même s'il se passe lui aussi d'éclairage frontal sur sa tête principale.
Le Dyson V8 Cyclone coûte 61,99 € de moins que le Samsung Jet 85 Pet VS20C85G2TW à son tarif remisé, mais l'appareil de Samsung conserve l'avantage d'une estimation précise de l'autonomie à la seconde près et d'un équipement fourni avec deux batteries.
Dyson V8 Cyclone
Points forts
- Belles performances d'aspiration.
- Entretien facile.
- Relativement discret, aussi bien visuellement qu'acoustiquement.
Points faibles
- Autonomie trop faible à la puissance turbo.
- Extraction de la brosse pénible.

articles.title: Apple no tira la toalla con el iPad plegable, pero no te hagas muchas ilusiones
articles.text:
Los rumores de que Apple trabaja en un iPad plegable no son nuevos. Las especulaciones en torno a este dispositivo son tan antiguas como las del recientemente lanzado iPhone Duo, pero todo apunta a que, a pesar de varios desafíos técnicos y de diseño, los de Cupertino siguen firmes con su desarrollo.
Así lo sostuvo Mark Gurman en la más reciente edición de su pódcast. El periodista de Bloomberg, el insider más confiable en lo que respecta al mundo Apple, indicó que los californianos siguen preparando un iPad plegable. El mismo tendrá la pantalla más grande jamás vista en el catálogo de tablets de la manzana, con un panel flexible de entre 19 y 20 pulgadas.
Gurman ha mencionado que el iPad plegable se está desarrollando bajo el nombre clave Project J312. El susodicho afirma que el diseño del dispositivo se parece al de un iPhone Duo, pero gigante y sin una pantalla exterior. Todavía no hay detalles sobre otras características técnicas; por ejemplo, qué chip podría impulsarlo.
Lo que sí sería un hecho es que el presunto iPad plegable estaría muy lejos de ser asequible. De acuerdo con el periodista, el dispositivo se lanzaría con un precio de entre 3.000 y 5.000 dólares. Así que si te interesa la idea de cargar un dispositivo de este tipo en tu mochila, vas a tener que desembolsar a lo grande.
El iPad plegable todavía está en marcha, pero afronta varios problemas
Los comentarios de Mark Gurman apuntan a que, si bien el iPad plegable continúa en desarrollo, ha enfrentado varios problemas. Esto se condice con un reporte previo del periodista, quien en octubre del año pasado reveló que Apple habría postergado su lanzamiento hasta 2029.
Los de Cupertino habrían apuntado a estrenarlo en 2027, pero luego lo retrasaron hasta 2028 y, más tarde, hasta 2029. Por entonces comentó que uno de los grandes inconvenientes de los ingenieros de la manzana era cómo reducir el peso del aparato. El prototipo de iPad plegable supuestamente pesaba 1,6 kilos, casi un kilo más que el iPad Pro más pesado de la actualidad.
Gurman también plantea que Apple aún no se decide sobre el software del presunto iPad plegable. Desde la compañía no estarían del todo seguros respecto de dotarlo de iPadOS, o si dan el salto que tanto reclaman los usuarios y le instalan macOS. Al parecer, tampoco se descarta desarrollar un software totalmente nuevo para el factor de forma.
Sea como sea, el iPad plegable todavía está lejos de llegar al mercado. Si bien el proyecto estaría entre las prioridades de John Ternus, Apple todavía podría descartarlo y enfocar sus recursos en una iniciativa diferente.

South Africa’s mortgage provider hit by data breach
Image Source: Engineering News
Most people can’t afford to buy a house in one go. So they take out a home loan, also called a mortgage, and repay the money in monthly instalments.
In some countries, mortgages are a big deal. South Africa has one of Africa’s largest mortgage markets. As of June 2026, the country had 1.62 million mortgage accounts, with borrowers owing R1.31 trillion ($74.6 billion) in outstanding loans, according to the country’s National Credit Regulator (NCR).
To collect monthly repayments, lenders keep customers’ banking details. Keeping that information safe is as important as protecting the loans themselves.
However, in one unfortunate twist, South African mortgage provider SA Home Loans (SAHL) has disclosed a data breach that may have exposed customers’ banking information.
What happened? On November 13, an unknown attacker accessed some of SAHL’s systems, including one used to collect payments. Names, bank account numbers, branch codes, and certain payment details may have been compromised.
Explain like I’m new here: A debit order allows a company to collect payments directly from your bank account, usually for recurring bills. Stolen banking details could help fraudsters attempt unauthorised deductions or impersonate a legitimate company when contacting customers.
State of play: SAHL said it has removed the attacker’s access and brought in forensic investigators. It has also notified South Africa’s Information Regulator and law enforcement of the incident. So far, there’s no evidence that home loan accounts were accessed, customer records were changed, or money was lost.
Between the lines: This is the second data exposure affecting SAHL customers in three months. September’s incident involved its compliance service provider, RelyComply. The latest breach involves SAHL’s own systems, underscoring how customers’ information can be exposed through different parts of a financial company’s operations.
Zoom out: SAHL has told customers to check their bank statements for unfamiliar deductions and avoid sharing one-time passwords with anyone claiming to represent SAHL. Even when criminals cannot access your loan, knowing where you bank and how you pay can make their next scam more convincing.

The Nigerian stock market is about to welcome a new heavyweight. Investors who bought shares in Dangote’s refinery during its public offer that ended on October 27 are one step closer to trading them.
What happened? Bloomberg reported that shares in Dangote Refinery will begin trading on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) on December 1. This follows approval from Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 23 for the distribution of shares to investors who applied during the refinery’s initial public offering (IPO).
Explain like I’m new here: In September, the refinery began selling newly issued shares to the public. About 4 million investors applied to buy them through the offer, using investment platforms and stockbrokers. Now that the SEC has approved the share distribution, successful applicants can receive the shares they paid for in their investment accounts.
Why does it matter? Until trading begins, investors who bought into the IPO can’t sell their shares on the stock exchange. Once trading starts, they can sell their stake to cash out, or hold on when the business grows and their shares become more valuable.
Other investors who missed the IPO can also buy shares when trading begins, but entry may be above the ₦525 ($0.40) IPO price.

Raenest secures six US payment licences
Image Source: Raenest
There’s a difference between building an app that lets people receive dollars and having the legal permission to move those dollars. Many fintechs rely on licenced companies to do the second part. Raenest wants more control over both.
The Nigerian-founded fintech has secured money transmitter licences in six US states, including Florida, Georgia, and Maryland.
Explain like I’m new here: A money transmitter licence allows a business to transfer money on behalf of customers, subject to regulatory conditions. In the US, states issue these licences. Approval in Florida, for example, doesn’t automatically cover New York.
State of play: Raenest launched in 2022 to help African freelancers receive payments from foreign clients. Today, it offers multicurrency accounts, international transfers, cards, and investment products. The fintech said it currently has over 1.5 million registered customers and has processed more than $3 billion in lifetime transactions.
The US licences follow its acquisition of UK payments company Remitise this month. Raenest also holds regulatory registrations in Canada and a money transfer licence in Nigeria.
Between the lines: When a fintech depends on another company’s licence, that partner’s fees, rules, and technical capabilities can influence what the fintech offers customers.
Owning licences gives Raenest more room to negotiate partnerships and develop services. But it doesn’t eliminate the need for banks, and maintaining those licences comes with compliance costs.
Zoom out: Customers won’t see cheaper or faster transfers immediately. Raenest is investing in the foundations of a bigger payments business. Its advantage will become clearer when those licences translate into services competitors cannot offer as easily.

WorldRemit founder launches app to help US immigrants manage money at home and abroad
Image Source: Bloomberg
If you are an immigrant in the US, your paycheck might have two destinations. One part pays for rent, groceries, and transport in America; the other covers school fees, groceries, or a hospital bill back home. Managing both can mean juggling a regular bank account and a separate app for sending money abroad.
Ismail Ahmed, founder of money transfer company WorldRemit, built a solution for that.
What happened? Ahmed has launched Odola, a US financial app that combines salary payments, early access to wages, a Visa debit card, and international money transfers in one account. He has invested an initial $5 million of his own money and plans to put in more. He is building the company with Dr Abdigani Diriye, a technology entrepreneur who has worked at Amazon, IBM, and Microsoft Research.
Explain like I’m new here: The US is home to more than 52 million migrants. Ahmed knows this market. He founded WorldRemit in 2010, growing it into a digital money transfer business serving more than 130 countries.
What does Odola do? With Odola, customers can receive their salaries, spend using a Visa debit card, access eligible wages up to two days early, and send money home through the same app. The app also offers Early Salary Release, which lets eligible customers access their pay before payday. It tracks spending, how much they have sent home, and what remains for future expenses.
Banking services and the debit card are provided through Lead Bank, a US bank that is a member of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
Odola is not the only one chasing immigrant wallets: MAJORITY offers a US account, debit card, international transfers, early access to direct deposits, and credit-building services. Remitly and Wise also compete for the business of people sending money across borders, although their core offerings are centred heavily on transfers.
Odola’s opportunity is to bring salary management and international transfers together. It plans to introduce secured credit-building charge cards in the coming months and investment products in 2027.

articles.title: Waymo passenger finds loaded gun on seat, says support staff implied it was his
articles.text:
WTF?! What's worse than getting into a Waymo robotaxi and finding a loaded gun on the seat next to you? Calling customer service to inform them only for the agent to imply the gun was yours, then for another operator to say they'll tell the police you're in the vehicle "with a gun." As a result of this incident, which could have become even more serious, Waymo says it is now reviewing its customer support.
Stefano Scalia got into the Waymo in North Beach about 4:16 pm on November 17, according to the San Francisco Police Department. On the seat next to him was what he initially thought was a handgun-shaped novelty lighter, but it was a real Colt .25.
Scalia writes that he was a firearms instructor, so he "rendered the gun safe." He also noticed there was a round in the chamber. As the firearm uses a grip safety, simply holding it in a normal firing position disengages one of its safety mechanisms, though Colt .25 pistols typically feature additional safeguards, including a manual safety.
As Scalia put it, "if a kid or someone picked this up and pulled the trigger it would have fired."
 – Stefano (@stefanoscalia) November 25, 2026
But the story doesn't end there. Scalia said he pressed the support button in the robotaxi to inform the company of what he found, but the agent didn't understand him and said weapons weren't allowed in the vehicle, implying that they thought it belonged to Scalia.
Scalia pleaded to have the case escalated and for the car to be remotely stopped. After Scalia told the second operator the whole story, they proposed telling the police that Scalia was "in a Waymo in north beach with a gun," which sounds like a sure way to get someone accidentally shot.
Scalia then got out of the car and dialed 911 himself. He emphasized that he was not armed, that the gun was in the car, and that he would be standing outside the vehicle.
Waymo disputes parts of Scalia's account. A company spokesperson said the incident was escalated to an event response specialist, who assured Scalia that he was not at fault and that the specialist would tell police exactly what had happened.
Waymo added that it has reviewed trip data to identify the account holder who left the weapon in the car and has taken appropriate action against them for breaching its terms of service. It also said that it was reviewing how its customer service team handled the incident. Scalia said he was only given two free rides as a result of what happened, adding that he doesn't think he can support the company anymore.
