articles.title: Dacia prépare un Jogger électrique 7 places pour 2028, et personne ne semble prêt à s’aligner sur son prix
articles.text:
Dacia Jogger : la familiale 7 places va passer à l’électrique pour bousculer le marché, mais il faudra être patient
Attendu en 2028 avec la prochaine Sandero, le futur Dacia Jogger passerait à l’électrique tout en gardant ses 7 places et un prix plancher de 28 000 €.
En retard sur l’électrification de ses véhicules, Dacia devrait revenir en force dès 2028. En plus de la Sandero, la prochaine génération du Jogger s’apprêterait, elle aussi, à passer pour la première fois à une motorisation 100 % électrique. Sans renier la recette qui fait son succès, la marque roumaine de Renault ferait tout pour préserver son positionnement économique. De premières informations détaillent déjà les choix techniques et tarifaires envisagés.
Une base de Renault 5 et un tarif contenu pour rester sans rival sur le segment des 7 places
Pour réussir cette transition vers l’électrique sans faire grimper la facture, le futur Dacia Jogger s’appuierait tout d’abord sur la plateforme CMF-B du groupe Renault. Cette base polyvalente permettrait ainsi de proposer des motorisations essence, GPL, hybride et 100 % électrique, et donc de limiter les frais de développement. Le diesel resterait en revanche absent du catalogue.
Sur la version électrifiée, cette plateforme déjà utilisée par les Renault 5 E-Tech et 4 E-Tech impose ses limites d’encombrement, ce qui orienterait vers leur batterie de 52 kWh. Plus adaptée à un usage familial qu’un pack de 40 kWh, elle permettrait de viser environ 400 km d’autonomie, avec une charge rapide culminant à 100 kW. Renault faisant constamment évoluer sa technologie, un accumulateur plus compact et moins onéreux reste toutefois envisageable d’ici 2028.
Côté conception, Dacia miserait toujours sur un levier clé pour limiter les coûts : le partage de la face avant et de la ligne d’assemblage avec la Sandero. Le style devrait néanmoins se moderniser dans l’esprit du Striker, avec de nouvelles optiques en équerre et un habitacle légèrement revu pour gagner en qualité tout en restant abordable. À l’arrière, la voiture conserverait son format entre break et monospace afin de préserver les 7 places et une capacité de coffre convenable.
Interrogé par Auto Express, David Durand, directeur du design chez Dacia, souligne l’absence de rival direct : “il n’y a aucune marque européenne ou chinoise face à nous ; il n’existe aucun vrai 7 places sur le marché à ce prix ou à ce poids”, évoquant un écart d’environ 10 000 € et 300 kg. Un positionnement à part que la PDG, Katrin Adt, entend pérenniser auprès d’une clientèle fidèle, avec une version électrique espérée autour de 28 000 € (soit légèrement plus cher que le modèle familial hybride actuel, débutant à 26 500 €).

articles.title: “Se transferirá el próximo mes”: Elon Musk promete entregar dos acciones de SpaceX a cada niño de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Elon Musk anunció que cada niño de Estados Unidos recibirá dos acciones de SpaceX, la compañía aeroespacial que dirige y que también desarrolla proyectos de inteligencia artificial. La promesa duplica el beneficio que había adelantado en octubre y contempla que una de las participaciones sea entregada por la empresa y la otra provenga de su patrimonio personal.
El empresario comunicó la decisión mediante una publicación en X, la red social de su propiedad. Según explicó, SpaceX transferirá sus acciones en diciembre, mientras que las que aportará directamente se entregarán en junio de 2027, cuando termine el período de bloqueo que impide vender o transferir determinados títulos.
“Cada niño en Estados Unidos recibirá dos acciones de SpaceX, una de la empresa y otra mía personal”, escribió Musk. También recomendó a las familias conservarlas como una inversión a largo plazo.
La iniciativa está vinculada a las llamadas Trump Accounts, cuentas de inversión destinadas a menores y promovidas por el Gobierno estadounidense. Para acceder a las acciones, los padres o tutores deberán solicitar y activar una cuenta a nombre de sus hijos.
Cómo recibirán los niños las dos acciones de SpaceX
SpaceX confirmó que entregará una acción nueva de clase A a cada cuenta infantil que se encuentre activa y cumpla con las condiciones del programa. Musk igualará esa contribución con una acción de su propiedad.
Esto significa que el beneficio no se entregará automáticamente a todos los menores del país. Para participar, los padres o tutores deberán completar el trámite correspondiente y activar la cuenta de inversión de sus hijos.
Las Trump Accounts fueron creadas para que los niños puedan acumular ahorros desde edades tempranas. El Gobierno estadounidense contempla una aportación única de 1.000 dólares para los ciudadanos que cumplan los requisitos y hayan nacido entre 2025 y 2028.
El dinero de estas cuentas suele destinarse a fondos de bajo costo que replican el comportamiento del mercado bursátil estadounidense. Además, las retiradas están restringidas, por lo general, hasta el año en que el beneficiario cumple 18 años.
La Casa Blanca informó que hasta octubre se habían creado cerca de 70 millones de cuentas. Sin embargo, no precisó cuántas estaban activas, un dato importante para calcular el alcance real de la propuesta de Musk.
Cuánto dinero representan las acciones prometidas por Musk
El valor de las dos acciones dependerá de la cotización de SpaceX en el mercado. Con un precio de cierre de 127,44 dólares por título el miércoles, cada niño recibiría participaciones valoradas en 254,88 dólares.
Si los 70 millones de cuentas anunciados por la Casa Blanca estuvieran activas y todas recibieran las dos acciones, el valor conjunto de la promesa alcanzaría aproximadamente los 17.800 millones de dólares.
No obstante, esa cifra es una estimación basada en el número total de cuentas creadas y en la cotización registrada ese día. No representa el monto definitivo que recibirán las familias, ya que se desconoce cuántas cuentas cumplen las condiciones para acceder al beneficio y el precio de las acciones puede cambiar.
Musk había adelantado en octubre que cada niño estadounidense recibiría una acción de SpaceX y describió aquella participación como “la primera de muchas”. El nuevo anuncio amplía el compromiso inicial al incorporar una segunda acción financiada directamente por él.
Musk apuesta por el futuro de SpaceX
El empresario también defendió la posibilidad de que las acciones aumenten considerablemente su valor con el paso del tiempo. En su mensaje, sostuvo que SpaceX podría alcanzar una valoración extraordinaria si consigue desarrollar proyectos para establecer vida humana fuera de la Tierra y aprovechar una parte de la energía solar.
Musk reconoció que se trata de objetivos extremadamente difíciles, aunque afirmó que existe un camino para alcanzarlos. Por esa razón, recomendó a los beneficiarios conservar los títulos en lugar de venderlos.
La promesa llega después de que SpaceX recaudara unos 85.700 millones de dólares en su salida a bolsa en junio de 2026, según los datos incluidos en el anuncio. La operación convirtió a la compañía en uno de los actores más relevantes del mercado tecnológico y aeroespacial.
Aun así, el beneficio para cada familia dependerá de que la cuenta infantil esté activa, de que se cumplan las condiciones del programa y de que las transferencias anunciadas se concreten en las fechas previstas. Por ahora, Musk ha fijado diciembre para la aportación de SpaceX y junio de 2027 para la entrega de sus acciones personales.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
  November 14, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ziad Obermeyer, Alexander Schubert, James Ross, Sendhil Mullainathan, Markus Lingman. An ECG biomarker for sudden cardiac death discovered with deep learning. Nature, 2026; 655 (8121): 210 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10674-6

articles.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
articles.text:
Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
The change is to meet EU regulations, but Apple gives its developers more privacy.
Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.
If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.
Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.
Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

articles.title: Feds will now pay 80 percent of costs under AI Compute Access Fund if purchased from a sovereign provider
articles.text:
Small and medium-sized businesses will only have to pay 20 cents on the dollar for AI compute costs under the latest updates to the federal government’s compute access fund, if that compute is purchased from a “sovereign provider.”
AI Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase of the AI Compute Access Fund in Toronto on Thursday. The government is now seeking proposals from health and life sciences projects looking to access the fund. The re-opening of submissions follows the AI Compute Access Fund’s $700-million top-up under the refreshed AI strategy earlier this year, bringing its total available funds to $1 billion.
The AI Compute Access Fund aims to help Canadian SMBs with compute costs between $100,000 and $5 million by covering up to 50 percent of eligible costs for cloud-based AI compute services, or up to 80 percent of eligible costs for the same services from a sovereign, Canadian-owned compute provider. Previously, the program only covered 67 cents on the dollar if applicants used Canadian compute providers.
The AI Compute Access Fund originally launched in March 2025, with $300 million allocated for applicants, but the government quickly discovered that demand vastly exceeded that earmark
“Canadian companies are developing AI that can help detect disease earlier, improve access to home care, and keep critical networks running,” Solomon said in a statement. “By encouraging more companies to use Canadian computing providers, we are also helping create the demand that supports investment in infrastructure owned, operated, and governed in Canada.”
The AI Compute Access Fund is open to Canadian-incorporated companies with fewer than 500 employees that are generating revenue or have raised Series A financing. Applicants must be developing AI products or services and have a commercialization plan with an existing AI compute service agreement in place.
Solomon also announced on Thursday an additional 45 companies being supported by more than $52 million in funding under the program. Recipients include Ottawa-based surveillance tech company Solink, Kitchener-based virtual healthcare platform myStoria, and Calgary-based regulatory AI company Ultimarii. This follows the $66 million sent to 44 SMBs this past May, bringing the fund’s total commitments to more than $118 million for 89 Canadian companies.
The program’s previous call for proposals ended in July 2025. According to its website, the AI Compute Access Fund is now accepting proposals for the health and life sciences sector until Jan. 4, 2027.
The AI Compute Access Fund originally launched in March 2025, with $300 million allocated for applicants, but the government quickly discovered that demand vastly exceeded that earmark, Solomon recounted on a recent episode of The BetaKit Podcast.
RELATED: Canada’s AI strategy contains $2.3 billion in spending but few details on new privacy regulations
“We thought … we’ll get a couple hundred people who need compute; [we got] 1,500 asks,” Solomon said, explaining why the program was topped up with $700 million earlier this year.
The program forwards the goals of the federal government’s AI strategy announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney alongside Solomon this past June. The strategy is built on six pillars, including increasing AI adoption and building Canada’s sovereignty. Thursday’s announcement follows the government pledging 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute for Canadian AI companies as part of the 2026 federal budget earlier this month.
“What we’re making sure is that, if there’s this race to get compute, it’s not just the big hyperscalers that can take the compute and grab it,” Solomon said on The BetaKit Podcast.
Feature image courtesy Evan Solomon via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Après Riemann, ce chercheur de renom est « quasiment certain » que l’IA a trouvé autre chose, et ça concerne vos données
articles.text:
Le titre du billet donne le ton : « HOLY SHIT », répété pas moins de quatre fois. Pourtant, Scott Aaronson n’a rien d’un exalté. Informaticien théoricien à l’université du Texas à Austin et ancien chercheur chez OpenAI, il compte parmi les voix les plus respectées de son domaine, et il a longtemps été l’une des plus sceptiques face aux annonces fracassantes, notamment en informatique quantique.
Dans ce billet publié sur son blog Shtetl-Optimized le 25 novembre 2026, à la veille de Thanksgiving, il raconte un dîner entre amis et collègues. Toute la soirée, téléphones et ordinateurs en main, ils ont suivi en direct les fichiers qu’OpenAI et Anthropic déposaient sur GitHub. Les deux entreprises ne prennent même plus la peine de publier des communiqués, note-t-il : elles mettent simplement leurs articles en ligne.
Il faut dire que le terrain était bien préparé. Le 20 novembre, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, a annoncé avoir prouvé avec Claude l’hypothèse de Riemann. Cette conjecture de 1859 sur la répartition des nombres premiers est l’un des sept problèmes du millénaire, dotés chacun d’un million de dollars. Sa preuve, formalisée en Lean, un logiciel qui vérifie mécaniquement chaque étape d’un raisonnement, compte plus de 17 millions de lignes de code. Le chercheur avait même affirmé qu’une version dépasserait 250 000 pages, avant de préciser le 23 novembre qu’il plaisantait.
Le 22 novembre, Alexandr Wang, directeur de l’IA chez Meta et patron de ses Superintelligence Labs, en a tiré une conclusion qui a le mérite d’être cliare : « La superintelligence arrive. » Il y décrit une preuve obtenue avec l’aide « d’un esprit extraterrestre que nous ne comprenons pas », et prévient que ce que l’humanité fera dans l’année à venir aura de « grandes conséquences ». Et voilà que ce nouveau texte publié par Scott Aaronson vient à nouveau secouer ce petit monde.
« Quasiment certain » : des révélations explosives sur le chiffrement
Le 24 novembre, OpenAI et Anthropic ont chacun publié une preuve que VP ≠ VNP, la version « algébrique » du célèbre problème P ≠ NP. Puis, le soir du dîner, OpenAI a affirmé avoir trouvé la valeur exacte de ω, l’exposant qui mesure la vitesse à laquelle on peut multiplier deux matrices, l’opération au cœur de toutes les IA : 9/4.
Pour Scott Aaronson, on assiste à la découverte d’« un tout nouveau continent de vérité mathématique », comparable à Galilée pointant sa lunette vers les étoiles. Il interpelle les sceptiques qui pinaillent sur des détails des preuves Lean : « ne soyez pas un crétin enragé » (« raging doofus », dans le texte). Il part désormais du principe que toute preuve venant d’OpenAI ou d’Anthropic est correcte, sauf preuve du contraire, même quand d’autres chercheurs n’ont pas encore pu la vérifier.
Mais c’est un passage de deux paragraphes, presque glissé en fin de billet, qui a mis le feu aux poudres. Scott Aaronson s’y dit « quasiment certain, d’après plusieurs sources fiables », que les laboratoires d’IA détiennent « une ou plusieurs révélations explosives » en cryptographie.
Il multiplie aussitôt les précautions : il ignore leur nature exacte, craint qu’elles aient été déformées de bouche en bouche et refuse de parler d’ECDSA, l’algorithme qui signe les transactions bitcoin. Interrogé depuis, il a seulement précisé avoir entendu « beaucoup, beaucoup de rumeurs » selon lesquelles un labo aurait prouvé que la factorisation est « dans P ». Au soir du 25 novembre, ni OpenAI ni Anthropic n’avait réagi.
P, NP et Q-Day : pourquoi le chiffrement tremble
Le problème P = NP, ouvert depuis 1971, demande si tout problème dont la solution se vérifie vite, comme une grille de sudoku remplie, peut aussi se résoudre vite. Presque tout le monde pense que non, sans l’avoir jamais prouvé. Scott Aaronson sent désormais « viscéralement » qu’une preuve de P ≠ NP n’est plus très loin.
Ce serait plutôt une bonne nouvelle pour la cryptographie. Le danger vient des algorithmes. Le chiffrement RSA, qui protège encore une bonne partie du web et des paiements, parie que retrouver les deux nombres premiers qui composent une clé prend trop de temps. Si une IA trouve une méthode rapide, RSA tombe, même si P ≠ NP.
Jusqu’ici, la menace venait des ordinateurs quantiques et du « Q-Day », le jour où l’un d’eux pourra casser RSA et la cryptographie sur courbes elliptiques. Google s’est fixé 2029 pour s’y préparer. Le scénario qui inquiète aujourd’hui est un Q-Day sans ordinateur quantique, déclenché par une simple découverte mathématique.
Charles Guillemet, directeur technique de Ledger, appelle pourtant à garder la tête froide. Dans un post sur X, il passe en revue trois rumeurs : la factorisation serait dans P, les courbes elliptiques qui protègent bitcoin seraient cassées, et Ring-LWE, à la base des nouveaux standards post-quantiques, ne résisterait pas aux ordinateurs quantiques. Il n’y croit pas : il ne serait pas surpris que ces systèmes soient un peu moins solides que prévu, mais « très surpris » qu’ils s’effondrent complètement. Il note surtout qu’un labo qui casserait l’une de ces briques aurait le plus grand mal à le révéler sans provoquer une exploitation massive. Si une telle découverte existait, les labos auraient donc toutes les raisons de se taire, et ce silence suffit à alimenter les rumeurs.

articles.title: Uber appoints former Zomato CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India, South Asia
articles.text:
Uber appoints former Zomato CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India, South Asia
Ranjan, who spent eight years at Zomato, will take charge of Uber’s India and South Asia operations from January 4, 2027.
Uber has appointed former Zomato food delivery CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India and South Asia, effective January 4, 2027, as the mobility platform looks to strengthen its presence in one of its largest global markets.
Ranjan will report to Dom Taylor, Uber’s Regional General Manager for Asia Pacific. He joins Uber from Allen Online, where he currently serves as CEO.
Ranjan joined Zomato in 2017 and spent eight years at the company. During his tenure, he led its food ordering and delivery business as CEO, having previously held leadership roles across Zomato Gold and sales.
“Uber has built a business that matters to how people move and earn across India and South Asia. The opportunity ahead is significant, and it starts with the everyday experience: dependable rides, value across different journeys and better earning opportunities for drivers. I’m excited to join the talented team and build on a great foundation,” said Ranjan in a statement.
Announcing the appointment, Taylor said: “After a search spanning more than three months, we’re delighted to welcome Rakesh to Uber. We set a high bar for this role, and his experience running large consumer businesses in India, combined with his ambition for what comes next, stood out."
"India and South Asia matter enormously to Uber’s future. Rakesh joins a business with real scale and enduring strength and he brings valuable experience to lead the next chapter of growth and innovation for our business in the region,” Taylor added.
India is Uber’s third-largest market globally by trips, after the US and Brazil, and its second-largest by the number of earners. The company operates in more than 225 cities across the country, offering multiple mobility options, including bikes, autos, cars and metro services. More than two million monthly active drivers earn through its platform.
India is also home to Uber’s largest technology centres outside the US, located in Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The company entered the Indian market in 2013 and has since expanded its presence across mobility categories.
Edited by Megha Reddy

articles.title: « Des crimes graves » : Huawei reconnu coupable de fraude, de blanchiment et d’espionnage aux États-Unis
articles.text:
Ce 24 novembre 2026, un procès de 11 semaines contre Huawei s’est achevé à New York. Au total, 12 chefs d’accusation ont été retenus contre le géant chinois. L’entreprise chinoise a été acquittée pour deux d’entre eux, à savoir association de malfaiteurs et entrave à la justice. En revanche, elle a été reconnue coupable pour les dix autres, et autant dire qu’ils sont lourds.
Huawei reconnu coupable de 10 chefs d’accusation
Comme le rapporte Bloomberg, Huawei a notamment été reconnu coupable de fraude bancaire, de blanchiment d’argent et de vol de secrets industriels appartenant à des entreprises américaines, comme Cisco, T-Mobile ou encore Motorola. L’entreprise chinoise aurait ainsi mis en place un véritable système de vol de secrets commerciaux pendant une période de 20 ans, avec notamment des détournements de code source et de technologies de concurrents.
Huawei a également été reconnu coupable d’avoir violé des sanctions américaines en menant des activités commerciales illégales en Iran, via sa filiale Skycom, spécialisée dans les télécommunications. L’entreprise chinoise aurait dissimulé ses liens avec Skycom auprès de banques comme HSBC afin de pouvoir continuer à mener ses activités en Iran.
Pour Tysen A. Duva, procureur général adjoint de la division pénale du ministère américain de la Justice, la conclusion de ce procès est claire : « Pendant plus de deux décennies, Huawei a bâti un empire sur la fraude, le pillage et le mensonge et les crimes de l’entreprise ont menacé le système financier américain […] et porté atteinte à notre sécurité intérieure ». De son côté, James Barnacle, chef du bureau du FBI à New York, a qualifié les chefs d’accusation retenus de « crimes graves », et a déclaré : « Le succès de Huawei repose sur la tromperie et le vol, et le FBI n’hésitera jamais à poursuivre ceux qui profitent de la loi ».
Rappelons que Washington envisage de nouvelles restrictions envers Nvidia à la suite de l’affaire Jensen Huang. Il est désormais fort probable que Huawei suive le même chemin.
Le géant chinois estime ces accusations sans fondement
L’entreprise chinoise s’est particulièrement félicitée d’avoir été acquittée de deux chefs d’accusation (association de malfaiteurs et entrave à la justice). En ce qui concerne les 10 autres chefs d’accusation retenus, elle considère qu’ils ne sont tout simplement pas fondés. Dans un communiqué, Huawei explique que les accusations retenues sont « sans base factuelle ou fondement juridique ». Le géant chinois l’affirme : « aucun tribunal n’a jamais reconnu la responsabilité de Huawei pour détournement délibéré de propriété intellectuelle, et l’entreprise n’a jamais été condamnée à verser des dommages-intérêts pour détournement de secrets d’affaires ».
De son côté, le porte-parole du ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères, Guo Jiakun, a dénoncé un acharnement et a déclaré que son pays « s’oppose fermement à la répression et à l’endiguement des entreprises chinoises par les États-Unis ».
Quoi qu’il en soit, Huawei risque désormais de sérieuses amendes. L’entreprise a d’ores et déjà fait part de son intention de faire appel.

articles.title: Pour 45 €, ce lampadaire SwitchBot éclaire le salon et change de couleur
articles.text:
Black Friday - Le lampadaire connecté SwitchBot perd près de la moitié de son prix
Lumière sur une bonne affaire
Le lampadaire connecté SwitchBot RGBICWW passe de 89 à 45 € pour le Black Friday. Nous l'avions pris en main : voici ce qu'il permet de faire pour éclairer le salon et varier les ambiances.
Un peu de lumière derrière le canapé, des couleurs autour du sapin ou un éclairage d'ambiance près du téléviseur : le lampadaire SwitchBot RGBICWW peut trouver sa place dans plusieurs coins du salon. Proposé à 89 € à l'origine, il passe à 45 € pour le Black Friday, soit une réduction d'environ 49 %.
Lors de notre prise en main, nous avions d'abord apprécié sa simplicité d'installation. Le SwitchBot peut ensuite diffuser plusieurs couleurs à la fois grâce au contrôle segmenté de ses LED. Il sait aussi produire une lumière blanche, du chaud au froid. La luminosité atteint, selon le fabricant, 1 200 lumens. Nous avions trouvé son éclairage assez puissant et son rendu réussi.
L'application SwitchBot permet de régler l'intensité, les couleurs et la température du blanc, mais aussi de choisir parmi de nombreux effets animés. Le lampadaire peut même faire varier son éclairage au rythme de la musique. Des boutons placés près du pied servent également à changer la couleur et le type d'éclairage sans sortir son téléphone.
Compatible Matter, il peut être piloté depuis des applications comme Apple Home, Alexa ou Google Home. Placé près d'un téléviseur ou associé à un second lampadaire, il permet de compléter l'éclairage d'une pièce tout au long de l'année.

articles.title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins
articles.text:
An ongoing phishing campaign dubbed "GoodGuys" impersonates major brands, including Google, Nvidia, Accenture, and SpaceX, to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars.
The attacks offer recipients up to $600 for a 45-minute interview in an attempt to get them to sign in with their work accounts to participate.
The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American Express, Coca-Cola, Culver's, Google Cloud, Nvidia, SpaceX, and Spotify.
The threat actors abuse legitimate email and event platforms, including HireVue, SendGrid, Mandrill, and Cvent, to distribute phishing links.
In one attack, a phishing email sent through HireVue invited recipients to attend a Google Cloud webinar about deploying AI applications into production.
The threat actors use domains themed around interviews, webinars, and research studies, creating brand-specific subdomains to host the phishing pages, such as:
- accenture[.]international-interviews[.]com
- nvidia[.]feedback-study[.]com
- google[.]webinar-cloud[.]com
- spotify[.]interview-experts[.]com
Clicking the phishing links typically takes recipients to a CAPTCHA challenge before displaying a website impersonating the company that supposedly sent the invitation.
Each website features customized branding and lures, with the Nvidia phishing site offering $500 to participate in an AI feedback study and the Accenture site offering $600 for an expert interview.
The sites ultimately prompt visitors to sign in with their Google accounts to validate their invitations, allowing the attackers to steal their credentials. The phishing kit specifically targets corporate accounts and rejects email addresses associated with Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.
Unlike adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that use reverse proxies to relay legitimate login pages, GoodGuys uses fake authentication forms controlled by an attacker-controlled server.
After victims enter their Google credentials, the phishing page can display various multifactor authentication (MFA) challenges, including requests for SMS codes, authenticator codes, and Google sign-in prompts requiring users to select a matching number on their phones.
The kit also includes fake Okta authentication forms and support for Okta Verify push notifications.
Push Security believes the threat actors manually attempt to log in using the stolen credentials, instructing the phishing page to display whatever MFA or security challenges Google or Okta show during authentication.
Similar techniques were used in vishing-based data theft attacks linked to the ShinyHunters extortion gang earlier this year to steal corporate single sign-on (SSO) credentials.
Once the process is completed, the phishing kit redirects victims to another website or displays a message thanking them for their application.
The researchers believe the phishing kit may have been developed using an AI coding assistant, based on hidden accessibility labels found in every analyzed version of the kit.
"The sign-in card in every build carries two hidden labels: "Sign-in simulation" and "GoodGuys sign-in simulation." They sit in accessibility text that only screen readers announce, so a visitor never sees them. We think the label is a leftover from how the kit was first built," explained Push Security.
"Calling the page a sign-in "simulation" for a made-up company is the kind of framing someone would use to get an AI coding assistant past its guardrails when asking it to build a phishing page. The label then stayed in every build we've collected."
The researchers also discovered a potentially related phishing campaign that uses fake Coca-Cola interview invitations and the Evilginx phishing kit to target Google Ads accounts.
While both campaigns used the same abused SendGrid click tracker and identical Coca-Cola branding assets, differences in their code and infrastructure prevented researchers from conclusively linking the attacks to the same threat actor.

articles.title: La IA ha encontrado nuevas pistas para uno de los grandes problemas matemáticos del milenio: P=NP
articles.text:
Con pocas horas de diferencia, Anthropic y OpenAI han subido a sus respectivas cuentas de GitHub dos trabajos casi gemelos en los que se abren nuevos caminos para resolver uno de los Siete problemas matemáticos del Milenio. Ambas compañías aseguran haber demostrado que cierto tipo de cálculos son difíciles de verdad, y no solo lo parecen.
Lo relevante de esta aportación de los dos principales laboratorios de IA es que ninguno de ellos resuelve el gran enigma que hay detrás del gran problema conocido como P=NP o teoría de la complejidad computacional, pero ofrecen nuevos caminos para llegar a su resolución. La resolución de ese enigma impactaría de forma directa con la clave de bóveda que sustentan sistemas de seguridad tan importantes como el cifrado de los correos o la seguridad de los pagos online.
Fácil de comprobar, difícil de resolver. Tratar de explicar el problema P=NP de forma sencilla supone todo un reto en sí mismo. Piensa en un sudoku enorme. Rellenarlo correctamente puede llevarte horas o días, pero comprobar si uno ya resuelto es correcto es cuestión de minutos. Los informáticos llaman P a los problemas que un ordenador puede resolver deprisa. NP, en cambio, son aquellos problemas en los que solo se necesita poder comprobar deprisa que existe una solución para ellos. En este caso, el término "deprisa" significa que el tiempo que se tarda en resolverlo no se dispara más allá de un crecimiento exponencial cuando el problema crece.
La pregunta del millón de dólares que quita el sueño a los matemáticos es si los dos grupos (P y NP) son en realidad el mismo. Dicho de otro modo: si todos los problemas que se comprueban rápido también tienen un método rápido de resolución, aunque no lo conozcamos. Lo habitual es pensar que no, y Scott Aaronson, experto en complejidad computacional, cifraba en su blog en un 96% su confianza en que son distintos. Es decir, que un problema que puede ser fácil de comprobar, puede ser difícil de resolver.
P=NP podría ser la llave del cifrado RSA. Cuando pagas online, tus datos viajan cifrados y convertidos en un galimatías que solo entiende quien tiene la llave. Uno de los sistemas más usados es RSA. Su truco es multiplicar dos números primos muy grandes. El truco en este caso es que multiplicarlos es fácil, pero calcular qué números eran a partir del resultado es algo casi imposible en la actualidad sin echar mano de los ordenadores cuánticos.
Esa dificultad en la resolución es la que protege la seguridad de los pagos, porque nadie conoce un método rápido para romperlo. Si P fuera igual a NP, en teoría existiría un plano sobre el que se podría encontrar una ruta para solucionar este y otros muchos problemas computacionales. El experto en la teoría de complejidad computacional Fulgencio López, del departamento de matemáticas de la Universidad de Toronto, advertía de que las claves criptográficas "se descifrarían de forma muy fácil". El otro riesgo conocido es el algoritmo de Shor, que factoriza con un ordenador cuántico muy potente. Un método rápido en máquinas normales abriría el candado de esa seguridad sin espera.
Lo que publicó Anthropic. Ambas empresas abordan una versión algebraica del problema P frente a NP llamada VP frente a VNP. En vez de problemas de sí o no, usa polinomios, que son expresiones hechas de sumas y multiplicaciones. Según explicaba Aaronson, desde los años setenta esta variante se ve como un calentamiento para resolver P frente a NP.
Anthropic publicó un preprint que todavía debe verificarse por humanos en el que se asegura que hay polinomios que exigen circuitos enormes. Uno está ligado al problema de recorrer todas las ciudades de un mapa sin repetir ninguna. El tamaño del circuito crece más rápido que cualquier polinomio. Según la empresa, lo halló un modelo interno de Claude, que escribió también una versión comprobable por ordenador en Lean.
Lo que aporta OpenAI. Seis horas más tarde que Anthropic, OpenAI colgó su propio preprint asegurando que hay otro camino. El texto de OpenAI compara el circuito con una red de cables. Imagina que un ordenador es una ciudad de calculadoras unidas por cables, y que cada cable cuesta según su longitud. Si esos cables no se pueden acortar. Entonces es fácil demostrar que ciertos problemas necesitan una cantidad gigantesca de cables, así que son difíciles.
En cambio, si los cables se pueden acortar, ese ahorro permite construir un circuito que repite el trabajo de otro supuestamente pequeño y lo contradice. Así, falle una vía o la otra, la dificultad siempre queda demostrada. Sin embargo, OpenAI avisa de que su trabajo no vale para los problemas de sí o no, que son los de P contra NP. Es decir, deja sin respuesta justo la pregunta que preocupa a los criptógrafos.
Cuánto acerca esto al gran enigma. Varun Kanade, de la Universidad de Oxford, cree que estos avances ayudarán, pero señala que "necesitaremos nuevas técnicas para la cuestión P vs. NP".
Aun así, Tom Gur, de Cambridge, admitía a NewScientist su sorpresa ante el avance en la resolución del problema de la mano de la IA: "Estamos presenciando décadas de progreso en cuestión de días", aunque añade que la comunidad necesita tiempo para estudiar los resultados antes de saber su alcance real.

articles.title: Ainoa, una camionera en España: "La ruta cambia cada día. Si voy a Madrid, calculo las horas que puedo hacer del tirón para saber dónde parar"
articles.text:
Ainoa Blasco es una camionera de 30 años que comparte el día a día de su profesión en sus redes sociales. Y en una entrevista con La Vanguardia sobre los retos de su oficio, también contó que la ruta que le toca hacer cambia cada día, algo que la obliga a calcular cuántas horas puede conducir del tirón para saber dónde va a parar.
Una ruta que se decide a última hora. Una de las cosas que más pesan en su día a día es la falta de rutina, porque aunque normalmente duerme en casa, no sabe con mucha antelación qué recorrido le tocará al día siguiente. Por eso tiene que planificar cada viaje y, a la vez, estar dispuesta a cambiar esos planes sobre la marcha. “Hasta última hora del día no sabes lo que vas a hacer al día siguiente. Te puede salir alguna ruta de dormir fuera, que a veces agradezco, porque vas cambiando y es muy diferente la rutina de los viajes si son más cortos o más largos”, explicaba en la entrevista.
Parar bastante antes de Madrid. Cuando le toca ir a la capital, por ejemplo, calcula cuántas horas puede conducir seguidas y las reparte de manera que el viaje se pueda hacer con seguridad, aunque eso suponga no llegar ese día a su destino. Si sale desde Valencia y necesita dormir por el camino, prefiere detenerse bastante antes de llegar. El motivo es la seguridad, ya que, según cuenta, en algunas zonas es más probable que intenten abrir el camión: “Si llegas a Madrid, es más fácil que te intenten abrir el camión, ya no la cabina, sino también el remolque. Y al final, eres el responsable de la carga que llevas. Es tu responsabilidad”.
Los consejos de los veteranos. Eso sí, asegura que hasta ahora nunca ha sufrido un intento de robo, algo que atribuye en parte a lo que le han ido enseñando su padre, su hermano y otros compañeros con más experiencia en la carretera. Y es que para ella es fundamental hacer caso a quienes llevan años en el oficio, porque gracias a lo que le cuentan puede ver venir las situaciones peligrosas antes de encontrárselas en ruta.
Atascos y cuestas. Pero el cálculo inicial no siempre aguanta hasta el final de la jornada, porque un atasco, una retención o cualquier otro imprevisto pueden obligarla a buscar otra zona donde detenerse, de modo que conocer bien la carretera cuenta mucho. También influye lo que lleva detrás: cuando va con mucho peso, procura escoger carreteras más largas si con ello puede evitar pendientes pronunciadas, porque las cuestas exigen un mayor esfuerzo al camión. Vamos, que prefiere sumar kilómetros antes que castigar al vehículo en cada subida.
Camionera de familia. Ainoa no llegó al transporte desde fuera, ya que su padre y su hermano son chóferes y en su casa siempre se había hablado de camiones y de carretera. Fue con la pandemia cuando decidió seguir esa tradición y sacarse el carnet C para conducir camiones, y la entrada en el sector también llegó de la mano de su familia. Su hermano habló con su jefe y la respuesta fue directa: “Que no busque trabajo, que se viene con nosotros”.
Reconoce que el trabajo es duro, por las horas y por la responsabilidad que recae sobre quien conduce, pero también destaca lo que le ha aportado a nivel personal, sobre todo en autonomía y en capacidad para resolver problemas por su cuenta. “A nivel personal te espabila mucho porque te pones en situaciones en las que vas a estar sola y vas a tener que buscarte la vida para poder salir de ello. Te hace muy autosuficiente”, resume.

articles.title: Cognition’s new engineers aren’t even downloading code anymore — they build entirely through Devin
articles.text:
Cognition’s new engineers aren’t even downloading code anymore — they build entirely through Devin
Some engineers joining Cognition no longer set up local development environments. Instead, Devin has become their primary interface for software development.
Speaking to Patrick O’Shaughnessy on Tuesday’s episode of Invest Like the Best, Cognition co-founder and CEO Scott Wu describes how the company’s internal engineering practices have changed as coding agents have become more capable.
No terminal, no download
“The funniest moment for me, I would say, was actually around like four or five months ago when we started to realize that new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer,” Wu says. “Like they didn’t pull up a terminal. They didn’t run a command line or anything.”
“new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer … They didn’t run a command line or anything.”
Over roughly a year, Cognition doubled its engineering headcount while increasing its rate of merged pull requests 20-fold, Wu says. That amounts to approximately ten times as many merged pull requests per engineer, despite the company’s already extensive use of AI coding tools a year earlier.
Perhaps more significant, Wu estimates, is that approximately 90% of Cognition’s internal Devin usage is now automated in some form.
When Devin runs itself
Wu cites incident response as an example of Cognition’s automated Devin workflows, where an error can trigger an investigation before an on-call engineer intervenes.
“It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off.”
“It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off,” Wu says.
Although Wu does not specify whether the 90% figure represents session count, token consumption, or another metric, automated execution has implications for compute provisioning and budget allocation as inference demand becomes less dependent on individual developer activity.
Cognition has already introduced hierarchical budgets for Devin, which give enterprises spending controls across organizational levels.
250,000 pull requests monthly
Wu says one of Cognition’s largest banking customers was on track to merge 250,000 pull requests with Devin in October. Until a few months earlier, the entire organization had been merging approximately 400,000 pull requests per month.
The bank has approximately 80,000 engineering personnel, according to Wu, and only a fraction of the organization had been fully onboarded to Devin at the time of the interview.
Separately, Citi CEO Jane Fraser says during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call that 14,000 engineers use Devin.
Neither Cognition’s internal figures nor the banking customer’s projected PR volume account for the complexity of individual changes. Wu does not provide corresponding data on change failure rates or review workloads, metrics that would help establish whether the rest of the SDLC has kept pace with implementation.
The disparity between implementation and review capacity has already prompted vendors such as CodeRabbit to expand into agentic change management.
Wu argues that enterprise adoption also requires engineering leaders to reconsider their roadmaps and organizational structures to accommodate additional implementation capacity.
Watching the agent swarms
The shift from individual background agents to swarms is a particular concern for Wu because monitoring becomes more difficult when multiple agents work together.
Cognition has been exploring this execution model with its recently introduced Devin Bots, persistent agents that manage other agents’ work.
Wu stresses the need to catch unintended agent behavior early and limit what agents can access, especially when workflows run without an engineer supervising them.
The engineering skill ceiling hasn’t changed
“The barrier to entry has for sure gotten a lot lower,” Wu says. “However, I think the skill ceiling and, you know, a lot of the particular skill sets that you need are still very much the same as they always have been.”
“I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable.”
For Wu, writing code is only one part of software engineering. Engineers still have to figure out what an incomplete or ambiguous specification actually means and make architectural decisions that could affect the business for years, even if an agent handles the implementation.
“I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable,” Wu says.
