articles.title: Forscher sind entsetzt: SpaceX darf eine Million weitere Satelliten ins All bringen
articles.text:
SpaceX darf eine Million Satelliten für KI-Rechenzentren ins All schicken – Forscher schlagen Alarm
Das Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX des Milliardärs Elon Musk darf bis zu eine Million Satelliten zur Errichtung von Weltraum-Rechenzentren für KI-Anwendungen in den Erdorbit schicken. Die US-Regulierungsbehörde FCC erteilte dem Projekt des Konzerns mit dem Namen „Starmind“ laut einer Mitteilung vom Mittwoch eine entsprechende Genehmigung.
SpaceX muss technische Hürden überwinden
„Indem sie Rechenkapazitäten über die Erdoberfläche hinaus verlagern, werden SpaceX und die zahlreichen Wettbewerber, die an ihren eigenen Datenzentren im Orbit arbeiten, den Anforderungen der Zeit gerecht“, sagte FCC-Chef Brendan Carr. Die Befürworter von Rechenzentren im All argumentieren mit der reichlich verfügbaren Sonnenenergie für deren Betrieb und den Kühlmöglichkeiten.
Die Genehmigung ebnet nun den Weg für ein Konzept, das im Mittelpunkt von Musks Präsentation im Rahmen des Börsengangs von SpaceX gestanden hatte. Allerdings gibt es für die Errichtung von weltraumgestützten Rechenzentren auch technische Hürden. Sie brauchen sehr große Solarmodule zur Stromerzeugung sowie ausgefeilte Kühltechnologien, und auch Systeme zur Übertragung riesiger Datenmengen zur Erde.
Forscher schlagen Alarm wegen Mega-Konstellation im All
    „„Die Entscheidung der FCC, den Start von einer Million SpaceX-Starmind-Satelliten zu genehmigen, ist eine katastrophale Entscheidung“.
Forscher sehen dagegen ganz andere Herausforderungen. Für die Zukunft. Sie befürchten mehr Weltraumschrott und eine deutlich schlechtere Sicht auf die Sterne. „Die Entscheidung der US-amerikanischen Federal Communications Commission, den Start von einer Million SpaceX-Starmind-Satelliten zu genehmigen, ist eine katastrophale Entscheidung, die massive Auswirkungen auf die erdnahe Umlaufbahn, unsere Atmosphäre und den Nachthimmel haben könnte“, sagt etwa Michael Brown, Associate Professor an der School of Physics and Astronomy, gegenüber dem Science Media Center (SMC).
Wenn die Satelliten eine Lebensdauer von fünf Jahren hätten, bedeute dies, dass täglich über 500 Satelliten gestartet werden müssten, so Brown weiter. Aber die künstlichen Trabanten müssten nicht nur in Serie ins All befördert, sondern von dort auch wieder entsorgt. „Die FCC hat ihre Entscheidung darüber, wie die Satelliten nach Beendigung ihrer Mission entsorgt werden sollen, vertagt, doch 500 Satelliten, die täglich in die Erde zurückkehren, würden die Verschmutzung der oberen Atmosphäre erheblich verstärken und die Ozonschicht schädigen“, erklärt Brown.
„Die geplante Starmind-Konstellation würde die Anzahl der aktiven Satelliten in der Umlaufbahn um mehr als das 50-Fache erhöhen. Dies steigert das Risiko von Kollisionen mit Weltraummüll erheblich, was zum Kessler-Syndrom führen könnte – einer Kaskade von Kollisionen, die die erdnahe Umlaufbahn unbrauchbar machen würde.“ Die enorme Zunahme der Satellitenanzahl werde zudem den Abendhimmel mit Satelliten überfüllen und den Blick jedes Einzelnen auf den Himmel grundlegend verändern.
Ähnlich besorgt äußern sich viele weitere Wissenschaftler aus Australien und Neuseeland gegenüber dem SMC. Schon vor diesem neuen Vorhaben von Elon Musk warnten Forscher immer wieder vor den Auswirkungen großer Satellitenkonstellationen, wie dem ebenfalls zu SpaceX gehörenden Starlink-Netzwerk. Schon 2023 klagten Astronomen über die zunehmende Lichtverschmutzung, die durch Satelliten und das reflektierte Sonnenlicht ausgelöst wird und die Sicht auf den Nachthimmel erschwert. Andere sorgten sich 2024 um die Auswirkungen der Starlink-Satelliten auf Radioteleskope. Diese könnten durch die Strahlung geblendet werden.
Die Lage am Nachthimmel wird sich nun aber wohl rasant verschlechtern. Laut der FCC muss SpaceX zehn Prozent der maximal genehmigten Satelliten bis November 2035 ins All bringen, bis November 2038 müssen es dann 50 Prozent sein.
(Mit Material der dpa.)
Die Idee ist doch gut.
Gibt es doch tatsächlich Sonnenenergie zu genüge und Kühlung durch das Vakuum.
Eigentlich der Traum jedes Grünen Politikers, sie können die neuen KI System nutzen, um endlich etwas über die Wissenschaft zu lernen, bei Null CO2 Emission.
Man könnte das ganze aber halt auch einfach mal in „klein“ angehen, und ein kleines Rechenzentrum-Netzwerk aufbauen.
Dann braucht es keine 500 Satelitten.
Ich denke, das Thema Daten übertragung wird Musk schon in den griff bekommen.
Kann er doch für den Anfang auf Starlink zurückgreifen.

articles.title: Dell 14 ou Dell 15: qual notebook escolher em 2026?
articles.text:
Resposta rápida: o Dell 14 é a escolha para quem quer um notebook compacto, com acabamento em metal e processadores Intel® Core™ 5 ou Core™ 7, que acompanha a sua rotina aonde estiver. O Dell 15 é ideal para quem prefere uma tela maior de 15,6 polegadas com 120 Hz e teclado com bloco numérico. Os dois rodam Windows 11 Home, têm SSD NVMe, Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3.
Os dois modelos fazem parte da linha Dell, família que ocupa o lugar dos tradicionais Inspiron e atende estudo, home office e uso diário. Veja abaixo as diferenças e descubra qual combina mais com a sua rotina.
| Característica | Dell 14 | Dell 15 | 
|---|---|---|
| Tela | 14″ 16:10 WUXGA, antirreflexo | 15,6″ Full HD, 120 Hz, antirreflexo | 
| Processador | Intel® Core™ 5 120U ou Core™ 7 150U | Intel® Core™ i5-1334U ou Core™ i7-1355U | 
| Memória | Até 32 GB de RAM | 8 ou 16 GB + slot extra para ampliar | 
| Armazenamento | SSD NVMe Gen4, 512 GB ou 1 TB | SSD NVMe Gen4, 512 GB ou 1 TB | 
| Teclado | ABNT2 retroiluminado | ABNT2 com bloco numérico dedicado | 
| Acabamento | Tampa e apoio em metal | Design preto sóbrio | 
| Conexões | HDMI, USB-C, leitor de cartões e biometria | Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Webcam | Full HD (1080p) | Integrada | 
| Preço inicial | Consulte no site da Dell | Consulte no site da Dell | 
Dell 14: compacto, elegante e pronto para levar a qualquer lugar
O Dell 14 une mobilidade e visual sofisticado. Tampa e apoio para as mãos em metal prateado dão um ar semi-premium ao conjunto, e a tela de 14 polegadas facilita carregar o notebook na mochila para a faculdade, o escritório ou o café.
- Tela: 14 polegadas, proporção 16:10, resolução WUXGA (1920 x 1200) e tratamento antirreflexo, com mais área útil na vertical para documentos e planilhas
- Processador: Intel® Core™ 5 120U ou Intel® Core™ 7 150U (até 10 núcleos e 12 threads, com picos de até 5,4 GHz)
- Memória: até 32 GB de RAM DDR5, com 16 GB nas configurações mais vendidas
- Armazenamento: SSD NVMe Gen4 de até 1TB, para abrir o sistema e os programas em segundos
- Teclado e webcam: teclado ABNT2 retroiluminado e webcam Full HD (1080p) para videochamadas nítidas
- Conexões: HDMI, USB-C com DisplayPort, USB, leitor de cartões e leitor biométrico
- Conectividade: Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3, com carregador de 65 W
- Preço: a partir de R$ 7.699 no site da Dell Brasil
Dell 15: tela grande e 120 Hz para trabalhar e estudar com conforto
O Dell 15 aposta no espaço: a tela de 15,6 polegadas Full HD dá mais área para trabalhar com duas janelas lado a lado, e a taxa de atualização de 120 Hz deixa a rolagem de páginas e documentos mais fluida. É um notebook funcional, pensado para quem passa muitas horas diante da tela.
- Tela: 15,6 polegadas Full HD (1920 x 1080), painel WVA com 120 Hz, tratamento antirreflexo e ângulos de visão amplos
- Processador: Intel® Core™ i5-1334U ou Core™ i7-1355U de 13ª geração, com 10 núcleos e 12 threads
- Gráficos: Intel Iris Xe integrado, suficiente para vídeos, aulas on-line e jogos leves como The Sims 4 e Stardew Valley
- Memória: opções com 8 GB ou 16 GB e slot adicional para ampliar
- Armazenamento: SSD NVMe Gen4 de 512 GB ou 1 TB, conforme a versão
- Teclado: ABNT2 com bloco numérico dedicado, ótimo para planilhas e cálculos
- Conectividade: Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3, com carregador de 65 W
- Sistema: Windows 11 Home
Dell 14 ou Dell 15: qual combina com o seu perfil?
- Estudantes que levam o notebook todo dia: Dell 14, pelo formato compacto e pelo acabamento em metal
- Quem trabalha com planilhas e números: Dell 15, pelo teclado numérico dedicado e pela tela ampla
- Quem faz muitas videochamadas: Dell 14, com webcam Full HD
- Quem passa horas lendo e navegando: Dell 15, com tela de 15,6″ e 120 Hz
- Quem quer mais desempenho e ampliação de memória: Dell 14 com Intel® Core™ 7 150U e até 32 GB de RAM
- Quem busca facilidade para conectar periféricos: Dell 14, com HDMI, USB-C, leitor de cartões e biometria
Perguntas frequentes sobre Dell 14 e Dell 15
Qual é a diferença entre o Dell 14 e o Dell 15?
O Dell 14 tem tela de 14 polegadas 16:10, acabamento em metal e processadores Intel® Core™ 5 ou Core™ 7. O Dell 15 tem tela de 15,6 polegadas Full HD com 120 Hz, teclado com bloco numérico e processadores Intel® Core™ i5 ou i7 de 13ª geração.
Qual Dell é melhor para estudar?
Os dois atendem bem. O Dell 14 é mais prático para levar na mochila; o Dell 15 oferece mais espaço de tela para pesquisar e escrever.
Quanto custa o Dell 14?
O Dell 14 parte de R$ 7.699 no site da Dell Brasil. O valor varia conforme processador, memória, armazenamento e promoções.
O Dell 14 e o Dell 15 vêm com Windows?
Sim. Os modelos têm versões com Windows 11 Home.
Dá para aumentar a memória RAM?
Nas versões com slot de memória livre, sim. Confira a configuração do modelo escolhido antes de comprar.
Dell 14 e Dell 15 rodam jogos?
Com gráficos Intel integrados, rodam jogos leves e casuais, além de filmes, séries e aulas em alta qualidade.
Onde comprar
Veja as configurações e condições atuais do Dell 14 e do Dell 15 no site da Dell Brasil. Preços e disponibilidade podem mudar sem aviso.
Atualizado em 10/11/2026. Especificações e preços iniciais divulgados pela Dell e por fichas técnicas de varejo; confirme a configuração e o valor final antes de comprar.

articles.title: Shein pagará USD 100 millones a la FTC por demoras en envíos y reseñas negativas ocultas
articles.text:
Shein pagará USD 100 millones para cerrar la demanda de la Comisión Federal de Comercio (FTC), la agencia de Estados Unidos que protege a los consumidores. La FTC la acusó de engañar a sus clientes sobre los plazos de entrega, las reseñas de productos y el origen del algodón de su ropa.
El acuerdo se presentó el 24 de noviembre de 2026 ante un tribunal federal del Distrito Central de California y debe ser aprobado por un juez para entrar en vigor. El dinero se destinará a compensar a consumidores.
La compañía no admite ni niega las acusaciones. En un aviso a la bolsa de Hong Kong, donde cotiza, Shein afirmó que sigue en desacuerdo con parte de la descripción que hace la FTC de sus prácticas y que el pago no tendrá un efecto adverso significativo en su negocio.
El pago debe hacerse dentro de los 30 días posteriores a que la orden quede firme. Según el documento, el dinero está depositado en una cuenta de garantía de los abogados de la empresa hasta entonces.
Por qué multaron a Shein en Estados Unidos
Según la FTC, Shein promocionaba un procesamiento rápido de los pedidos, pero los clientes esperaban semanas o meses, y algunos nunca recibían lo comprado. La agencia sostiene que la empresa tampoco ofrecía la opción de aceptar la demora o cancelar el pedido con reembolso inmediato, como exige la ley.
La demanda describe un servicio de atención deficiente. De acuerdo con la agencia, el chat solía estar desconectado o respondía con mensajes genéricos. Shein no tuvo un número de teléfono de atención durante años y que hasta septiembre de 2025 contaba con solo cinco agentes.
Sobre las reseñas, la FTC afirma que la empresa ocultaba las opiniones negativas. Según la agencia Reuters, que cita la demanda, una guía interna indicaba a los empleados excluir los comentarios “extremadamente malos”, como el de que una joya manchaba la piel.
La tercera acusación se refiere a las prendas de la línea “evoluSHEIN” y al algodón. La FTC dice que Shein no pudo respaldar con auditorías independientes sus afirmaciones sobre proveedores con buenas calificaciones sociales. También afirma que algodón presentado como cultivado en Estados Unidos resultó, en pruebas, ser de China.
Qué debe cambiar la empresa de comercio digital
La orden propuesta prohíbe a Shein hacer afirmaciones sobre auditorías a proveedores o sobre la trazabilidad del algodón sin una base razonable. También le impide decir que sus reseñas reflejan la opinión de todos los compradores si se retiraron comentarios por su tono negativo, y le exige guardar un registro de cada reseña eliminada.
Asimismo, la empresa se comprometió a mantener canales de atención que ofrezcan ayuda oportuna y efectiva, según el presidente de la FTC, Andrew Ferguson. Este caso cobra especial atención porque Shein concentra cerca de la mitad de las ventas de moda rápida en Estados Unidos.
Un portavoz de Shein dijo a Reuters que la compañía no reconoce responsabilidad y que seguirá reforzando sus prácticas con los consumidores y su cumplimiento normativo.
La investigación de la FTC ya aparecía como un riesgo en el prospecto de la salida a bolsa de Shein, el 24 de agosto de 2026, según el propio aviso de la compañía. La FTC aún no detalló cómo ni cuándo se repartirá el dinero entre los clientes; su alerta para consumidores anticipa que publicará más detalles conforme avance la ejecución del proceso judicial en curso.
El siguiente paso es la decisión del tribunal sobre la orden. Solo después de su aprobación comenzará a correr el plazo de 30 días para el pago de los USD 100 millones.

articles.title: The FCC approves SpaceX's plan for up to a million data-center satellites
articles.text:
What just happened? The vision of millions of data-center satellites orbiting Earth has seemed like a far-off concept, but the FCC has just given SpaceX approval to launch up to one million of these structures into Earth orbit, and the company says the first could be launched as early as 2028 Chairman Brendan Carr said the satellites will use solar power to extend America's lead in AI, or "Super Intelligence," as US executive agencies must now call it in most official communications.
SpaceX filed its application back in January, giving the FCC a little under ten months to sign off on the first constellation of its kind in the US. The Starmind satellites will process data in low Earth orbit and use lasers to communicate with one another and with Starlink satellites. Radio links will serve as a backup.
The FCC statement makes the bold claim that the system will "bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation – one that can harness the full power of the sun." Proposed in 1964 by astrophysicist Nikolai Kardashev, a Kardashev Type II civilisation is a hypothetical advanced society capable of capturing and using the entire energy output of its host star.
 – Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) November 25, 2026
Musk kept his response to Carr's announcement on X short but sweet. "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world," the SpaceX CEO wrote.
We got a look at what SpaceX plans to put up there back in June, when Musk showed off the first-generation AI1 satellite. With its wings fully deployed, the thing measures almost 230 feet across, making it wider than a Boeing 747-8. SpaceX says it can deliver 120 kilowatts of sustained power to its computing hardware, peaking at 150 kW. For comparison, a single Nvidia GB300 rack is rated at 140 kW.
Getting the first satellite into orbit should be the easy part, at least by SpaceX's standards. Under the FCC licence, the company has until November 25, 2033, to get a single satellite up and running, though SpaceX told investors it could start deploying them as early as 2028. The deadlines get considerably more demanding from there. SpaceX needs 100,000 operational by November 2035, half a million by November 2038, and the full million by November 2040.
Unsurprisingly, astronomers aren't quite as enthusiastic about the prospect as Musk. The American Astronomical Society, which asked the FCC to reject the application, warned that satellites this large would appear brighter and remain visible for longer, making it harder for ground-based telescopes to observe the night sky.
There's also the question of what happens to all that hardware when it stops working. SpaceX wants the option of sending retired satellites into orbit around the sun. The FCC says it needs more detail before it will sign off on that idea. SpaceX must also submit a final debris plan before deploying any Starmind satellites that will operate above 600 kilometers (373 miles).
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," astrophysicist and author Adam Becker told CNBC. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX is far from alone in its plans for deploying data-centers in space. Google's Project Suncatcher sent its first prototype into orbit aboard a SpaceX rocket in October. Google switched on the satellite's Tensor Processing Unit, sent it a prompt, and got a haiku back. For a bigger test, Google has booked a ride with one of Musk's rivals. Blue Origin's New Glenn is scheduled to carry several Google computing satellites into orbit in early 2029.
Jeff Bezos' company has orbital data center ambitions of its own, having asked the FCC for permission to deploy up to 51,600 satellites under the name Project Sunrise.
Then there's Washington startup Starcloud, which sent an Nvidia H100 GPU into space last year. The company used it to run one of Google's Gemma models and train a small language model on the complete works of Shakespeare. Its plans for a second satellite include something a little less literary: Starcloud wants to see if it can mine Bitcoin in orbit.

articles.title: Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance
articles.text:
Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.
CEO Satya Nadella opened the keynote by acknowledging the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage, then positioned Copilot as the operating system for work, combining chat, coding, and autonomous agents in one experience. In his edited keynote remarks, Nadella argued that customers must be able to examine and independently verify what AI does, announced an AI Transparency Initiative aligned with NIST's Agent Standards Initiative, and rejected setups where models audit other models:
These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable.
The Book of News groups the announcements by product area, and many of them ship as previews rather than in general availability.
Compute and Infrastructure
Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines are now generally available, a year after InfoQ reported on Microsoft introducing the chip at Ignite 2025 and two and a half years after the preview of Cobalt 100 VMs. According to the Azure announcement, the processor combines 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores on TSMC's 3nm process, and the VMs run in 14 regions today, with 23 planned by the end of 2026. Microsoft claims up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100, plus up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS through Azure Boost. Customers can run cores at a fixed 3.2 GHz in Deterministic Mode or let them boost up to 3.6 GHz in Opportunistic Mode, and the lineup adds Mpsv4 VMs for high-memory workloads and storage-optimized Lpsv5 VMs. Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput than on Cobalt 100, and OpenAI's Vadim Filanovsky described a similar result:
We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200.
Confidential computing gains three previews: multi-GPU confidential computing on VR72 for models larger than a single GPU, Azure Confidential Enclaves with AKS Kata CoCo containers, and Azure Confidential Clean Room for multiparty analytics without exposing raw data.
Customers can now deploy Foundry open-weight models and agents to their own AKS clusters. At the same time, an Agent Sandbox extension provides VM-level isolation for agent-written code, and Agent Grid applies central policy to agent, model, tool, and service interactions. Flex nodes extend AKS clusters to servers outside Azure. According to the AKS team's Ignite post, managed GPU node pools, which handle GPU drivers, device plugins, and Azure Monitor metrics, are generally available, with NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 support and mixed multi-instance GPU in preview. Confidential VM node pools on Azure Container Linux are also generally available on both Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP VM sizes.
On the operations side, Azure Monitor health models are generally available and build a real-time health graph from telemetry, ranking incidents by business impact. The Azure Copilot deployment agent, also generally available, turns natural-language requirements into deployed workloads, and Azure SRE Agent picks up previews for customer-managed keys, Entra Agent ID integration, cross-agent communication, and multicloud investigations. For migration projects, Azure Catalyst is now generally available, with its agent (formerly the Azure Copilot migration agent) handling discovery, assessment, and planning. Separately, GitHub Copilot modernization adds a preview of BizTalk-to-Logic Apps migration.
Hybrid, Sovereign Cloud, and Windows Server
Microsoft now pitches Sovereign Private Cloud as a full stack on Azure Local, with VMs and AKS at the base, followed by data services, Foundry Local, GitHub Enterprise Local, and Microsoft 365 Local. Darryl van der Peijl, a Microsoft MVP for Azure Local, Hyper-V, and Azure Arc, listed what shipped in his Azure Local Insider newsletter: Foundry Local on Azure Local and GitHub Enterprise Local are generally available, while a Sovereign control panel, Blob Storage and DocumentDB on Azure Local, multi-tenancy, and rehoming are in preview. The control panel assesses data residency, encryption, network exposure, and business continuity for Azure resources without enforcing any controls, and during the preview it runs in European regions only, with the service hosted in Sweden.
Van der Peijl singled out rehoming, which moves an Azure Local instance from Azure management to local management while VMs, AKS clusters, and data stay in place:
Until now, going from connected to disconnected meant a migration project. Microsoft showed a script that does the rehoming in one run.
Azure Local also runs on arm64 for the first time, in public preview on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Development Kit, which hosts containers on bare metal without a hypervisor. Windows Server 2028 entered preview through the Windows Server Insider Program, bringing a hardened Server Core, post-quantum cryptography, native NVMe enabled by default, NVMe over Fabrics, and boot from ReFS. According to van der Peijl, Microsoft added inference as a new pillar for the release, calling on-premises inference servers token factories, and is moving network drivers from kernel mode to user mode as part of its Windows resiliency work. Windows Admin Center vMode is now generally available at no extra cost and manages up to 1,000 Hyper-V hosts and 25,000 VMs, which Microsoft described on stage as "kind of a replacement for SCVMM."
AI, Models, and Microsoft Foundry
Foundry's main theme was continuous improvement. Multi-turn evaluation and production insights that group recurring failures and rank fixes are now generally available, while the agent optimizer, human annotation, rubric evaluators, Managed Training, and Programmed Training for custom SFT and reinforcement learning loops on open-weight models are in preview. The optimizer adjusts an agent's instructions, skills, and model choice, with a human approving each change before it ships.
(Source: Microsoft blog)
In a separate engineering post, the Microsoft team behind the optimizer described how the loop works. They reported that the reflector, a separate model that reads failing traces and diagnoses why an agent scored poorly, influenced results more than switching the agent's own model, for example between gpt-4o and gpt-4.1-mini. Developers drive the loop from the Azure Developer CLI:
azd ai agent eval init                         # generate dataset & evaluator from a one-paragraph description
azd ai agent eval run                          # score the current version (baseline)
azd ai agent optimize                          # search over candidates
azd ai agent optimize apply --candidate <id>   # apply the winner locally
azd deploy                                     # ship as the next version
Writing on DEV Community, Hector Flores advised readers to treat Microsoft's claim that the model router saves up to 65% compared with a frontier model as a ceiling rather than a forecast, and he welcomed the human approval step in the optimizer loop:
Self-modifying agents with no review gate are an incident waiting to happen.
On the model front, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is generally available in Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Built on Gemma 4 26B A4B with added image input, it scores 68 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 and runs more than twice as fast as its predecessor, and Copilot uses it to route requests. MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash are generally available on GitHub, MAI-Image-2.7 is in preview, and the model router now covers the top 50 models in a catalog of more than 11,000. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol became generally available in Foundry, with Global Standard deployments covering 28 regions. On Standard deployments with short context, Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Astra costs $8 and $40. Foundry IQ added knowledge graphs and an iterative retrieval model, Microsoft-Retriever-1, both in preview.
Microsoft also made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone product, split out of the API Management AI tier, to govern, route, and monitor access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. It includes 10,000 free requests per gateway per month, with paid billing starting January 1, 2027, across 17 regions.
Microsoft IQ, which Nadella described as an externalization of the context system behind Copilot, is now generally available without a new SKU. It exposes Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ context to Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and MCP-compatible harnesses, and Web IQ is now available to all Azure customers at a lower price. Business plugins, which package reusable context, skills, and tools with hierarchical inheritance and governance, are available through the Frontier program.
Data
PostgreSQL got most of the attention on the data side. Azure HorizonDB is now generally available as a managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database with built-in vector indexing, and teams can lock it down with Entra ID, private endpoints, and their own encryption keys. Calling models from SQL through AI Functions and AI Pipelines is still in preview. The same holds for Fabric HorizonDB, a serverless variant inside Fabric that provisions in seconds and pauses when nobody uses it, and for a DMS path that moves existing Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers onto HorizonDB.
Teams moving off Oracle can test a new Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration in Azure DMS, also in preview. Cosmos DB developers now have a generally available Rust SDK and semantic reranker, and Cosmos DB Shell lets them query from VS Code or the portal with MCP support built in. On Azure Managed Redis, the Redis 8 preview folds JSON, search, time-series, and vector search into a single version. Anyone who wants to develop against Azure SQL Database on a laptop can pull a preview container that needs no Azure subscription.
Developer Tools
The Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0 is generally available, built on a native Rust runtime, supported in six languages, and using the same agent harness Microsoft and GitHub run internally. The GitHub Copilot app now takes Azure DevOps repositories from clone to merge and runs tests in a real, signed-in browser. Copilot code review adds local reviews in the CLI and app, secret detection, adaptive review effort, and cross-repository context. Copilot Code, a natural-language app builder with cloud and local sandboxes, is in the Frontier program, with general availability planned for December and a macOS local sandbox still to come.
Copilot and Business Applications
The Copilot app now brings Chat, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot into one experience, and Office in Copilot puts Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside it as a generally available feature. Autopilot, a long-running personal agent with its own identity, memory, and tool access, is rolling out to Frontier customers. Salesforce in Copilot entered preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, and zero-copy data federation between Salesforce Data 360 and Fabric OneLake is generally available. For spend control, Agent 365 FinOps previews cost visibility, policies, alerts, and Fabric-based chargeback.
Cost tracking also featured in practitioner reactions. In his newsletter, Microsoft principal AI apps architect Anurag Karuparti wrote that tokenomics is among the top challenges his customers raise, and he proposed a different unit for agent ROI:
The metric that matters isn't just tokens consumed. It's cost per successful business outcome. That's how I think enterprises should start measuring agent ROI.
Writing for business leaders, Aaron Reich, CTO of the Accenture and Microsoft joint venture Avanade, built his Ignite analysis around trust rather than speed:
Speed isn't the bottleneck anymore, trust is. As AI drives the cost of knowledge toward zero with apps being easier to build, agents doing more work, and abundant intelligence, the scarce things are hard and need more attention: institutional knowledge, judgment, accountability and trust.
Security, Identity, and Governance
At the Microsoft Hub, where he spent the week answering customer questions, Microsoft MVP Muhammad Atif noticed a change in what customers wanted to know:
How do we actually put this into production? How do we scale AI and agents across the organisation? How do we govern and secure them? How do we control the cost as adoption grows?
Entra now assigns Agent IDs automatically to discovered local agents, starting with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, and previews an MCP Firewall that controls access to MCP servers, tools, prompts, and transports. The Microsoft MCP Server for Enterprise, which gives agents permission-controlled access to Entra data, is generally available. Defender's runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows is generally available to Defender for Endpoint P2 customers, while Intune previews local agent governance that marks devices with unapproved agents as noncompliant. Agent 365 now has a generally available tools registry that lists the plugins, skills, MCP servers, and connectors agents use; MCP governance is in preview through Azure AI Gateway and LiteLLM; and Dynamic Agent Risk combines runtime, posture, and blast-radius signals into risk levels for each agent. Microsoft Perception, formerly Project Perception, is now generally available, with its Triage Agent covering about 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue.
(Source: Microsoft Tech Community, Agent 365 blog)
In her Ignite recap, cloud and identity consultant Shannon Kuehn warned against handling agents as ordinary applications:
Treat agents like apps and you'll spend 2027 cleaning up after them.

articles.title: Comprar una GPU de NVIDIA está a punto de volverse más difícil (y aún más caro)
articles.text:
Si planeas armar un PC gaming, conseguir una GPU de NVIDIA tal vez se vuelva todavía más difícil y caro que ahora. Según reporta VideoCardz, el gigante verde implementaría un fuerte recorte a la asignación de chips para los fabricantes de sus tarjetas gráficas. Esto impactaría de forma directa en la disponibilidad del hardware en el mercado minorista y ya se teme por nuevas subidas de precio.
Todavía no hay anuncios oficiales en tal sentido, pero rumores que circulan en foros chinos sostienen que NVIDIA planea reducir la distribución de chips para GPU destinadas a uso comercial gaming entre un 20 y un 30 por ciento. Este cambio se implementaría en el trimestre fiscal que se inició en noviembre y que se extiende hasta enero de 2027, inclusive.
Si esto se confirma, será el segundo recorte a la asignación de chips para GPU que implementa NVIDIA, al menos en China. De acuerdo con la información disponible, algo similar ya sucedió en el trimestre previo. Todavía no hay detalles sobre si el presunto recorte que implementaría el gigante verde podría impactar solo en el gigante asiático, o si también se verá en el resto del mundo.
La citada publicación menciona que reportes anteriores apuntaban a que los principales socios fabricantes de GPU de NVIDIA se estaban quedando sin stock de modelos de la línea RTX 50. Asimismo, se indica que algunas marcas estarían tratando de cubrir huecos de demanda con modelos de entrada y de gama media con algunos años de antigüedad, tales los casos de las RTX 3050 y 3060.
NVIDIA recortaría la asignación de chips para sus GPU de uso comercial y gaming
Como ya indicamos, NVIDIA no ha confirmado la veracidad del rumor sobre un nuevo recorte en la asignación de chips para sus GPU de uso comercial y gaming. Las principales especulaciones apuntan a que la presunta reducción busca liberar chips para los productos destinados puntualmente a la inteligencia artificial. Y no es descabellado pensar que algo de esto hay, si la historia realmente es así, considerando que la firma californiana es la principal empresa de hardware de IA del mundo.
Pero la disponibilidad más acotada de chips gráficos podría no impactar únicamente a quienes quieren una GPU de NVIDIA para su PC gaming. Otros dispositivos de la industria, incluyendo consolas como la Nintendo Switch 2, también dependen de los componentes de la firma. Ya veremos qué sucede con todo esto.
Por lo pronto, NVIDIA tiene varios temas de resolver más allá del aparente recorte de sus GPU para usuarios finales. La compañía viene de semanas bastante convulsionadas tras la renuncia de Jensen Huang por el escándalo de sus relaciones extramatrimoniales y su posterior regreso a la conducción.

articles.title: Closing Canada’s AI adoption gap starts with talent and AI literacy
articles.text:
Canada’s national AI strategy projects that wider use of artificial intelligence could add nearly $200 billion to the economy and create up to 250,000 jobs by 2031.
But there’s a hitch. Only 12.2 percent of Canadian firms used AI in 2025, close to the lowest among international peers. That rate climbed to 19.2 percent in Q2 this year, but most businesses are still on the sidelines.
“The challenge isn’t finding people who can use AI tools. It’s finding people who can combine AI capabilities with deep business expertise.” 
Kevin d’Entremont,
TECHNATION
A big part of the problem is a skills gap, said Kevin d’Entremont, president and CEO of TECHNATION, a national association representing Canada’s tech sector. A shortage of specialized expertise—particularly in complex areas like data architecture and advanced technical problem-solving—could slow the spread of AI across the economy and limit the potential productivity gains it can deliver.
Employers already face growing competition and rising wages for specialists in complex areas such as data architecture and advanced technical problem-solving. Across the broader workforce, there’s also a need to boost AI literacy and build trust in the technology so employees can use it confidently and responsibly.
“The challenge isn’t finding people who can use AI tools,” said d’Entremont. “It’s finding people who can combine AI capabilities with deep business expertise. Organizations need professionals who understand data, technology, governance, and business outcomes simultaneously.”
Understanding the tech advantage
Closing that skills gap is the focus of TECHNATION’s FutureWave 2026. The Nov. 30 conference at Northeastern University in Toronto brings together leaders from industry, education, and government to talk through the skills Canada’s fastest-growing tech sectors will need over the next decade. They’ll also dig into how smaller businesses can hire as they grow and how workforce programs can help bring AI skills and literacy to more Canadians.
Ideas from the day will help shape The Tech Advantage Playbook, a set of practical recommendations to help businesses across sectors, including small and medium-sized companies, nurture talent and develop partnerships with educators.
For d’Entremont, talent is one piece of a bigger agenda. “AI can significantly increase productivity, but we need to build the skills, investment, regulatory frameworks, and AI literacy for responsible AI adoption,” he said.
Hiring for judgment
One big question facing companies today is how to tell whether promising candidates actually have the AI skills they need to do the job.
d’Entremont said employers are seeing a growing gap between what applicants list on their résumés and what they can demonstrate. At the same time, automation and generative AI are disrupting some of the early-career opportunities that have traditionally helped workers gain valuable on-the-job experience.
As AI takes on tasks like drafting content and writing code, employers are now putting more weight on judgment when they hire, he noted. Can a candidate spot a flaw in an AI-generated analysis and decide what to do about it?
The technical depth that takes depends on the role. Engineers, data scientists, and AI risk specialists need advanced skills because they’re accountable for model performance, deployment, security, and compliance. In other roles, such as finance or customer service, it’s more about knowing when the tools can help and when the results need a critical eye to ensure accuracy.
“Not every role requires AI experts, but every role will increasingly require AI literacy,” he said.
From training to results
d’Entremont said closer ties between employers and schools are key to making AI training more widely available and keeping it relevant to today’s jobs. That could mean updating what’s taught about AI, giving teachers more support, and offering short, industry-led certifications so people already in the workforce can build in-demand skills.
Government has a role, too, he noted, pointing to the funding for training and work placements in Ottawa’s AI strategy as a sign of federal support. What really counts, though, is what that support delivers.
“Training is an input; adoption and economic impact are the outcomes that matter,” he said.
The stakes are high. Companies are more likely to expand research and product development where they can find the expertise they need, said d’Entremont. If Canada fails to develop and retain that talent, he warned, the country risks becoming “a purchaser of AI rather than a producer of AI.”
“AI is one of the areas where Canada has a natural advantage in technology and the potential to be a world leader. By building ecosystems of companies around global champions, we can increase the potential for commercialization, jobs, and IP growth in Canada,” he said.
PRESENTED BY
Ready to be part of the conversation? Visit our website to learn more and register for FutureWave 2026.
Feature image courtesy TECHNATION.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
  November 13, 2026
- Source:
  Princeton University
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: Brasil lidera ranking de vítimas de ransomware; veja os números
articles.text:
O Brasil lidera a América Latina em publicações de vítimas de ataques de ransomware em sites de vazamento de dados. Entre abril e setembro de 2026, foram identificados 102 registros envolvendo organizações brasileiras, contra 56 da Argentina, segunda colocada no levantamento. Os dados são do Relatório de Ameaças Cibernéticas de novembro de 2026, divulgado pela empresa de segurança digital Trellix.
O estudo também identificou cenário global de expansão e fragmentação do mercado de ransomware. Ao todo, 5.505 publicações de vítimas foram registradas em sites de vazamento de dados, atribuídas a 124 grupos criminosos ativos. Segundo a empresa, é o maior volume já observado em um período de seis meses.
A América Latina respondeu por 8,3% das vítimas publicadas globalmente. O Brasil concentrou o maior número de registros da região, seguido pela Argentina.
Para Rodrigo Buosi, country manager da Trellix no Brasil, a liderança brasileira representa sinal de alerta. Segundo ele, criminosos exploram vulnerabilidades conhecidas, credenciais comprometidas e relações de confiança com fornecedores para invadir organizações.
Ransomware tenta desativar ferramentas de segurança
- Outro ponto destacado pelo levantamento é a tentativa de neutralizar mecanismos de proteção antes da execução dos ataques;
- Das 94 campanhas de ransomware analisadas pela Trellix, 40 apresentaram tentativas de desativar ou modificar ferramentas de segurança. Em 14 delas, foram identificados recursos desenvolvidos para neutralizar soluções de detecção e resposta em endpoints (EDR) ou explorar drivers vulneráveis;
- Esse tipo de estratégia busca dificultar a identificação da invasão e permitir que os criminosos avancem pelos sistemas comprometidos antes que as equipes de segurança consigam reagir;
- A telemetria da empresa também registrou mais de 2,2 milhões de detecções relacionadas a ransomware em 775 campanhas diferentes. O volume representa crescimento de 4,7% em relação ao período anterior.
Leia mais:
- 1Password é invadida por hackers e tem dados de clientes roubados
- Fifa confirma ataque cibernético com acesso a dados pessoais
- Falha crítica em sistema de criação de sites é explorada por hackers
Ataques à cadeia de suprimentos e inteligência artificial (IA) ganham espaço
O relatório também aponta mudanças nas estratégias utilizadas pelos criminosos digitais. A proporção de campanhas que mencionaram IA ou grandes modelos de linguagem (LLMs, na sigla em inglês) passou de 5,3% para 10,4%, praticamente dobrando no período analisado.
Os ataques à cadeia de suprimentos de software também cresceram, passando de 9,1% para 11,9%. Nesse tipo de operação, os invasores exploram fornecedores, ferramentas de desenvolvimento ou outros componentes utilizados por diferentes organizações. Assim, o comprometimento de um único elemento pode abrir caminho para atingir vários ambientes conectados.
A Trellix também identificou agentes de IA e malwares autônomos capazes de executar diversas etapas de uma invasão com supervisão humana mínima. Segundo a empresa, essa evolução representa mudança em relação ao uso inicial de IA, principalmente para produzir mensagens de phishing.
O levantamento ainda destaca que vulnerabilidades conhecidas, mesmo quando já existem correções disponíveis, continuam entre os principais alvos dos criminosos.
Como o relatório foi elaborado?
O Relatório de Ameaças Cibernéticas de novembro de 2026 reúne informações coletadas entre 1º de abril e 30 de setembro. A metodologia combina dados de telemetria das soluções de segurança da Trellix com informações de fontes abertas e da dark web, incluindo sites utilizados por grupos de ransomware para divulgar vítimas e ameaçar o vazamento de informações.
A empresa ressalta que os resultados representam retrato das ameaças identificadas durante o período. Os números são baseados em detecções e publicações monitoradas, não necessariamente em infecções confirmadas, e não incluem ameaças que escaparam dos mecanismos de identificação.
O relatório completo está disponível no site da Trellix.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: From selling drones to intelligence: Where will the next wave of value come from?
articles.text:
From selling drones to intelligence: Where will the next wave of value come from?
As the drone industry evolves, the focus is shifting from aircraft specifications to the value delivered to customers. The next phase of growth will be shaped by AI, software, integrated technologies and service-led business models.
When we look at the value of a drone, it is easy to focus on the aircraft itself. How long can it fly? How much weight can it carry? How far can it travel? These are important questions, and they will continue to matter. But there is another question that deserves equal attention: what does the customer actually get from that flight?
A drone may spend several hours monitoring an area and return with a large volume of footage. Yet, if the operator has to spend several more hours reviewing that footage to identify something important, much of the benefit is lost. The real value lies not simply in collecting information, but in making sense of it and using it at the right time.
I believe this is where the next phase of the drone industry will take shape.
The value does not end when the drone lands
As drones become more widely used across defence, infrastructure, mapping, and homeland security, customer expectations are changing. Buying a drone is increasingly becoming the beginning of a larger operational requirement.
Consider a team monitoring a long stretch of border or inspecting a large infrastructure project. The drone can capture images, video and location data, but the customer needs more than these individual inputs. They need to know what has changed, whether something requires attention and what action should follow.
This is where software and artificial intelligence (AI) have a pivotal role to play. Automated video summaries, event detection, and searchable annotations can make it easier to find relevant information without having to watch hours of recordings. The idea is not to remove people from the decision-making process but to help them focus on what matters and make better-informed decisions.
Experience is difficult to replicate
There is something about technology that becomes clear only when it is used regularly in the field. A drone may perform well during testing, but actual operating conditions can be very different. Terrain, weather, temperature and connectivity can all affect how a system performs.
This is why the experience gained from real deployments matters. Across the industry, drone manufacturers are learning that building a reliable product is not just about getting the engineering right. It is also about understanding how customers use the technology, what difficulties they encounter and where improvements are needed.
The scale of deployments is important in this regard. Every mission provides an opportunity to understand how the aircraft, payload, software and communication systems perform in real conditions. Repeated operations can also reveal patterns that may not emerge during controlled testing.
Over time, this learning becomes an advantage. Companies that stay closely connected to actual operating conditions are better placed to develop technology that works outside controlled testing environments. It also helps them understand what customers need, rather than relying only on what they initially ask for.
Technology must work together
Intelligence is not limited to what happens to the data after a flight. It also depends on whether the drone can complete its mission reliably in the first place.
For instance, a drone operating in a challenging environment needs dependable communication and navigation. In defence applications, electronic interference, jamming and spoofing can create additional complications. Similarly, operations in remote locations may have limited network connectivity, making it important to process certain information closer to where it is collected.
This is why the industry needs to look at the entire technology stack rather than treating the aircraft, software, payload and communication systems as separate elements. Secure command-and-control systems, resilient navigation, edge computing and specialised payloads all contribute to the final outcome.
This shift is also reflected in India's evolving defence procurement priorities. The Defence Acquisition Council's recent approval of capital acquisition proposals worth approximately Rs 2.12 lakh crore includes requirements for Long Range UAS, Surveillance UAV, Integrated Surveillance and Strike Systems, and Long Range Kamikaze Drone Systems. With approximately 82% of the proposed procurements earmarked for the Indian industry, the direction is significant. It signals an opportunity for domestic manufacturers to move beyond building individual platforms towards developing integrated, mission-ready capabilities that address increasingly complex operational requirements.
This also helps reduce dependence on external technologies in areas where control, security and reliability are particularly important.
The business model will evolve with the technology
This shift also has implications for how drone companies build sustainable businesses. Hardware sales will remain an important part of the industry. However, the opportunity extends well beyond the initial sale of an aircraft. A drone has an operating lifecycle that involves software, analytics, maintenance, upgrades, training and support. Each of these can contribute to the value delivered to a customer over time.
Models such as Drone-as-a-Service, software subscriptions and analytics-led solutions can allow customers to access drone capabilities without having to manage every aspect of ownership and operations themselves. For providers, these models can create opportunities for longer-term customer relationships and a more diversified revenue mix.
From a business perspective, this also creates opportunities for repeat engagements and more predictable customer relationships. But these models will succeed only when they offer a clear economic or operational benefit. A customer will continue paying for a service if it helps reduce manual effort, improve efficiency or deliver information that was previously difficult to access.
The objective should not simply be to introduce more software or services. It should be to make the overall solution more useful to the customer.
The next opportunity is in delivering outcomes
The drone industry is still evolving, and there are challenges to address, particularly around data security, system integration, reliability and the economics of scaling these solutions. Not every application will require the same level of automation or intelligence. What matters is understanding the customer's actual requirement and developing technology accordingly.
As the market matures, I expect customers to place greater emphasis on the outcome rather than the specifications of the aircraft alone. They will want to know whether a drone can help them monitor an area more effectively, complete an inspection faster or respond to an incident with better information.
The aircraft will remain at the centre of this ecosystem, but it will be one part of a much larger solution. The companies that understand this shift early and invest in the right capabilities will be better positioned for the industry's next phase of growth.
Ultimately, the future of drones will not be determined only by how far they can fly or how long they can stay in the air but it will depend on how effectively every flight can be translated into intelligence, action and measurable value for the customer.
(Vipul Joshi is the CFO at ideaForge, an Indian aerospace and defense company)

articles.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension
articles.text:
The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service.
On November 8, the Remus infostealer developer started advertising the alleged Gmail zero-day flaw that allowed the malware to collect emails even if victims changed their passwords and revoked all sessions.
Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock investigated the claims but came to inconclusive results. The researchers noted that evidence from the malware customers matched the seller's pitch, although there was no technical proof that a zero-day vulnerability was being exploited.
GenDigital and Invoke RE researchers published their independent findings yesterday, explaining that the advertised “zero-day” was just a malicious Chrome extension installed on the victims' browsers.
The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts. It can also survive password changes and session revocations because it remains installed in the victim's Chrome browser.
Its access to Gmail stops when the active session ends, and resumes again when the victim signs back in.
GenDigital discovered the extension after reverse-engineering the Remus infostealer. The researchers found no trace of an email-stealing module, suggesting that the functionality is implemented via an add-on.
“In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets,” GenDigital explains.
“The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its .rdata section.”
GenDigital explains that Chrome versions 137 and later removed a command-line option that allowed malware to load extensions.
Remus takes a complex route to overcome this restriction, editing the victim’s Chrome profile to register the malicious extension and then enabling ‘Developer Mode’ in the browser, which is required to run unpacked extensions.
The extension uses the name “Google Sheets,” copies the description of Google Docs Offline, and requests access to all websites.
Once active in the browser, it checks for unread emails every minute across up to 10 account slots and retrieves them in full, in raw format.
The extension sends the email subject, message body, sender, and victim’s email address to its command-and-control server, along with a campaign identifier.
Failed uploads are queued and retried, while a local record helps the extension keep track of what has succeeded so it doesn’t send duplicates.
Although the extension also parses attachment filenames, it does not send those to its operators, so this feature may not be fully implemented yet.
To defend against this threat, users are advised to download software only from trusted sources and scrutinize “chrome://extensions” for rogue installations or unexpected activation of Developer Mode.

articles.title: BYD a peut-être poussé la ressemblance trop loin : son SUV est interdit en Europe
articles.text:
Il arrive qu’il y ait des ressemblances entre certains modèles de la production automobile, mais parfois, cette ressemblance va trop loin. BYD en fait maintenant les frais, car son Ti7, un tout-terrain hybride rechargeable, se voit interdire d’importation en Europe parce qu’il est trop proche du Land Rover Defender. Un tribunal vient de donner raison à la marque britannique et complique les plans du constructeur chinois.
Un SUV fortement inspiré du Land Rover
BYD a lancé l’année dernière en Chine le tout-terrain Ti7 avec une motorisation hybride rechargeable Super DM-i. Et avec la forme de ses boucliers avant et arrière, sa roue de secours sur le coffre, sa silhouette avec un capot et un toit plats, des barres de toit ou encore des protections de bas de caisse, la ressemblance avec un Land Rover Defender est frappante.
Pour BYD, il ne s’agit pas d’une copie et la marque avance des différences au niveau des passages de roues, du capot, des fenêtres, des phares ou encore des boucliers. Il est vrai qu’il ne s’agit pas d’une copie conforme, comme la BYD F0 était une copie de la Toyota Aygo, mais quiconque a déjà vu un Land Rover Defender reconnaîtra une ressemblance marquée. Et un tribunal européen a été du même avis.
Un tribunal européen statue en faveur de Land Rover
Jaguar Land Rover a entamé une action en justice contre BYD devant le tribunal du district de La Haye, aux Pays-Bas. La société britannique, appartenant au groupe indien Tata Motors, n’a certainement pas apprécié de découvrir les ressemblances entre son modèle et celui de BYD. Le tribunal vient toutefois de donner raison à Land Rover en interdisant à BYD d’importer son tout-terrain Ti7 en Europe.
Le tribunal a notamment retenu plusieurs caractéristiques stylistiques propres au Land Rover Defender pour justifier sa décision. Parmi elles figurent les épaules et les angles arrondis de la carrosserie, l’habillage spécifique du montant C, les passages de roues aux contours arrondis, ainsi que la ligne de vitrage et la silhouette générale du véhicule. Selon le juge, c’est l’association de ces différents éléments qui confère au Defender son identité visuelle, une identité que le BYD Ti7 reprendrait de manière trop similaire.
Le tribunal prévoit une pénalité de 100 000 dollars par jour si BYD enfreint la décision d’interdiction de commercialisation, d’importation, de production et de stockage du BYD Ti7 en Europe. Jaguar Land Rover pourrait opter pour une pénalité de 25 000 dollars par jour, dans la limite de 10 millions de dollars.
Le tribunal est donc sévère et donne raison à Jaguar Land Rover. Toutefois, le BYD Ti7 n’était pas encore commercialisé en Europe. Le constructeur chinois devrait donc s’en sortir sans avoir d’amende à payer. Même si BYD devrait faire appel, il apparaît clair que les autorités européennes sont en faveur du constructeur britannique.
Tout n’est pas gagné pour Land Rover
Toutefois, ce dernier n’a pas obtenu tout ce qu’il souhaitait puisque le tribunal de La Haye ne peut pas prendre de décision pour le Royaume-Uni, qui a quitté l’UE. Jaguar Land Rover doit donc continuer de travailler pour obtenir une interdiction également au Royaume-Uni, au risque de voir le BYD Ti7 y être commercialisé.
De son côté, BYD explique que le Ti7 a été développé indépendamment et n’enfreint aucun des droits de propriété intellectuelle de JLR. « Le BYD Ti7 est le résultat du travail de conception indépendant de BYD et n’enfreint aucun des droits de JLR. Nous poursuivrons toutes les voies légales pour démontrer que cette décision est incorrecte. »
Du côté de BYD, il serait judicieux de renoncer à la bataille pour le Ti7 avant que les autorités européennes ne se rendent compte que le Denza Bao 5, déjà commercialisé en Europe, présente lui aussi des similitudes avec le Land Rover Defender.

articles.title: Vous regardez du football via un moyen illégal ? La LFP va bientôt pouvoir bloquer les services en plein match
articles.text:
Football pirate : la LFP annonce un dispositif pour bloquer en temps réel les services pendant la diffusion des matchs
Grâce à une décision de justice, d'ici les prochaines semaines la LFP sera en mesure de bloquer automatiquement et en temps réel les services pirates pendant la diffusion d'un match de football de Ligue 1 ou de Ligue 2.
Alors que l'identité du ou des lieux de diffusion légale des prochaines saisons du championnat de France de football reste encore inconnue, la Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) vient de faire une annonce qui risque de déplaire aux adeptes de ballon rond regardé depuis un service pirate. Dans un communiqué, l'entité se dit "en ordre de marche" pour déployer un nouveau dispositif dans les prochaines semaines afin de bloquer au plus vite les flux illégaux.
La LFP veut siffler au plus vite la fin des matchs pirates
Cette annonce s'appuie sur un jugement rendu le 20 novembre 2026 par le Tribunal judiciaire de Paris, le premier obtenu dans le cadre du nouveau dispositif prévu par la loi du 3 août 2026. Jusqu'à présent, le blocage des services pirates reposait sur une actualisation hebdomadaire des mesures de blocage et sur une validation manuelle par l’Arcom des nouveaux services pirates identifiés. De quoi concrètement ralentir tout le processus et arriver littéralement après la fin des matchs.
Mais avec ce jugement, le groupe LFP pourra, via un système automatisé, permettre aux fournisseurs d'accès à Internet de bloquer sans délai les services visés dès leur détection au moment des rencontres. Les matchs de Ligue 1 McDonald’s et de Ligue 2 BKT sont concernés, tandis que la LFP espère que ce dispositif permettra "d’accroître considérablement la rapidité et l’efficacité de son action contre le piratage et de renforcer la protection de ses compétitions, de ses diffuseurs et des revenus du football professionnel."
Toujours selon la LFP, "la lutte contre le piratage constitue un enjeu majeur pour l’économie du football professionnel. Protéger les contenus au moment même où ils sont diffusés, c’est protéger la valeur des droits audiovisuels, les investissements consentis par les diffuseurs et les revenus qui permettent aux clubs de se développer."
Reste maintenant à voir dans quelle mesure ce dispositif sera efficace pour couper les flux et identifier les personnes qui en profitent, et s'il sera adopté par d'autres entités pour empêcher le piratage de davantage de sports.

articles.title: « Le véhicule autonome n’a aucun avenir » et ne ferait pas « 3 mètres dans Paris » : non, c’est faux (on a testé)
articles.text:
C’est un grand classique des plateaux télévisés français : dès qu’il s’agit d’innovation automobile, les vieux réflexes ont la vie dure (voiture électrique, conduite autonome…). Ces dernières heures, un extrait diffusé sur LCI a fait réagir sur X après avoir été partagé par l’utilisateur Dominique Peretti le matin du 25 novembre 2026. On y entend Benjamin Cuq, journaliste et chroniqueur spécialisé dans l’automobile, présenter le véhicule autonome comme une impasse totale, balayant le sujet d’un revers de main : selon lui, ces voitures seraient incapables de parcourir ne serait-ce que « 3 mètres dans le Marais à Paris », le tout appuyé d’un argument d’autorité : « j’ai écrit 2 000 articles sur le sujet », que je me permet de juger largement exagéré.
Le problème n’est pas d’être sceptique face aux promesses parfois délirantes de certains constructeurs, Tesla en tête. Le problème, c’est d’asséner à une heure de grande écoute des affirmations factuellement fausses, restées bloquées dix ans en arrière. La technologie évolue très vite : les barrières d’hier ne sont souvent plus d’actualité quelques mois plus tard.
Les voitures savent déjà se conduire seules dans Paris, sous surveillance
Chez Numerama, nous n’avons peut-être pas (encore) écrit 2 000 articles sur le sujet, mais nous testons régulièrement les avancées technologiques. Du robotaxi Waymo dans les rues de San Francisco aux systèmes d’aide à la conduite intelligente développés en Chine, nous avons notamment pu expérimenter cette année plusieurs technologies dans Paris.
Que ce soit lors de nos différents essais du système FSD (Full Self-Driving) supervisé de Tesla dans le trafic chaotique des rues étroites parisiennes, ou plus récemment avec les technologies embarquées de Xpeng, nous avons vu ces voitures gérer les piétons qui traversent hors des clous, les scooters qui se faufilent, les vélos qui grillent les feux, les livreurs en double file et les ruelles serrées sans sourciller. Elles passent même l’épreuve redoutée de l’Arc de Triomphe. Tout n’est pas encore à 100 % parfait, mais rassurez-vous, la conduite de Benjamin Cuq ne l’est probablement pas non plus.
Bien sûr, en Europe, la réglementation impose encore que le conducteur reste vigilant et responsable derrière le volant. Mais techniquement, le cap du « 3 mètres dans le Marais » est franchi depuis belle lurette. D’ailleurs, là où la conduite FSD de Tesla est autorisée, comme aux Pays-Bas depuis le mois d’avril, la cohabitation entre les vélos, le tram et les piétons dans le cœur d’Amsterdam se fait sans gros titres relayant tous les deux jours des accidents. Cela n’exclut pas qu’il puisse y avoir des accrochages, ou qu’un accident grave arrive un jour.
Pourquoi l’intelligence artificielle change toute la donne
Si ces « experts » de plateau se trompent d’époque, c’est parce qu’ils jugent la voiture autonome d’aujourd’hui avec les lunettes d’hier. Pendant longtemps, la conduite autonome reposait sur des règles codées à la main et sur une cartographie haute définition au centimètre près de chaque rue. Avec cette ancienne méthode, le moindre chantier imprévu ou une rue complexe du centre de Paris suffisait effectivement à paralyser le véhicule.
Sauf que l’approche technologique a radicalement basculé vers l’intelligence artificielle de bout en bout (end-to-end), alimentée uniquement par des caméras et des réseaux neuronaux.
Concrètement, ces systèmes sont devenus agnostiques à leur environnement : la voiture n’a plus besoin de connaître une rue par cœur pour s’y déplacer. Elle analyse la scène en temps réel et réagit par apprentissage, un peu comme un humain qui débarque dans une ville inconnue. Ce qui explique pourquoi un même logiciel entraîné aux États-Unis ou en Chine s’adapte aujourd’hui en quelques semaines aux pièges de la circulation parisienne.
Il reste encore de nombreux défis réglementaires, économiques et éthiques avant de voir des flottes de robotaxis sans volant envahir nos centres-villes. Mais prétendre que la technologie n’a « aucun avenir » parce qu’elle ne saurait pas gérer une rue étroite avec beaucoup de piétons revient à avoir un train de retard.
Il est probablement temps que certaines chaînes de télévision renouvellent un peu leur panel d’« experts ». Entre un Luc Julia qui clame que « l’intelligence artificielle n’existe pas » et un Benjamin Cuq qui affirme que « le véhicule autonome n’a aucun avenir », les plateaux télévisés français ont décidément encore du chemin à parcourir pour parler correctement des nouvelles technologies.
